section: Romans 8:6 — The Thought Pattern of the Old Sin Nature; the Sin Unto Death; Reversionism and the Justice of God
text: Romans 8:6 “For to set the mind on the flesh is death, but to set the mind on the Spirit is life and peace.” (ESV)

section: Romans 8:6 — The Thought Pattern of the Old Sin Nature; the Sin Unto Death; Reversionism and the Justice of God
text: Corrected translation: Consequently, the thought pattern of the old sin nature is death; but the thought pattern of the Spirit is life and peace.

section: Romans 8:6 — The Thought Pattern of the Old Sin Nature; the Sin Unto Death; Reversionism and the Justice of God
text: Romans 8:5 established that believers dominated by the old sin nature concentrate on the things of the old sin nature, while believers dominated by the Holy Spirit concentrate on the things of the Spirit — that is, Bible doctrine. Verse 6 now states the consequence of those two contrasting thought patterns. This chapter focuses on the first half of the verse: the thought pattern of the old sin nature and its result — the sin unto death.

section: I. Exegesis of Romans 8:6a
text: I. Exegesis of Romans 8:6a

section: The Inferential Conjunction
text: The Inferential Conjunction

section: The Inferential Conjunction
text: The verse opens with the inferential use of the conjunctive particle gar (γάρ), properly rendered consequently or so then. It draws a logical conclusion from the contrast presented in verse 5.

section: Phronēma — Thought Pattern
text: Phronēma — Thought Pattern

section: Phronēma — Thought Pattern
text: The subject is the nominative singular noun phronēma (φρόνημα), meaning thought pattern or mindset. This is the operative category of the soul's orientation — what a person habitually thinks about, what frames his perception of reality.

section: Sarx — The Old Sin Nature
text: Sarx — The Old Sin Nature

section: Sarx — The Old Sin Nature
text: The possessive genitive singular noun sarx (σάρξ) here refers not merely to physical flesh but to the old sin nature — the fallen capacity inherited at birth through the male genetic line. The phrase renders: consequently, the thought pattern of the old sin nature.

section: Thanatos — Death
text: Thanatos — Death

section: Thanatos — Death
text: The predicate nominative singular thanatos (θάνατος) completes the clause. In this context thanatos does not refer to spiritual death, physical death in the ordinary sense, or retroactive positional death. It refers specifically to the sin unto death — maximum punitive discipline from the justice of God administered to the reversionistic believer.

section: Thanatos — Death
text: Corrected translation of the first clause: Consequently, the thought pattern of the old sin nature is death — that is, the sin unto death. The human viewpoint orientation of the reversionistic believer, sustained over time, terminates in this maximum discipline.

section: II. The Justice of God as the Point of Reference
text: II. The Justice of God as the Point of Reference

section: II. The Justice of God as the Point of Reference
text: The controlling framework for understanding both blessing and discipline in Romans 8 is the justice of God — not the love of God, not the sovereignty of God, not any other divine attribute operating independently. All divine blessing flows through the justice of God as the giving end of the pipeline, and all discipline originates from the same source. This is what gives absolute security to blessing and absolute certainty to discipline.

section: II. The Justice of God as the Point of Reference
text: At physical birth, human life was imputed to its divinely prepared home — the human soul. Simultaneously, Adam's original sin was imputed to the genetically formed old sin nature. Adam's original sin plus the old sin nature equals spiritual death. Every person is born a facsimile of Adam after the fall. The old sin nature is therefore the sovereign of human life from physical birth until the new birth.

section: II. The Justice of God as the Point of Reference
text: At the new birth, eternal life is imputed to the divinely prepared home of regeneration, and divine righteousness is judicially imputed to every believer. This imputed righteousness is the foundation of the believer's pipeline to blessing. The integrity of God — composed of divine righteousness and divine justice — encapsulates the entire blessing mechanism. Justice on the giving end, righteousness on the receiving end. This encapsulation excludes all human good, human ability, and human talent from the equation. Blessing flows through the pipeline when the believer cracks the maturity barrier.

section: II. The Justice of God as the Point of Reference
text: The reversionistic believer also possesses imputed righteousness. But without capacity — maximum Bible doctrine resident in the soul — there is no target to receive the imputation of divine blessing. The reversionistic believer is therefore outside the blessing bracket and inside the cursing bracket. The justice of God, which cannot bless where there is no capacity, administers instead progressive discipline: warning discipline, intensive discipline, dying discipline, and finally the sin unto death.

section: III. Doctrine of the Sin Unto Death
text: III. Doctrine of the Sin Unto Death

section: 1. Definition and Description
text: 1. Definition and Description

section: 1. Definition and Description
text: Physical death is the ordinary means of transferring from time into eternity. For the mature believer — one who has cracked the maturity barrier and is in supergrace A, supergrace B, or ultra-supergrace — physical death is an event of maximum blessing. The soul departs the body and moves from phase two (the Christian life in time) to phase three (resurrection life in eternity) across what may be described as the high golden bridge of dying grace. No matter how long or how brief the dying process, it is entirely within the design of God's blessing. It is, in fact, the ultimate expression of blessing to the mature believer at the terminus of his earthly life.

section: 1. Definition and Description
text: For the reversionistic or carnal believer, the departure from time is entirely different. The sin unto death is characterized by painful, miserable, and horrific dying. It is God's final and greatest expression of divine discipline — the concentrated dose of all the discipline the reversionistic believer has avoided or resisted during his life. Once any believer dies, there is no sorrow, no tears, no pain, no regrets in eternity. The sin unto death therefore compresses all disciplinary consequences into the dying moment before that final transition.

section: 2. Three Categories of Christian Death
text: 2. Three Categories of Christian Death

section: 2. Three Categories of Christian Death
text: First, dying grace: the death of the growing or mature believer, associated entirely with blessing. Second, the sin unto death: disciplinary death for the reversionistic believer under the sustained influence of evil, associated with suffering and pain. Third, suicide: the reversionistic believer superimposes his volition over divine volition and takes his own life. The reversionistic believer in this category is often in psychological distress. However, suicide does not cancel salvation. The believer still possesses imputed righteousness, imputed eternal life, and all thirty-four grace assets that entered the pipeline at salvation. He still goes to heaven.

section: 3. Four Ways of Making the Transfer from Time to Eternity
text: 3. Four Ways of Making the Transfer from Time to Eternity

section: 3. Four Ways of Making the Transfer from Time to Eternity
text: First, the sin unto death — maximum discipline. Second, dying grace — maximum blessing in dying. Third, the rapture — the Lord Himself descends with a shout, the voice of the archangel, and the trumpet of God; the dead in Christ rise first; then those alive are caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17). The rapture is imminent — nothing must be fulfilled before it occurs — but imminence does not specify timing. It could occur at any moment or not for a thousand years. It is entirely within the Lord's timetable. Fourth, transfer from time to eternity without physical death and without resurrection — surpassing grace, of which the only recorded case is Enoch (Hebrews 11:5).

section: 4. Documentation
text: 4. Documentation

section: 4. Documentation
text: Old Testament: Psalm 118:17–18 — David speaks of reversion recovery: 'I shall not die, but live and declare the works of the Lord. The Lord has disciplined me severely, but He has not given me over to death.' David's reference is to reversion recovery — discipline short of the sin unto death because of his eventual positive response.

section: 4. Documentation
text: New Testament: 1 John 5:16 states plainly that there is a sin unto death. The context of Romans 8 itself is primary New Testament documentation.

section: 5. The Cause: Reversionism
text: 5. The Cause: Reversionism

section: 5. The Cause: Reversionism
text: The cause of the sin unto death is always reversionism — the retroactive spiritual regression of a believer who returns to the thinking and values of the old sin nature. Jeremiah 9:13–16 documents this in the national context: 'Because they have forsaken My doctrine which I set before them, and have not obeyed My voice, nor walked according to it, but have walked after the hardness of their own hearts' — the accumulated scar tissue of the right lobe — 'I will feed this people with wormwood and give them poisoned water to drink. I will scatter them among the nations... and I will send the sword after them until I have annihilated them.' The five cycles of discipline progress from warning to military disaster to national destruction. Jeremiah 44:12 adds that the remnant according to the election of grace — the pivot of mature believers — is always preserved even when the reversionistic population is destroyed.

section: 5. The Cause: Reversionism
text: Additional documentation: Philippians 3:18–19 (the reversionistic believer as the enemy of the cross); Revelation 3:15–16 (the Laodicean pattern of lukewarm reversionism drawing maximum discipline).

section: 6. The Sin Unto Death Does Not Mean Loss of Salvation
text: 6. The Sin Unto Death Does Not Mean Loss of Salvation

section: 6. The Sin Unto Death Does Not Mean Loss of Salvation
text: 2 Timothy 2:11–13 establishes the immutability of the believer's union with Christ. The first-class conditional chain reads: 'If we have died with Christ — and we have — at the same time also we shall live with Him.' This is retroactive positional truth: identification with Christ in His spiritual death (rejection of the old sin nature positionally), His physical death (separation from the old sin nature, analogous to divorce), and His burial (the finality of that separation). We are then identified with Christ in His session at the right hand of the Father — the new marriage. Verse 12: if we endure suffering as mature believers, we shall rule with Him. If we repudiate Him as reversionists, He will refuse us rewards and blessings. Verse 13: 'If we are unfaithful, He remains faithful, for He cannot deny Himself.' The sin unto death may be painful and is accompanied by total loss of temporal and eternal blessing, but it does not and cannot cancel salvation.

section: 7. Case Histories of the Sin Unto Death
text: 7. Case Histories of the Sin Unto Death

section: 7. Case Histories of the Sin Unto Death
text: Monetary reversionism: Ananias and Sapphira (Acts 5:1–10). Sexual reversionism: the Corinthian case (1 Corinthians 5:1–5). Ritual reversionism: abuse of the Lord's Table (1 Corinthians 11:30–31). Mental attitude reversionism: Saul (1 Samuel 13:9–14; 1 Chronicles 10:13–14). Verbal reversionism: Hymenaeus and Alexander (1 Timothy 1:19–20). Anti-establishment reversionism: Hezekiah's foreign policy failure (Isaiah 31:1–3; Isaiah 38).

section: 8. Reversion Recovery
text: 8. Reversion Recovery

section: 8. Reversion Recovery
text: Reversion recovery is possible and is God's purpose for every reversionistic believer still alive. Three elements are required: a change of mental attitude (repentance in the classical sense — Greek metanoia, a change of mind, not an emotional response), the consistent function of rebound, and the daily intake of Bible doctrine through the Grace Apparatus for Perception.

section: 8. Reversion Recovery
text: 2 Timothy 2:24–26 addresses the role of the pastor-teacher in this process: he must not be contentious but maintain objectivity toward the entire congregation, teaching skillfully and persistently in spite of opposition, 'so that perhaps God may give them a change of mind toward the full knowledge of doctrine, and they may come to their senses and be delivered from the devil's trap, having been held captive by him to do his will.' The reversionistic believer operating within the devil's plan is identified in Philippians 3 as the enemy of the cross.

section: 8. Reversion Recovery
text: 1 Corinthians 11:30–31 makes the connection explicit: 'Many among you are weak and sick, and a number sleep' — sleep here meaning the sin unto death — 'but if we judge ourselves, we shall not be judged.' The rebound technique — naming known sins to God — is the immediate recovery mechanism that returns the believer to fellowship and restores the possibility of blessing.

section: 8. Reversion Recovery
text: James 4:4–8 provides a comprehensive summary of reversion recovery factors: recognizing the conflict between worldliness and God, submitting to divine authority through the Word, resisting the devil, drawing near to God through daily doctrine intake, and cleansing the right lobe from the pollution of evil and reversionism. James identifies all reversionists as arrogant — they have assumed their own plan supersedes the Protocol Plan of God. The antidote is the humility of the advancing believer, to whom God gives greater grace.

section: IV. The Thought Pattern of the Old Sin Nature: Three Categories
text: IV. The Thought Pattern of the Old Sin Nature: Three Categories

section: IV. The Thought Pattern of the Old Sin Nature: Three Categories
text: The believer dominated by the old sin nature constantly programs his thinking in three categories: sin, human good, and evil. Sin is the overt expression of the old sin nature's trends — either the lasciviousness trend or the morality trend. Human good is the attempt to substitute self-generated righteousness for divine righteousness. Evil is the overarching satanic system of thought — the cosmic philosophy that frames and organizes both sin and human good into a coherent alternative to the Protocol Plan of God.

section: IV. The Thought Pattern of the Old Sin Nature: Three Categories
text: The justice of God cannot bless the reversionistic believer because blessing requires a prepared recipient. The carnal and reversionistic believer possesses imputed righteousness but has no capacity. Capacity for blessing, capacity for prosperity, capacity for life itself — all of it derives exclusively from maximum Bible doctrine resident in the soul. Without capacity, possession of material prosperity, social prominence, or any temporal blessing produces only misery. This is the answer to the ancient question of Proverbs: why do the wicked prosper? Blessing by association with a mature believer — a parent, spouse, child, or colleague who has cracked the maturity barrier — can produce temporal prosperity for the reversionistic believer in proximity. But without capacity, those blessings become a source of unhappiness rather than fulfillment.

section: V. The A Fortiori Arguments
text: V. The A Fortiori Arguments

section: V. The A Fortiori Arguments
text: Two a fortiori arguments establish the certainty of blessing for the mature believer. First a fortiori: if God accomplished the greater by imputing divine righteousness at salvation, it follows with greater logical force that God will provide the lesser blessing of time — temporal prosperity and maturity blessing. Second a fortiori: if God provided the greater temporal blessings at maturity, it follows that God will provide the even greater blessings of eternity at resurrection.

section: V. The A Fortiori Arguments
text: Primary potential: imputed divine righteousness plus capacity (maximum doctrine resident in the soul resulting in maturity adjustment to the justice of God) equals the reality of supergrace blessing in time. Secondary potential, grounded in Romans 6: the baptism of the Holy Spirit plus that same capacity produces the reality of the encapsulated environment of blessing — an inner environment superior even to Eden, regardless of historical adversity.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Two Hundred Eighty
text: Conclusions from Chapter Two Hundred Eighty

section: Conclusions from Chapter Two Hundred Eighty
text: 1. The sin unto death is maximum discipline from the justice of God to the reversionistic believer. The reversionistic believer is completely dominated by the old sin nature — the sovereign ruler of human life through spiritual death. The justice of God cannot bless, but only discipline, such a believer.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Two Hundred Eighty
text: 2. The thought pattern of the believer dominated by the old sin nature is programmed in three categories: sin, human good, and evil. These three categories constitute the full expression of the old sin nature's control over the believer's mental life.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Two Hundred Eighty
text: 3. The justice of God is the sole point of reference for both blessing and discipline. Not divine love, not sovereignty, not omnipotence — the justice of God is what gives absolute security to blessing and absolute certainty to discipline.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Two Hundred Eighty
text: 4. The sin unto death does not mean loss of salvation. The reversionistic believer retains imputed righteousness and imputed eternal life. He goes to heaven. But he dies in maximum pain and enters eternity with no rewards, no blessings above positional sanctification, and zero parlay of zero at resurrection.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Two Hundred Eighty
text: 5. The cause of the sin unto death is always sustained reversionism: negative volition toward Bible doctrine maintained over time until the old sin nature achieves complete domination of the soul, producing scar tissue, blackout, and the vacuum of the soul fully occupied by evil.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Two Hundred Eighty
text: 6. Reversion recovery requires three concurrent factors: a change of mental attitude toward Bible doctrine (repentance), the consistent function of rebound (1 John 1:9), and daily positive volition toward doctrine through the Grace Apparatus for Perception.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Two Hundred Eighty
text: 7. Capacity for blessing is the exclusive product of maximum doctrine resident in the soul. Without capacity, no imputation of divine blessing can occur. Temporal prosperity received without capacity produces misery rather than fulfillment. This is the mechanism behind blessing by association.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Two Hundred Eighty
text: 8. The worst thing that can ever happen to a born-again believer is to die the sin unto death. Since there is no sorrow, no regret, and no discipline in eternity for any believer, all disciplinary consequences must be concentrated in the dying moments before the final transfer from time to eternity.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Two Hundred Eighty
text: 9. There are four ways to transfer from time to eternity: the sin unto death (maximum discipline), dying grace (maximum blessing), the rapture (imminent, on the Lord's timetable, nothing preceding required), and surpassing grace — the rare translation of the mature believer without physical death or resurrection, of which Enoch is the only recorded example.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Two Hundred Eighty
text: 10. The maturity adjustment to the justice of God is the alternative to the sin unto death. Filling of the Spirit plus maximum doctrine resident in the soul equals experiential sanctification. This is the substance of the second half of Romans 8:6, to be examined in the following chapter: the thought pattern of the Spirit is life and peace.

Chapter Two Hundred Eighty-One

section: Romans 8:6b — The Thought Pattern of the Spirit: Capacity for Life and Prosperity
text: Romans 8:6b — The Thought Pattern of the Spirit: Capacity for Life and Prosperity

section: Romans 8:6b — The Thought Pattern of the Spirit: Capacity for Life and Prosperity
text: Romans 8:6 “For to set the mind on the flesh is death, but to set the mind on the Spirit is life and peace.” (ESV)

section: Romans 8:6b — The Thought Pattern of the Spirit: Capacity for Life and Prosperity
text: Corrected translation: Consequently, the thought pattern of the old sin nature is dead, but the thought pattern of the Spirit is capacity for life and prosperity.

section: Romans 8:6b — The Thought Pattern of the Spirit: Capacity for Life and Prosperity
text: This chapter continues the exegesis of Romans 8:6. The first clause — the thought pattern of the old sin nature is death — was established in the previous session as a reference to the sin unto death: the terminal consequence of sustained human viewpoint dominating the soul. The present session treats the contrasting clause: the thought pattern of the Spirit is life and peace. The Greek terms behind that translation open into a developed doctrinal statement about divine blessing in time, the a fortiori of grace, and the mechanism by which the justice of God imputes real blessing to the mature believer.

section: I. Grammatical Analysis of the Contrasting Clause
text: I. Grammatical Analysis of the Contrasting Clause

section: I. Grammatical Analysis of the Contrasting Clause
text: The clause opens with the post-positive conjunctive particle δέ (de), which connects two antithetical clauses. The contrast is deliberate: the thought pattern of the old sin nature versus the thought pattern governed by the Holy Spirit.

section: I. Grammatical Analysis of the Contrasting Clause
text: The subject is the nominative singular noun phrōnēma (φρόνημα), meaning thinking, mindset, or thought pattern. What a person thinks determines what that person is. The recurring use of this noun throughout Romans 8:6–8 underscores the epistle’s concern with the orientation of the inner life.

section: I. Grammatical Analysis of the Contrasting Clause
text: This is followed by a processive genitive from the noun pneuma (πνεύμα), used here for God the Holy Spirit. The full phrase, to phrōnēma tou pneumatos, the thought pattern of the Spirit, refers to Bible doctrine as the content of that thinking — the divine viewpoint deposited in the soul through the daily function of the Grace Apparatus for Perception (GAP).

section: I. Grammatical Analysis of the Contrasting Clause
text: The verb is supplied by ellipsis: the present active indicative of εἰμί (eimi), to be. Two predicate nominatives follow.

section: I. Grammatical Analysis of the Contrasting Clause
text: The first predicate nominative is zōē (ζωή), life. In this context zōē does not refer to eternal life received at salvation but to the function of life in phase two — the period between salvation and physical death. The emphasis is on capacity for life: the mature believer’s ability to receive, contain, and enjoy divine blessing in time. This capacity is the product of maximum doctrine resident in the soul.

section: I. Grammatical Analysis of the Contrasting Clause
text: The second predicate nominative is eirēnē (εἰρήνη). The standard translation “peace” is insufficient here. In the context of Romans 8 and the a fortiori argument of the chapter, eirēnē carries the sense of prosperity — the full-orbed blessing and well-being that attends the mature believer who has cracked the maturity barrier. The verse is therefore a statement about the objective of the Christian life in time: capacity for life and prosperity, both of which are the direct product of doctrine resident in the soul.

section: II. The A Fortiori of Blessing in Time
text: II. The A Fortiori of Blessing in Time

section: II. The A Fortiori of Blessing in Time
text: Romans 8:6b points toward the governing argument of Romans 8:31–32, which will be examined in full at that passage. The present verse, however, requires a foundational statement of the a fortiori principle as it operates between salvation and maturity.

section: A. The Mechanism: Two Judicial Imputations
text: A. The Mechanism: Two Judicial Imputations

section: A. The Mechanism: Two Judicial Imputations
text: All blessing from God to man flows through the justice of God. The justice of God is the single point of contact between divine integrity and human experience. Blessing and discipline alike originate there. No attribute of God other than justice directly dispenses either. This has a specific consequence for how blessing reaches the believer.

section: A. The Mechanism: Two Judicial Imputations
text: Divine justice can only bless perfect righteousness. Since no member of the human race possesses perfect righteousness antecedently, a mechanism had to be established by which perfect righteousness could be present in the believer as a divinely prepared home — a target — for the imputation of divine blessing. That mechanism operates through two judicial imputations.

section: A. The Mechanism: Two Judicial Imputations
text: A real imputation always involves an antecedent affinity: something is imputed to a divinely prepared home where there is an inherent correspondence. Human life imputed to the human soul at birth is a real imputation — there is and always will be an affinity between human life and the soul. Adam’s original sin imputed to every member of the human race at birth is likewise a real imputation — the old sin nature, created at the moment of Adam’s transgression, constitutes a genetically prepared target.

section: A. The Mechanism: Two Judicial Imputations
text: A judicial imputation, by contrast, involves no antecedent affinity. Something is imputed to a target where there is no inherent correspondence. The two judicial imputations that constitute the foundation of all blessing in time are these:

section: A. The Mechanism: Two Judicial Imputations
text: Judicial imputation number one: at the cross, the personal sins of the entire human race were imputed to Jesus Christ. These sins were not antecedently His. There was no affinity between the impeccable, sinless Son of God and the aggregate of human sin. The revulsion expressed in the cry of dereliction — “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” — testifies to the total absence of affinity. Nevertheless, the judicial imputation was executed, the sins were judged, and the basis for salvation was established.

section: A. The Mechanism: Two Judicial Imputations
text: Judicial imputation number two: at the moment of faith in Christ, the righteousness of God is imputed to the new believer. There is no affinity. The finest moral specimen of the human race has no correspondence with the perfect, infinite, eternal righteousness of God. Human righteousness cannot serve as a qualifying ground for divine blessing. The imputation is entirely judicial — it establishes a divinely prepared home, designated “plus R” (imputed righteousness), which serves as the target for all subsequent blessing from the justice of God.

section: A. The Mechanism: Two Judicial Imputations
text: This second judicial imputation is what is called justification — not a moral transformation but a forensic qualification. It means that the justice of God now has a legitimate target in the believer to which divine blessing can be imputed as a real imputation.

section: B. The Real Imputation of Blessing at Maturity
text: B. The Real Imputation of Blessing at Maturity

section: B. The Real Imputation of Blessing at Maturity
text: The two judicial imputations combine to make possible a real imputation at a later point: the imputation of divine blessing to its divinely prepared home, the imputed righteousness of God in the believer. This real imputation occurs when the believer cracks the maturity barrier through sustained doctrine intake under the filling of the Holy Spirit.

section: B. The Real Imputation of Blessing at Maturity
text: Prior to that point, all that the believer receives constitutes logistical grace — the provision of everything necessary to sustain physical existence and to carry the believer toward maturity. Food, shelter, clothing, transportation, relationships: these are not divine blessings in the technical sense. They are logistical support. They are real and often excellent, but they are incomparable to what awaits the believer who advances to spiritual maturity.

section: B. The Real Imputation of Blessing at Maturity
text: When the maturity barrier is cracked, the justice of God imputes the blessings of supergrace — supergrace A, supergrace B, and ultra-supergrace — to the divinely prepared home. These blessings are real imputations: they have perfect affinity with imputed righteousness. They are secure. They cannot be lost. And the believer at this stage has both the capacity to receive them and the capacity to enjoy them.

section: B. The Real Imputation of Blessing at Maturity
text: The a fortiori logic runs as follows: if the justice of God accomplished the greater work at salvation — the judicial imputation of divine righteousness to the undeserving believer — it follows with certainty that the justice of God will accomplish the lesser, which is the real imputation of divine blessing to that now-prepared home at maturity. This argument will be stated explicitly in Romans 8:32.

section: III. The Sin Unto Death Does Not Complete the A Fortiori
text: III. The Sin Unto Death Does Not Complete the A Fortiori

section: III. The Sin Unto Death Does Not Complete the A Fortiori
text: The sin unto death — the terminal discipline executed by the justice of God upon the believer who sustains maximum negative volition and reversionism — represents a failure to complete the a fortiori. The believer who dies the sin unto death departs this life with imputed righteousness intact but without the real imputation of divine blessing having been executed. The divinely prepared home exists, but nothing has been imputed to it in the supergrace categories.

section: III. The Sin Unto Death Does Not Complete the A Fortiori
text: This condition is described in Romans 8:6a: the thought pattern of the old sin nature is dead — it produces the sin unto death. The contrasting clause of Romans 8:6b is the positive alternative: the thought pattern of the Spirit, doctrine resident in the soul, produces the capacity for life and the prosperity that constitute the completed a fortiori in time.

section: III. The Sin Unto Death Does Not Complete the A Fortiori
text: The only state from which the a fortiori of blessing in time can be completed is experiential sanctification: the filling of the Spirit combined with maximum doctrine resident in the soul, sustained to the point of cracking the maturity barrier. No system of human righteousness, self-effort, vows, or religious performance contributes anything to this process. Our righteousness has no affinity with divine blessing and cannot serve as a qualifying ground. The entire work is accomplished by the grace of God through the daily function of GAP.

section: IV. Blessing Without Capacity Equals Misery
text: IV. Blessing Without Capacity Equals Misery

section: IV. Blessing Without Capacity Equals Misery
text: The two predicate nominatives of Romans 8:6b — capacity for life and prosperity — are not incidental. The sequence is theologically significant. Capacity precedes blessing. Divine justice cannot impute the blessings of supergrace until there is a prepared recipient who can contain and enjoy them. Blessing imputed to a believer without capacity produces misery rather than joy. The preparation of capacity is precisely the work that doctrine accomplishes in the soul over time.

section: IV. Blessing Without Capacity Equals Misery
text: This is why the believer is left in this life after salvation. The purpose of phase two is not endurance of suffering until the release of death. The purpose is the progressive development of capacity — doctrinal content in the soul — until the justice of God can impute blessing in the supergrace categories, and through that blessing, glorify Jesus Christ. The greatest things that ever happen to the believer in time glorify God. They do so because the real imputation of divine blessing to its divinely prepared home is the justice of God demonstrating the wisdom of its own plan in the resolution of the angelic conflict.

section: V. Undeserved Suffering as a Category of Blessing
text: V. Undeserved Suffering as a Category of Blessing

section: V. Undeserved Suffering as a Category of Blessing
text: A sixth category of supergrace blessing, beyond those previously enumerated, must be noted here because the subsequent context of Romans 8 will develop it. This is the category of undeserved suffering assigned to the mature believer.

section: V. Undeserved Suffering as a Category of Blessing
text: The mature believer who has cracked the maturity barrier possesses the capacity to receive a form of suffering that does not destabilize, does not produce misery, and does not require explanation or self-defense. This suffering is assigned only to believers whom God honors with it. Abraham’s offering of Isaac is the paradigm case: profound suffering executed without hesitation, without complaint, and without loss of orientation to the divine plan. That response was possible only because Abraham had the capacity — the doctrinal content in the soul — to sustain it.

section: V. Undeserved Suffering as a Category of Blessing
text: The mature believer who receives undeserved suffering has no need to circulate explanations or corrections of false impressions. The justice of God handles the believer’s case. Security in the blessings of supergrace means, among other things, that maligning, misjudgment, and false accusation cannot strip those blessings away. They are imputed to their target and secured there.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Two Hundred Eighty-One
text: Conclusions from Chapter Two Hundred Eighty-One

section: Conclusions from Chapter Two Hundred Eighty-One
text: 1. The contrasting clause of Romans 8:6b: The post-positive particle de (\u03b4\u03ad) introduces a deliberate antithesis. The thought pattern of the Holy Spirit — phrōnēma tou pneumatos — is defined by doctrine resident in the soul and produces two results: zōē, capacity for life, and eirēnē, prosperity.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Two Hundred Eighty-One
text: 2. The two predicate nominatives define the completed a fortiori: Zōē (life) refers to capacity for phase two existence under the supergrace categories. Eirēnē (prosperity) refers to the real imputation of divine blessing to its divinely prepared home at maturity. These are not descriptions of a comfortable religious life but of the objective completion of the divine plan for the Church Age believer.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Two Hundred Eighty-One
text: 3. At salvation, the greater a fortiori from the justice of God: The greater a fortiori was accomplished through the judicial imputation of divine righteousness to the new believer at salvation adjustment. This established a divinely prepared home — imputed righteousness — which is the target for all subsequent blessing from the justice of God.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Two Hundred Eighty-One
text: 4. The greatest things that ever happen to the believer glorify God: The real imputation of divine blessing to imputed righteousness at maturity is the mechanism by which Jesus Christ is glorified through the believer’s life in time. This is the reason the believer remains in phase two after salvation. The angelic conflict requires a demonstration in time.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Two Hundred Eighty-One
text: 5. At spiritual maturity, the less in a fortiori from the justice of God: The less a fortiori is accomplished through the real imputation of divine blessings to the divinely prepared home, imputed righteousness. If the justice of God performed the greater work at salvation, it will certainly perform the lesser work at maturity. This argument will be stated explicitly in Romans 8:32.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Two Hundred Eighty-One
text: 6. Two judicial imputations preceded this real imputation: Judicial imputation number one — the personal sins of the human race imputed to Christ on the cross — and judicial imputation number two — the righteousness of God imputed to the believer at salvation. These two judicial imputations, involving no antecedent affinity in either case, combine to establish the only ground on which divine blessing can legitimately be imputed to a member of the human race.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Two Hundred Eighty-One
text: 7. There is no a fortiori blessing in time until maturity: Logistical grace sustains the believer during the advance toward maturity but does not constitute supergrace blessing. The justice of God cannot impute supergrace blessings until there is capacity to receive them. Blessing without capacity produces misery, not joy. The development of capacity is the specific work of doctrine in the soul over time.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Two Hundred Eighty-One
text: 8. The sin unto death does not complete the a fortiori: The believer who dies under the sin unto death departs with imputed righteousness intact but with no real imputation of supergrace blessing having been executed. The divinely prepared home exists but remains unoccupied by the blessings for which it was prepared. Only the state of experiential sanctification — the filling of the Spirit plus maximum doctrine resident in the soul — can complete the a fortiori.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Two Hundred Eighty-One
text: 9. Blessing without capacity equals misery: The sequence of the two predicate nominatives — capacity for life first, then prosperity — is not incidental. Capacity must precede blessing. This is why doctrine intake is the single non-negotiable requirement for the reception of supergrace blessings. No system of human performance, religious activity, or self-righteousness can substitute for or supplement it.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Two Hundred Eighty-One
text: 10. Undeserved suffering is a category of supergrace blessing: A sixth supergrace category, beyond those in the standard enumeration, is undeserved suffering assigned to the mature believer. It differs from ordinary suffering in that the mature believer possesses the capacity to sustain it without destabilization, without self-defense, and without loss of orientation to the divine plan. Abraham’s offering of Isaac is the paradigm. This category will be developed further in the subsequent context of Romans 8.

Chapter Two Hundred Eighty-Two

section: Romans 8:6 — Real and Judicial Imputation; Divine Blessing; Prosperity as the Objective of the Believer in Time
text: Romans 8:6 — Real and Judicial Imputation; Divine Blessing; Prosperity as the Objective of the Believer in Time

section: Romans 8:6 — Real and Judicial Imputation; Divine Blessing; Prosperity as the Objective of the Believer in Time
text: Romans 8:6 “For to set the mind on the flesh is death, but to set the mind on the Spirit is life and peace.” (ESV)

section: Romans 8:6 — Real and Judicial Imputation; Divine Blessing; Prosperity as the Objective of the Believer in Time
text: Corrected translation: Consequently, the thought pattern of the old sin nature is death, but the thought pattern of the Spirit is capacity for life and prosperity.

section: Romans 8:6 — Real and Judicial Imputation; Divine Blessing; Prosperity as the Objective of the Believer in Time
text: Romans 8:6 has been under sustained examination. The corrected translation renders the verse's second clause as 'capacity for life and prosperity.' This chapter focuses on the word 'prosperity' — the objective of the believer's life in time — and develops the doctrinal foundation that makes prosperity intelligible: the distinction between real and judicial imputation, the two judicial imputations that together produce the real imputation of divine blessing, and the six categories of divine blessing that constitute that prosperity.

section: I. Rightly Dividing the Word: Real Imputation vs. Judicial Imputation
text: I. Rightly Dividing the Word: Real Imputation vs. Judicial Imputation

section: I. Rightly Dividing the Word: Real Imputation vs. Judicial Imputation
text: The command to 'rightly divide the word of truth' (2 Timothy 2:15) applies not only to dispensational distinctions but to the minutiae of doctrine, including the doctrine of imputation. A failure to distinguish real imputation from judicial imputation produces confusion at the heart of the plan of God.

section: A. Real Imputation
text: A. Real Imputation

section: A. Real Imputation
text: A real imputation has two essential factors: (1) that which is imputed, and (2) a target or home — a recipient that possesses a natural affinity for what is being imputed. The affinity is the basis on which the imputation 'resides.' Without a prepared home with affinity, there can be no real imputation.

section: A. Real Imputation
text: Two real imputations occur at physical birth. First, human life is imputed to the divinely created human soul — the soul has affinity for human life. Second, Adam's original sin is imputed to the old sin nature — the old sin nature has genetic affinity for that sin. The result is that every member of the human race is simultaneously physically alive and spiritually dead. Death rules life: the old sin nature, operating through spiritual death, dominates the human life resident in the soul.

section: B. Judicial Imputation
text: B. Judicial Imputation

section: B. Judicial Imputation
text: A judicial imputation has only one factor: that which is imputed. There is no prepared home, no affinity, no natural target. The imputation is made by a sovereign judicial act of God, not because the recipient has affinity for what is given.

section: B. Judicial Imputation
text: Two judicial imputations lie at the foundation of the plan of God for the human race in the Church Age. The first: at the cross, all personal sins of the entire human race were imputed to the Lord Jesus Christ and judged. Christ is absolutely perfect; there is no affinity in Him for human sin. This is therefore a judicial imputation. The second: at the moment of personal faith in Christ, the divine righteousness of God is imputed to the new believer. The believer has no natural affinity for God's perfect righteousness — it does not belong to him inherently. This too is a judicial imputation.

section: B. Judicial Imputation
text: The governing principle: it takes two judicial imputations to produce one real imputation of divine blessing. The first judicial imputation (personal sins to Christ at the cross) plus the second judicial imputation (divine righteousness to the believer at salvation) together constitute the necessary precondition for the real imputation of divine blessing in time.

section: II. Adam's Original Sin and the Basis for Grace
text: II. Adam's Original Sin and the Basis for Grace

section: II. Adam's Original Sin and the Basis for Grace
text: The two real imputations at birth — human life to the soul, Adam's original sin to the old sin nature — establish the human condition from which all subsequent divine dealing proceeds. Several observations are critical.

section: II. Adam's Original Sin and the Basis for Grace
text: First, one sin condemns the entire human race. Not multiple sins, not personal sins accumulated over a lifetime — one sin: Adam's original transgression in the garden (1 Corinthians 15:22, 'In Adam all die'). Personal sins are never the ground of condemnation. Every personal sin committed by every member of the human race has already been imputed to Christ at the cross and judged. No personal sin is imputed to the individual human being. The condemnation is based solely on Adam's one act.

section: II. Adam's Original Sin and the Basis for Grace
text: Second, Adam's original sin was unique in character. It carried no conventional moral content — no one was killed, no one was directly harmed. It was a violation of a specific divine prohibition by an act of volition. God ensured it could never be repeated. Its absolute uniqueness is what makes it the single point of condemnation for all humanity.

section: II. Adam's Original Sin and the Basis for Grace
text: Third, the condemnation of the entire race at birth is, paradoxically, the greatest blessing the human race could receive. It accomplishes two things simultaneously: it maintains the integrity of all the divine attributes — justice cannot wink at transgression — and it provides the basis for grace. Grace as a policy did not exist in the Garden of Eden. In an environment of sinless perfection, there was no necessity for grace. It was the fall that made grace both possible and necessary. Grace is the policy of the justice of God in providing blessing for a condemned race.

section: II. Adam's Original Sin and the Basis for Grace
text: Fourth, being born at the bottom — spiritually dead, condemned, with no merit of one's own — means there is only one direction to go: upward. The justice of God imputed the worst possible deficit at birth precisely so that all subsequent movement is movement toward blessing. No room is left for human arrogance. Not one member of the human race can claim spiritual death as the result of personal performance. Spiritual death is universal, uniform, and entirely the consequence of Adam's act, not one's own.

section: III. The Integrity of God and the Mechanism of Blessing
text: III. The Integrity of God and the Mechanism of Blessing

section: III. The Integrity of God and the Mechanism of Blessing
text: All blessing from God to man flows through the justice of God. The integrity of God is composed of two attributes in tandem: divine righteousness and divine justice. Righteousness is the standard; justice is the administrator of that standard. What righteousness demands, justice executes. What righteousness rejects, justice condemns. What righteousness approves, justice blesses.

section: III. The Integrity of God and the Mechanism of Blessing
text: Divine justice can only bless perfect righteousness. This is not a limitation — it is the logical consequence of the consistency of God's attributes. God's righteousness will accept nothing less than God's own righteousness as a standard. Therefore the source of all direct divine blessing — the justice of God — is free to provide blessing only where divine righteousness exists.

section: III. The Integrity of God and the Mechanism of Blessing
text: At the moment of faith in Christ, the believer receives the judicial imputation of divine righteousness. From that moment forward, the believer carries divine righteousness as a permanent possession — not because he earned it or has affinity for it, but because God imputed it judicially. This imputed righteousness functions as a magnet: the justice of God is drawn to bless wherever its own righteousness resides. Justification, rightly understood, does not mean 'justice as if I had never sinned' — it means 'qualified for blessing in time and eternity'; it means being a candidate for the positive side of the grace of God.

section: III. The Integrity of God and the Mechanism of Blessing
text: Because God loves His own integrity — the composite of His righteousness and justice — the imputation of half of that integrity (divine righteousness) to the believer at salvation is the mechanism by which the believer comes under the love of God as an attribute. The love of God as an attribute operates through the integrity of God, not apart from it.

section: III. The Integrity of God and the Mechanism of Blessing
text: The governing logical principle: if the justice of God can provide the greater — salvation through the imputation of divine righteousness — it follows by the lesser-to-greater argument that the justice of God can provide the less: the real imputation of divine blessing at the point of spiritual maturity. Matthew 6:33 states this exactly: 'Seek first the kingdom and His righteousness, and all these things shall be added to you.' The 'all these things' is the real imputation of divine blessing.

section: IV. The Real Imputation of Divine Blessing: Six Categories
text: IV. The Real Imputation of Divine Blessing: Six Categories

section: IV. The Real Imputation of Divine Blessing: Six Categories
text: Divine blessing — prosperity in the fullest sense — is a real imputation. It has two factors: (1) that which is imputed, namely divine blessing itself, the source of which is always God; and (2) the divinely prepared home with affinity for that blessing, which is the imputed divine righteousness resident in the mature believer. No human effort, self-righteousness, religious performance, or moral attainment constitutes a valid target for divine blessing. Only divine righteousness has affinity for what divine justice dispenses.

section: IV. The Real Imputation of Divine Blessing: Six Categories
text: The real imputation of divine blessing cannot be made until the believer has capacity. God would be unjust to impute blessing without the capacity to appreciate and participate in it. Capacity comes from maximum doctrine resident in the soul — the result of sustained intake and application of Bible doctrine through the Grace Apparatus for Perception. Capacity precedes blessing; life precedes prosperity in the corrected translation of Romans 8:6 for precisely this reason.

section: IV. The Real Imputation of Divine Blessing: Six Categories
text: Divine blessing in time is organized into six categories. The first five are experienced in time and in dying; the sixth is the category of undeserved suffering, which will be treated in detail when the commentary reaches Romans 8:18–30.

section: Category 1: Spiritual Blessings
text: Category 1: Spiritual Blessings

section: Category 1: Spiritual Blessings
text: Spiritual blessings are listed first because they are the blessings of capacity itself — they are produced by, and are coextensive with, the attainment of spiritual maturity. They include: occupation with Christ (maximum category-one love); sharing the happiness of God; capacity for life, capacity for love, capacity for happiness, and capacity for blessing; capacity for undeserved suffering; total appreciation for grace; ability to face suffering and pressure without destabilization; ability to correctly interpret contemporary history in light of divine viewpoint; freedom from slavery to circumstances; and adaptability to changing circumstances. The mature believer becomes the greatest innovator precisely when historical circumstances are most unstable.

section: Category 1: Spiritual Blessings
text: One distinction requires emphasis: capacity for undeserved suffering is possible for the mature believer; capacity for divine discipline is not. Divine discipline is designed to sting — if it did not produce pain, it would not function as discipline. No believer at any level of maturity has capacity for divine discipline. Undeserved suffering, by contrast, is a separate category that the mature believer handles with stability and turns into a basis for glorifying the Lord Jesus Christ.

section: Category 2: Temporal Blessings
text: Category 2: Temporal Blessings

section: Category 2: Temporal Blessings
text: Temporal blessings include success, promotion, and recognition in one's sphere of life. They are not exhaustively enumerated here but are representative: social prosperity; sexual prosperity (right man, right woman); technical prosperity in science and related fields; mental prosperity (increased concentration and perspicacity); cultural prosperity (maximum appreciation of music, art, literature, drama); establishment prosperity (enjoyment of freedom, privacy, property, and protection); and professional prosperity in law, medicine, engineering, military service, education, or any legitimate vocation. Every believer's prosperity is individualized; this list is representative, not exhaustive.

section: Category 3: Blessing by Association
text: Category 3: Blessing by Association

section: Category 3: Blessing by Association
text: Blessing by association is the mechanism by which unbelievers and reversionistic believers receive temporal blessing. Those in the periphery of a mature believer — whether in supergrace A, supergrace B, or ultra-supergrace — are blessed by their association with that believer. God may bless them directly, because of their proximity to the mature believer; or He may bless them indirectly through the visible instrumentality of the mature believer himself.

section: Category 3: Blessing by Association
text: The peripheries of blessing by association include: the loved-one periphery (right man, right woman, family, friends); the business periphery (investors, management, and labor associated in the same enterprise); the professional periphery (colleagues in the same institution, firm, or organization); the social periphery (friends, clubs, athletic teams — one mature believer can change the character of a team); the spiritual periphery (a local congregation or any assembly of believers); the geographical periphery (a neighborhood, city, state, or nation — the salt principle: the mature believer provides both flavor and preservation to society); the inheritance periphery (the greatest heritage a believer can leave is to have died in spiritual maturity — blessing by association extends to survivors); and the pastoral periphery (no congregation can exceed the spiritual growth of its pastor, whose consistent advance in doctrine is therefore the precondition of the congregation's advance).

section: Category 4: Historical Impact
text: Category 4: Historical Impact

section: Category 4: Historical Impact
text: The mature believer is the spiritual pivot of his generation. The ebb and flow of historical disaster does not disturb the stability or the effectiveness of the mature believer. He directly affects the trajectory of his generation. As the pivot goes, so goes the nation: if the pivot of mature believers in a client nation is large enough, the nation survives even the most severe historical adversities. The spinoff — reversionistic believers, believers operating in human good, and apostate believers — is always on the wrong side of history and subject to its disasters. The mature believer rises above historical catastrophe; the reversionist is swept away by it. Ultra-supergrace believers such as Moses, David, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Paul had historical impact not only in their own generation but in all subsequent generations.

section: Category 5: Dying Blessing
text: Category 5: Dying Blessing

section: Category 5: Dying Blessing
text: Dying grace is the physical death of the mature believer — in supergrace A, supergrace B, or ultra-supergrace. At the point of dying grace, the sting and fear of death are removed. Death becomes the greatest experience in the believer's life to that point, the antithesis of the sin unto death. Dying grace is the mature believer's permanent change of station from phase two (time) to phase three (eternity).

section: Category 5: Dying Blessing
text: Dying grace also operates by the lesser-to-greater argument: the greater is the blessings in time (paragraph SG2); the less is the rewards and blessings of eternity (paragraph SG3). If the justice of God provided the greater in time, He will certainly provide the less in eternity. The mature believer therefore has the best of life in time, something better still in dying grace, and the best of all in eternity. Psalm 116:15: 'Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of His godly ones.' The godly ones are the mature believers.

section: Category 6: Undeserved Suffering
text: Category 6: Undeserved Suffering

section: Category 6: Undeserved Suffering
text: Undeserved suffering is the sixth category of divine blessing for the mature believer. Its full treatment is reserved for Romans 8:18–30, where the apostle Paul addresses it directly: 'I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us' (Romans 8:18). The sufferings in view are the undeserved sufferings of the mature believer — not divine discipline, which would be deserved. For the mature believer, God not only provides the capacity to endure such suffering but transforms it into blessing. This is the true meaning of Romans 8:28: 'We know that all things work together for good to those who love God.' The 'we know' excludes those without doctrine; 'those who love God' identifies the mature believer characterized by maximum category-one love — occupation with Christ. Romans 8:28 is not a general promise for all believers; it is the operational reality of the mature believer for whom undeserved suffering belongs to the real imputation of divine blessing.

section: V. Prosperity and the Maturity Adjustment to the Justice of God
text: V. Prosperity and the Maturity Adjustment to the Justice of God

section: V. Prosperity and the Maturity Adjustment to the Justice of God
text: Returning to the corrected translation of Romans 8:6 — 'the thought pattern of the Spirit is capacity for life and prosperity' — note that life precedes prosperity. This ordering is not incidental. Capacity for life is the prerequisite for appreciating and participating in prosperity. A person may possess great wealth, a right man or right woman, social position, or any combination of temporal blessings, and be entirely miserable — because without capacity, participation in blessing is impossible. Capacity comes from maximum doctrine resident in the soul. The real imputation of divine blessing cannot be made to its target — imputed divine righteousness — unless the believer has the capacity to receive and appreciate what is being imputed.

section: V. Prosperity and the Maturity Adjustment to the Justice of God
text: Prosperity in Romans 8 is therefore more than material or circumstantial well-being. It is the objective of the believer in time: the means by which the believer, in tactical victory in the devil's world, glorifies the strategic victory of the Lord Jesus Christ at the cross. The maturity adjustment to the justice of God — cracking the maturity barrier through sustained doctrine intake and advancing to supergrace — is the path by which the believer arrives at the real imputation of divine blessing. When righteousness demands it, justice executes it: the justice of God opens the dikes of divine blessing to the one who has cracked the maturity barrier and stands before God qualified by His own imputed righteousness.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Two Hundred Eighty-Two
text: Conclusions from Chapter Two Hundred Eighty-Two

section: Conclusions from Chapter Two Hundred Eighty-Two
text: 1. Two judicial imputations produce one real imputation of divine blessing. The first judicial imputation — all personal sins imputed to Christ at the cross — and the second judicial imputation — divine righteousness imputed to the believer at salvation — together constitute the necessary and sufficient precondition for the real imputation of divine blessing in time.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Two Hundred Eighty-Two
text: 2. A real imputation requires both that which is imputed and a home with affinity. Divine blessing requires divine righteousness as its target. No human righteousness, religious performance, or moral effort constitutes a valid home for divine blessing. Only the imputed righteousness of God possesses the required affinity.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Two Hundred Eighty-Two
text: 3. Condemnation at birth is the basis for grace. Being born spiritually dead because of Adam's one sin — not personal sin — removes all ground for human arrogance and establishes grace as the exclusive policy of the justice of God toward the human race. Grace did not exist before the fall; the fall made grace both necessary and possible.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Two Hundred Eighty-Two
text: 4. Justification means qualified for blessing, not moral exoneration. The imputation of divine righteousness at salvation produces justification — standing before God as a candidate for the positive side of His grace, qualified in time and eternity. It is not a statement about the believer's personal moral history.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Two Hundred Eighty-Two
text: 5. The lesser-to-greater argument governs the entire structure of divine blessing. If the justice of God provided the greater — salvation through the imputation of divine righteousness — He will not withhold the lesser: blessing in time at spiritual maturity, and blessing in eternity at physical death.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Two Hundred Eighty-Two
text: 6. Capacity precedes prosperity; life precedes blessing. Romans 8:6 orders the clause deliberately: 'capacity for life and prosperity.' Without capacity — produced by sustained doctrine intake — the real imputation of divine blessing cannot be received or appreciated, regardless of outward circumstances.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Two Hundred Eighty-Two
text: 7. Six categories of divine blessing constitute prosperity in time. Spiritual blessings, temporal blessings, blessing by association, historical impact, dying blessing, and undeserved suffering together constitute the prosperity that is the objective of the believer's life in time. The sixth category — undeserved suffering — will receive full treatment at Romans 8:18–30.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Two Hundred Eighty-Two
text: 8. Romans 8:28 is addressed specifically to mature believers. 'We know that all things work together for good to those who love God' — the 'we know' excludes those without doctrine; 'those who love God' identifies the mature believer in occupation with Christ. This promise is not operative for every believer indiscriminately; it is the experience of those who have cracked the maturity barrier and for whom undeserved suffering belongs to the real imputation of divine blessing.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Two Hundred Eighty-Two
text: 9. The pivot of mature believers is the decisive factor in national history. The mature believer carries his generation in human history. As the pivot of mature believers in a client nation grows, the nation is preserved under historical adversity. The reversionist is on the wrong side of history and subject to its disasters; the mature believer rises above them and glorifies God on the crest of the wave.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Two Hundred Eighty-Two
text: 10. Prosperity is the means of glorifying the strategic victory of the Lord Jesus Christ. The believer remains in the devil's world after salvation not by accident but by divine design: to advance to maturity, receive the real imputation of divine blessing, and thereby demonstrate in time that the tactical victory of the mature believer vindicates the strategic victory won at the cross.

Psalm 116:15: 'Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of His godly ones.'
