section: Glossary
text: γάρ gar — for, indeed, certainly

section: Glossary
text: A post-positive particle with explanatory or emphatic force. At Romans 8:13 it introduces the explanatory reason for the preceding prohibition and carries emphatic force: "for indeed." It signals that the alternatives about to be stated are the explanation and consequence of the negative obligation just declared.

section: Glossary
text: εἰ ei — if (conditional conjunction)

section: Glossary
text: The standard conditional conjunction for the first-class condition in Greek. With the indicative mood it introduces a supposition stated from the viewpoint of reality — the premise is assumed to be true for the purpose of the argument. At Romans 8:13 the first-class condition assumes that the reversionistic trajectory is an actual present reality.

section: Glossary
text: mellō

section: Glossary
text: μέλλω mellō — to be about to, to be destined, to be on the point of

section: Glossary
text: A verb expressing imminence or destiny. At Romans 8:13 the futuristic present tense denotes a consequence not yet realized but certain and approaching. With the infinitive apothnēskō it indicates that the reversionistic believer is destined to die — a reference to the sin unto death as maximum divine discipline.

section: Glossary
text: apothnēskō

section: Glossary
text: ἀποθνῄσκω apothnēskō — to die

section: Glossary
text: Compound verb: apo (away, from) + thnēskō (to die). Used at Romans 8:13 as a present active infinitive of conceived result. In this context it refers specifically to the sin unto death — maximum divine discipline resulting in physical death — not to spiritual death or loss of salvation.

section: Glossary
text: Sin unto death

section: Glossary
text: The terminal stage of divine discipline for the believer who sustains reversionism without recovery. It is physical death imposed by the justice of God when the believer's capacity for blessing has been permanently destroyed. It involves no loss of eternal salvation but does involve the permanent forfeiture of supergrace blessings in time and corresponding rewards in eternity. Distinguished from dying grace, which is the normal and blessed exit from time for the mature believer.

section: Glossary
text: Retroactive positional truth

section: Glossary
text: The believer's identification with Christ in His spiritual death, physical death, and burial at the moment of salvation through the baptism of the Holy Spirit. This identification breaks the legal authority and power of the old sin nature, which had functioned as the first husband prior to salvation. It is analogous to the divorce described in Romans 7:1–6.

section: Glossary
text: Maturity adjustment to the justice of God

section: Glossary
text: The progressive stage of adjustment to the justice of God accomplished through sustained daily intake of Bible doctrine under the filling of the Holy Spirit. Distinguished from salvation adjustment (instantaneous, once only) and rebound adjustment (instantaneous, repeated as needed). Maturity adjustment culminates in supergrace and the release of maximum blessings through the grace pipeline.
Chapter Three Hundred One

section: Romans 8:13b–14 — Authority, Human Good, and Divine Guidance
text: Romans 8:13b–14 — Authority, Human Good, and Divine Guidance

section: Romans 8:13b–14 — Authority, Human Good, and Divine Guidance
text: Romans 8:13b–14 “But if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live. For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God.” (ESV)

section: Romans 8:13b–14 — Authority, Human Good, and Divine Guidance
text: Corrected translation: But if by means of the Spirit you recognize as dead the actions from the body, you shall live. For as many as are being led by the Spirit of God, these are sons of God.

section: Romans 8:13b–14 — Authority, Human Good, and Divine Guidance
text: Romans 8:13 presents two alternatives for the believer in time. The first half of the verse, studied in the preceding chapter, describes the reversionist living under the authority of the old sin nature and destined for the sin unto death. The second half of verse 13 opens the positive alternative: the believer who, by means of the Holy Spirit, condemns human good as dead and thereby advances toward maturity adjustment to the justice of God. Verse 14 then introduces the first result of that maturity — divine guidance.

section: I. The Two Authorities — Review of the First Half of Romans 8:13
text: I. The Two Authorities — Review of the First Half of Romans 8:13

section: I. The Two Authorities — Review of the First Half of Romans 8:13
text: All believers in time are oriented to one of two authorities. Either the Word of God and everything related to it serves as the governing authority of the soul, or the old sin nature and everything related to it does. There is no middle position. The first half of verse 13 presents the reversionist — the believer who neglects rebound and rejects Bible doctrine — living under the authority of the old sin nature. The corrected translation of that clause reads: Indeed, if you live under the authority of the old sin nature — a first-class condition, assumed as reality — you are destined to die.

section: I. The Two Authorities — Review of the First Half of Romans 8:13
text: This death is not physical death in the ordinary sense. It is the sin unto death: maximum divine discipline administered to the believer in reversionism who has persisted in malajustment to the justice of God.

section: The Sin Unto Death
text: The Sin Unto Death

section: The Sin Unto Death
text: There are four ways a believer may transfer from time into eternity. Two are honorable and two are dishonorable.

section: The Sin Unto Death
text: Dying grace is the honorable death of the mature believer. It is a death accompanied by maximum blessing and serves as a transition into the eternal rewards prepared for those who have reached maturity adjustment to the justice of God. The rapture or resurrection is the second honorable means of departure — the translation of the living generation of Church Age believers at the end of the Church Age.

section: The Sin Unto Death
text: The sin unto death is the dishonorable death of the reversionistic believer. It is painful, miserable, and represents the final and most severe expression of divine discipline. Suicide — the reversionistic imposition of one's own will over the will of God — is the fourth category. Both are dishonorable.

section: The Sin Unto Death
text: The administration of the sin unto death never involves the loss of salvation. The moment of death ends all sorrow, pain, and discipline. One second after that death, the old things have passed away. But the process leading to it is the most extreme divine discipline a believer can receive in time.

section: The Sin Unto Death
text: The doctrinal basis for the sin unto death is found in several passages. Psalm 118:17–18 records David's testimony that he had received severe discipline but had not been given over to death — he was not dying the sin unto death. First John 5:16 establishes the category directly. The causal passage is Jeremiah 9:13–16, where the Lord identifies the cause as the abandonment of His doctrine: because they have forsaken My doctrine, which I have set before them, and have not obeyed My voice, nor walked according to it, but have walked after the hardness of their right lobe. Philippians 3:18–19 describes the reversionistic believer as an enemy of the cross of Christ, whose termination of life is ruin, whose god is his emotion, whose fame is his means of dishonor.

section: The Sin Unto Death
text: Categories of reversionism that can culminate in the sin unto death include: monetary reversionism (Acts 5:1–10, Ananias and Sapphira); sexual reversionism (1 Corinthians 5:1–5, the incestuous Corinthian); ritual reversionism (1 Corinthians 11:30–31, abuse of the Lord's Table); mental attitude reversionism, involving complete divorce from reality (1 Chronicles 10:13–14); verbal reversionism, the sustained practice of gossip and maligning (1 Timothy 1:19–20); and anti-establishment reversionism, in which an abuse of authority produces national consequences. The means of recovery from reversionism involves repentance (2 Timothy 2:24–26), rebound (1 Corinthians 11:30–31), and the renewed function of the Grace Apparatus for Perception, GAP (James 4:4–8).

section: II. The Positive Alternative — Romans 8:13b
text: II. The Positive Alternative — Romans 8:13b

section: Grammatical Analysis
text: Grammatical Analysis

section: Grammatical Analysis
text: The second half of verse 13 opens with the adversative conjunctive particle de, establishing a contrast between the two clauses of the verse: the reversionist under the authority of the old sin nature, and the believer who is positive toward doctrine and advances in grace.

section: Grammatical Analysis
text: A conjunctive particle ei (εἰ) introduces a first-class condition — an assumption based on reality. As long as the believer remains alive, the option toward maturity adjustment to the justice of God remains open. Reversionism is never irreversible in time.

section: Grammatical Analysis
text: The instrumental of means from pneuma (πνεῦμα), the Holy Spirit, governs the clause. The Holy Spirit is the means by which doctrine is received, retained, and applied. He both controls the believer's soul under the filling of the Spirit and enables the perception of doctrine through the Grace Apparatus for Perception.

section: Grammatical Analysis
text: The main verb is the present active indicative of thanatoo (θανατόω), a classical Attic word meaning to kill, to deliver up to death, to condemn to death, or to recognize as dead. The last meaning is determinative here. The present tense is a retroactive progressive present — denoting what must begin at salvation and continue throughout the believer's life. The active voice indicates that the believer produces the action. The indicative mood is a potential indicative of obligation: this is the only way to live the Christian way of life.

section: Grammatical Analysis
text: The direct object is the accusative plural of praxis (πρᾶξις), meaning actions or functions, followed by the ablative of source singular from soma (σῶμα), the human body. The full construction reads: the actions from the body.

section: Grammatical Analysis
text: The corrected translation of the second half of verse 13 therefore reads: But if by means of the Spirit you recognize as dead — condemned to death — the actions from the body, you shall live.

section: The Actions from the Body: Human Good
text: The Actions from the Body: Human Good

section: The Actions from the Body: Human Good
text: The actions from the body do not refer to physical functions or ascetic renunciation of material existence. Asceticism, whether in its mutilating or its world-denying form, is not in view here. The passage is addressing human good — any system of self-righteousness, any program designed to improve the devil's world through human effort, any attempt to gain divine blessing through personal performance.

section: The Actions from the Body: Human Good
text: Human good comes in several recognizable categories. Emotional human good is the error of those who equate spiritual ecstasy or intense religious experience with closeness to God. Working human good is the error of the believer who regards Christian service activity — witnessing campaigns, organizational involvement, church programs — as the basis of spirituality or blessing. Self-righteous human good is the pattern of the legalist who measures divine favor by the height of personal moral standards and simultaneously persecutes those who do not conform to those standards.

section: The Actions from the Body: Human Good
text: Human good is the greatest temptation facing the believer precisely because it is attractive, respectable, and easily mistaken for genuine spiritual production. The old sin nature drives the believer toward self-improvement and world-improvement programs. The tree of the knowledge of good and evil presents the same danger to the believer in the Church Age as it did to the original parents in the garden. Good and evil together constitute the comprehensive alternative to the Word of God.

section: The Divorce from the Old Sin Nature
text: The Divorce from the Old Sin Nature

section: The Divorce from the Old Sin Nature
text: The verb thanatoo calls the believer to recognize as dead the actions that originate from the old sin nature. This recognition is not a physical act but a mental one. It is accomplished through the mentality of the soul, informed by doctrine and sustained by the filling of the Holy Spirit.

section: The Divorce from the Old Sin Nature
text: The basis for this recognition is retroactive positional truth — the believer's identification with Christ in His death, burial, and resurrection through the baptism of the Holy Spirit at salvation. At salvation, a judicial divorce from the old sin nature was effected positionally. The power of the old sin nature as the ruling authority has been broken. Experientially, this positional reality is exploited through the daily filling of the Spirit and the daily function of the Grace Apparatus for Perception.

section: The Divorce from the Old Sin Nature
text: Orthodox Judaism provides a useful parallel for understanding the mental dimension of this recognition. When a family member converts to another faith, Orthodox practice has sometimes required the family to regard that person as dead — conducting a funeral, entering mourning, refusing any ongoing relationship. The person is recognized as dead in the mind of those remaining, even though physically alive. The same principle applies here: the believer, operating on the basis of doctrine resident in the soul, regards human good as dead — as belonging to a former mode of existence that no longer has authority.

section: The Elimination of Both Human Good and Legitimate Good
text: The Elimination of Both Human Good and Legitimate Good

section: The Elimination of Both Human Good and Legitimate Good
text: The accusative plural direct object praxis encompasses two categories: human good and legitimate good. Human good refers to all illegitimate, self-righteous systems of earning divine favor — legalism, self-improvement programs, performance-based spirituality.

section: The Elimination of Both Human Good and Legitimate Good
text: Legitimate good refers to the divine commands found in the Word of God for believers: commands to pray, to witness, to exercise royal family prerogatives, to function in Christian service. These are genuine obligations of the Christian life. However, none of these legitimate commands are related to divine blessing — with the sole exception of the rebound command. Prayer, witnessing, service, and the use of spiritual gifts accomplished in the energy of the flesh — without the filling of the Spirit and without doctrine as the motivating capacity — are also eliminated from the divine blessing pipeline. Even when accomplished in the Spirit, these activities do not themselves produce blessing. Blessing comes through the intake of doctrine and the resultant capacity for life.

section: The Elimination of Both Human Good and Legitimate Good
text: The actions of the body — whether human good or legitimate good performed in the flesh — originate from human talent, human ability, human energy, and human motivation. All of these have been set aside in the divine plan for the believer in the Church Age. The divine plan operates entirely on the grace principle: all blessing flows through the pipeline of divine justice to the righteousness of God as a real imputation to the prepared recipient.

section: The Grace Pipeline and the Imputation System
text: The Grace Pipeline and the Imputation System

section: The Grace Pipeline and the Imputation System
text: No one ever receives blessing from God for being good. No one ever receives blessing from God for giving, for working, for witnessing, for prayer — when any of these is performed as a means of gaining divine favor. This is not a peripheral point; it is the organizing axis of the Epistle to the Romans. All blessing from God flows through the pipeline of divine justice to divine righteousness. The justice of God is on one end, the righteousness of God on the other. The pipeline is broken by no human performance and activated by no human merit.

section: The Grace Pipeline and the Imputation System
text: The imputation system operates as follows. At physical birth, Adam's sin and a sin nature are imputed to the human race — two real imputations that bring condemnation. At the new birth (salvation), there is one judicial imputation — the imputation of divine righteousness — which provides the target or home for all subsequent blessing. At maturity, a real imputation of divine blessing occurs to the prepared home of imputed righteousness. In eternity, blessing is imputed to the resurrection body, which is the divinely prepared home for eternal blessing. Two judicial imputations were required to establish the basis: sins imputed to Christ on the cross, and divine righteousness imputed to the believer at salvation. Without both of these, no real imputation of blessing is possible.

section: The Grace Pipeline and the Imputation System
text: Human good, in all its forms, is a distraction from the only mechanism that actually advances the believer toward blessing: the daily intake of Bible doctrine. Church attendance performed as an endurance exercise rather than as learning is human good. Prayer offered as a transaction with God — I will do this if you will bless me — is human good. Tithing performed to earn favor is human good. Even evangelism conducted in the energy of the flesh without the filling of the Spirit is human good. God cannot compromise His attributes to accommodate human good transactions. The divine character requires that blessing flow through its appointed channel.

section: The Result: You Shall Live
text: The Result: You Shall Live

section: The Result: You Shall Live
text: The apodosis of the conditional clause is the future middle indicative of zaō (ζάω), to live. The future tense is a progressive future, denoting advance in future time — specifically, the advance to maturity. The middle voice is a direct middle: the believer acts in a way that brings the results of the action back to himself, namely, the blessing from the justice of God and the glorification of Jesus Christ. The indicative mood is declarative — a statement of fact. You shall live means: you shall live the life that God has designed for the royal family of God — the new life of phase two, the life which is being unfolded throughout Romans 8.

section: The Result: You Shall Live
text: The entire verse in corrected translation: Indeed, if you live under the authority of the old sin nature — you are destined to die. But if by means of the Spirit you recognize as dead — condemned to death — the actions from the body, human good, you shall live — that is, live the life that God has designed for you.

section: III. The First Result of Maturity Adjustment — Romans 8:14
text: III. The First Result of Maturity Adjustment — Romans 8:14

section: Grammatical Analysis of Verse 14
text: Grammatical Analysis of Verse 14

section: Grammatical Analysis of Verse 14
text: Verse 14 opens with the postpositive conjunctive particle gar (γάρ), expressing cause or reason — connecting the result of maturity to the promise of verse 13b.

section: Grammatical Analysis of Verse 14
text: The subject is formed by the nominative plural of the correlative adjective hosos (ὅσος), as many as — referring to those believers who have attained maturity through the filling of the Spirit and maximum intake of doctrine.

section: Grammatical Analysis of Verse 14
text: The main verb is the present passive indicative of agō (ἄγω), to be led. The present tense is a retroactive progressive present — what was begun in the past continues into the present. The mature believer is continuously guided. The passive voice indicates that the mature believer receives the action of the verb — divine guidance is something received, not achieved. The indicative mood is declarative: a dogmatic statement of fact. The means is the instrumental of means from pneuma (πνεῦμα), followed by the descriptive genitive singular theou (θεοῦ), of God. For as many as are being led by the Spirit of God — these are sons of God.

section: The Doctrine of Divine Guidance
text: The Doctrine of Divine Guidance

section: The Doctrine of Divine Guidance
text: Divine guidance is the doctrine of determining the will of God for one's life — on specific matters, general matters, and the overall modus vivendi of the Christian life. Divine guidance is the communication of God's will through God's revelation. In the present dispensation, divine revelation is limited to the Word of God. The canon of Scripture contains everything relevant to divine guidance. There are no voices, no angelic instruction, no subjective impressions that supplement the Word.

section: The Doctrine of Divine Guidance
text: Divine discipline as a guidance mechanism is limited to a negative function. Warning discipline and intensive discipline can alert the reversionist that he is on the wrong road. But this is a painful and inefficient guidance system. Before the will of God can be known positively, the believer must recover from reversionism through rebound and resume the intake of doctrine. The only reliable positive guidance system is Bible doctrine resident in the soul.

section: Three Categories of the Will of God
text: Three Categories of the Will of God

section: Three Categories of the Will of God
text: The will of God operates in three historically recognized categories, each of which must be understood in relation to the justice of God.

section: Three Categories of the Will of God
text: First, the sovereign will of God. God's will must be consistent with His attributes and His personality. God is a person — self-conscious and self-determining. He thinks, decides, and acts rationally, forming policy in keeping with His character. The sovereignty of God is manifest in the decrees of God. The decree of God encompasses all that will ever occur, in its precise manner and order, to the exclusion of the alternatives that could have occurred. The decrees are God's immutable will regarding the future — the eternal plan by which God has rendered all things certain. They express the will of God by which all things are brought into being and controlled for His glory and pleasure.

section: Three Categories of the Will of God
text: The divine decrees exist in two categories of action. Those things intrinsic to the Godhead — the immanent actions of God within Himself. And those things extrinsic to God — transient actions that fulfill the functions of human history with divine justice as the constant point of reference. God did not decree Himself into existence. The decrees logically presuppose the eternal existence of God. The decrees are efficacious — they determine all that ever was or will be — used here in the technical sense, referring to the direct work of God as distinct from that which God merely permits.

section: Three Categories of the Will of God
text: A critical distinction must be maintained between the decrees of God in eternity past and the actions of God in time. The actions of God in time are the execution of the eternal decrees — they logically follow the decrees but are not identical with them. Additionally, what could have happened must be distinguished from what does happen. God's omniscience knows every alternative of every event, thought, and action in all of human history — the sum total of all possibilities. This is the domain of omniscience proper. Foreknowledge, by contrast, is a technical term referring only to what actually occurs. The laws of God are completely revealed in Scripture; the decrees of God are only partially revealed. The laws of God can be violated by human volition; the decrees of God cannot be broken or frustrated by human volition, angelic volition, or any subsequent act of God.

section: Three Categories of the Will of God
text: The foreknowledge of God does not make things certain. Foreknowledge perceives what is already certain — what has already been fixed by the divine decrees. The decrees originate from the sovereign will of God, not from His foreknowledge. Foreknowledge records for history what the decrees have established. Omniscience knows all the alternatives — what would have happened if any variable in history had been different. Foreknowledge deals only with what actually happens.

section: Three Categories of the Will of God
text: Second, the determinative will of God. God has permitted non-meritorious human volition to bring the believer either to the place of blessing through maturity or to the place of discipline through reversionism. The outcome is not mechanically imposed but flows through the believer's own volitional choices in relation to doctrine.

section: Three Categories of the Will of God
text: Third, the permissive will of God. Negative volition toward doctrine is permitted. Divine justice then provides painful discipline. Fourth, the preventative will of God. God provides doctrine, establishment laws, and discipline to keep human volition within the boundaries of His will.

section: Three Categories of the Will of God
text: All four principles together — directive, determinative, permissive, preventative — constitute the complete doctrine of the will of God as it relates to divine guidance. The exposition of verse 14 continues in the following chapter with the identification of the mature believer as a son of God and the full development of the guidance system.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred One
text: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred One

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred One
text: 1. The two alternatives of the Christian way of life are defined in this verse: either the sin unto death through reversionism and malajustment to the justice of God, or divine blessing through maturity adjustment to the justice of God. There is no third option.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred One
text: 2. The sin unto death is the antithesis of dying grace: it is painful, miserable, and represents the maximum expression of divine discipline. It does not result in loss of salvation, but it is the worst possible mode of departure from time into eternity for a believer.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred One
text: 3. The positive option requires the filling of the Holy Spirit and the daily intake of Bible doctrine: the present active indicative of thanatoo (θανατόω) is a retroactive progressive present, indicating that the recognition of human good as dead must begin at salvation and continue throughout the believer's life.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred One
text: 4. Human good is the greatest distraction from the Christian way of life: it is attractive, respectable, and masquerades as genuine spiritual production. The tree of the knowledge of good and evil presents the same danger in the Church Age as it did in the garden.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred One
text: 5. Both human good and legitimate good accomplished in the flesh are excluded from the blessing pipeline: no one is ever blessed by God for prayer, witnessing, service, giving, or any other performance when these are done as means of gaining divine favor. Blessing comes exclusively through doctrine resident in the soul and the resultant capacity for life.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred One
text: 6. All blessing from God is a real imputation through the pipeline of divine justice to divine righteousness: two judicial imputations at the cross and at salvation establish the necessary targets; real imputations of blessing then occur at maturity in time and at resurrection in eternity. God cannot compromise His attributes to accommodate human-good transactions.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred One
text: 7. The result of recognizing human good as dead is expressed in the progressive future of zaō (ζάω) — you shall live: this is the life of the royal family of God in phase two, advancing to maturity and glorifying Jesus Christ through the reception of divine blessing.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred One
text: 8. Divine guidance, the first identified result of maturity in verse 14, is not communicated through subjective impressions or supernatural voices: it is communicated exclusively through the Word of God. The foreknowledge of God perceives what the decrees have established; the believer learns the will of God only through the consistent daily intake of Bible doctrine.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred One
text: 9. The omniscience of God knows all alternatives — what could have happened under every possible variation of every decision: foreknowledge, by contrast, is a technical term referring only to what actually occurs. The decrees originate from the sovereign will of God, not from His foreknowledge, and cannot be frustrated by any human or angelic volition.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred One
text: 10. The mature believer is guided continuously — the retroactive progressive present of agō (ἄγω) indicates ongoing reception of guidance: this guidance is received, not achieved. It operates through the Spirit of God applying doctrine already resident in the soul, not through external signs, impressions, or circumstances interpreted apart from the Word.

Chapter Three Hundred Two

section: Romans 8:14 — Divine Guidance, the Three Wills in History, and the Decrees of God
text: Romans 8:14 — Divine Guidance, the Three Wills in History, and the Decrees of God

section: Romans 8:14 — Divine Guidance, the Three Wills in History, and the Decrees of God
text: Romans 8:14 “For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God.” (ESV)

section: Romans 8:14 — Divine Guidance, the Three Wills in History, and the Decrees of God
text: Corrected translation: For as many as are being led by the Spirit of God, these are sons of God.

section: Romans 8:14 — Divine Guidance, the Three Wills in History, and the Decrees of God
text: Romans 8:14 stands at the intersection of two major theological streams in this epistle: the doctrine of the indwelling and leading ministry of the Holy Spirit, and the broader framework of the adjustment to the justice of God. The phrase 'led by the Spirit of God' introduces the doctrine of divine guidance, which is the subject of this chapter. The present tense of the participle indicates a continuous pattern of life characteristic of the spiritually mature believer, whose advance through the grace pipeline has produced capacity and alignment with the will of God.

section: I. Divine Guidance — Definition and Scope
text: I. Divine Guidance — Definition and Scope

section: I. Divine Guidance — Definition and Scope
text: Divine guidance is the Bible doctrine dealing with the determination of the will of God for the believer's life. It encompasses not only the knowledge and execution of God's will but also the communication of that will. In the present dispensation — the Church Age — God communicates His will exclusively through the canon of Scripture. There are no supplementary channels: no audible voices, no impressions, no unusual physical sensations, no providential omens. The royal family of God occupies a unique category among all dispensational expressions of the family of God, and the mode of divine communication is correspondingly unique.

section: I. Divine Guidance — Definition and Scope
text: Divine discipline and logistical reverses may function as secondary indicators that something has gone wrong — that the believer has departed from the Word — but these are undesirable forms of guidance, analogous to the bit and bridle of a horse rather than the rational response of a mature person to doctrine already resident in the soul. They are always calls to return to the Word, never substitutes for it.

section: I. Divine Guidance — Definition and Scope
text: The implication of the passage is significant: while all believers are subject to divine will and receive some measure of guidance, the continuous leading of the Spirit described in verse 14 belongs specifically to the mature believer. Maturity — the product of sustained doctrine intake through the Grace Apparatus for Perception — produces the capacity to know, discern, and execute the will of God as a matter of reflexive response rather than anxious inquiry.

section: II. The Justice of God as the Point of Reference
text: II. The Justice of God as the Point of Reference

section: II. The Justice of God as the Point of Reference
text: Before examining the three categories of will in history, it is necessary to recall the framework within which divine guidance operates. All blessing from God flows through His justice, not through His love or sovereignty considered in isolation. The justice of God is the believer's point of reference. This was established at the very beginning of human existence through the doctrine of imputation.

section: A. Real Imputation at Physical Birth
text: A. Real Imputation at Physical Birth

section: A. Real Imputation at Physical Birth
text: Two imputations occur simultaneously at physical birth. First, God imputes human life to the soul — a real imputation, because the soul is the divinely created antecedent home for human life, carrying the necessary affinity. Second, Adam's original sin is imputed to the genetically formed old sin nature. This is also a real imputation: Adam's original sin is the origin of the old sin nature, and the affinity is therefore present. The result is physical life and spiritual death simultaneously.

section: A. Real Imputation at Physical Birth
text: The critical theological point is this: no member of the human race is spiritually dead because of personal sins. Every human being is spiritually dead at birth solely because of Adam's original sin. Personal sins have never been imputed to the individual for condemnation and never will be. The divine wisdom here is exact: by restricting condemnation to one sin — Adam's — all personal sins were made available for imputation to Christ on the cross. This is the precondition for judicial imputation.

section: B. Judicial Imputation at the Cross
text: B. Judicial Imputation at the Cross

section: B. Judicial Imputation at the Cross
text: The first judicial imputation occurred at the cross, when all personal sins of the human race were imputed to Christ and judged. This imputation was judicial rather than real: there was no antecedent home, no affinity. The sins were not Christ's own; He was judged as a substitute. The justice of God was satisfied in this act, opening the way for the second judicial imputation.

section: C. Judicial Imputation at Salvation
text: C. Judicial Imputation at Salvation

section: C. Judicial Imputation at Salvation
text: The second judicial imputation occurs at the moment of saving faith. The righteousness of God — divine integrity itself — is imputed to the believer. Again, there is no antecedent home and no affinity; this is pure grace. The believer does not earn or deserve this imputation. Yet the result is decisive: the believer now carries divine righteousness as the permanent target for all subsequent blessing.

section: C. Judicial Imputation at Salvation
text: Simultaneously, eternal life is imputed to its home — regeneration — in a real imputation. The believer therefore possesses both divine righteousness and eternal life as the foundation for all future grace provision.

section: D. The Grace Pipeline
text: D. The Grace Pipeline

section: D. The Grace Pipeline
text: The justice of God stands at one end of the grace pipeline; the righteousness of God carried by the believer stands at the other. All divine blessing in time is imputed from the justice of God to the believer's divine righteousness. This is the only mechanism by which God can bless without compromising any of His attributes. God cannot bless the believer directly through merit, works, morality, self-sacrifice, or human good — not because these things are necessarily sinful, but because they have no affinity with the justice of God as a source of blessing.

section: D. The Grace Pipeline
text: Before the justice of God will impute the six categories of blessing in time (the content of the believer's supergrace paragraph), there must be capacity. Capacity is maximum Bible doctrine resident in the soul. Without it, the blessings themselves become a source of misery: wealth without capacity, promotion without capacity, prosperity without capacity — each produces a corresponding degree of misery. Capacity must precede the imputation of blessing.

section: D. The Grace Pipeline
text: Logistical grace — housing, clothing, transportation, physical sustenance — is not to be confused with blessing in time. It is the provision God makes for the believer's continued existence and function, available to mature and immature alike. The six categories of supergrace blessing are distinct from logistical grace and are imputed only when capacity has been established through the maturity adjustment to the justice of God. These categories will be examined in detail beginning at Romans 8:28–32.

section: III. The Three Wills in History
text: III. The Three Wills in History

section: III. The Three Wills in History
text: Divine guidance must be understood within the framework of the three categories of will that coexist in human history. Each category has its own character and authority. Confusion among them is the source of most theological error regarding the will of God.

section: A. The First Will: The Sovereign Will of God — The Decrees
text: A. The First Will: The Sovereign Will of God — The Decrees

section: A. The First Will: The Sovereign Will of God — The Decrees
text: The will of God is rooted in His decrees. The decree of God is His eternal, holy, wise, and sovereign purpose, comprehending at once all things that ever were, are, or will be — in their courses, conditions, successions, and relations — and determining their certain future. Several defining characteristics must be noted.

section: A. The First Will: The Sovereign Will of God — The Decrees
text: First, there is one all-inclusive will and purpose of God concerning all that ever was or will be. This will and purpose originates entirely within Himself. God did not receive counsel from His creatures. No member of the human race or the angelic order advised or informed the divine plan. The will and plan of God were objectively designed for His own glory, His own pleasure, and His own satisfaction.

section: A. The First Will: The Sovereign Will of God — The Decrees
text: Second, the decrees of God are eternal and immutable. They concern the future existence of events in time and the precise order of their occurrence. All events of history — past, present, and future — are rendered certain by the divine decrees. Historical occurrence is the execution of what was already settled in eternity past. The execution is not the decree itself, but logically follows from it.

section: A. The First Will: The Sovereign Will of God — The Decrees
text: Third, the decrees of God are efficacious in the technical sense: they constitute the direct action of God, as distinguished from the permissive will of God, which is the will of God accomplished through the free will and action of His creatures. A believer who chooses to attend a Bible class exercises the permissive will of God. A believer who is brought back through divine discipline exercises the overruling will of God. All three modes — efficacious, permissive, and overruling — fall within the single comprehensive decree.

section: A. The First Will: The Sovereign Will of God — The Decrees
text: Fourth, the decrees are to be distinguished from the laws of God. The laws of God regulate human conduct and are fully revealed in Scripture; they can be broken by human volition. The decrees of God cannot be frustrated or broken by human or angelic volition. If they could be, Satan would long ago have overthrown the divine plan.

section: A. The First Will: The Sovereign Will of God — The Decrees
text: Fifth, a further distinction must be observed between the decrees of God and the foreknowledge of God — a distinction of critical importance for the passage that follows later in Romans 8 ('whom He foreknew He also predestined'). The omniscience of God is the source of the decrees. Foreknowledge is not a separate or superior faculty; it is a subset of omniscience that perceives what is certain. The decrees make all things certain; foreknowledge merely confirms what the decrees have established. In the logical order of eternity past, the decree precedes the foreknowledge. God did not foreknow a contingent future and then decree it; He decreed it from His own omniscience, and foreknowledge reflects that certainty.

section: A. The First Will: The Sovereign Will of God — The Decrees
text: Sixth, a distinction must be made between the decrees of God and the desires of God. These are not identical. Sin, spiritual death, suffering, good and evil as the policy of the old sin nature, and reversionism are not the desires of God. This was already revealed in the garden: God prohibited the tree of the knowledge of good and evil not because its fruit was morally evil in itself, but because good and evil as categories of self-determination were not what the human being needed. The prohibition was absolute: 'You do not need to know good. You do not need to know evil.' Self-righteousness — the attempt to stand before God on the basis of one's own goodness — is therefore not merely inadequate; it is a direct violation of the divine prohibition that goes back to the original divine instruction to the human race.

section: A. The First Will: The Sovereign Will of God — The Decrees
text: Nevertheless, sin, good and evil, suffering, and death are all in the decrees. They exist in human history not because God desires them but because the omniscience of God knew they would exist, and they were therefore incorporated into the decree. The decrees are reality-inclusive; the desires of God are His perfect will. The decrees do not contradict the desires; they encompass the full range of what actually occurs, including those things that fall short of the divine desire.

section: A. The First Will: The Sovereign Will of God — The Decrees
text: The practical consequence for divine guidance is this: the goal is not merely to be inside the decree — everything that happens is inside the decree — but to be aligned with the desires of God. Divine guidance, in its fullest expression, is the convergence of human volition with the perfect desires of God. This is what the mature believer achieves through sustained doctrine intake.

section: A. The First Will: The Sovereign Will of God — The Decrees
text: Additional characteristics of the will of God as expressed in the decrees: God is perfect, therefore His will is perfect. Since nothing can occur unknown to God, His will is unchangeable and certain. God does not gain knowledge over time. What He knows at any given moment He has always known — from before the creation of time itself. Every event of the believer's life, including the specific blessings of the supergrace paragraph, was known and settled in eternity past. God is bound by His own justice, truth, and faithfulness to complete what He has begun in the believer. The principle of the divine will, therefore, is grace: the policy of the justice of God in blessing the believer who has capacity.

section: A. The First Will: The Sovereign Will of God — The Decrees
text: The divine objective expressed in the decrees is the preservation and deliverance of believers, bringing them to the point of glorifying God — which is accomplished not by what believers do for God, but by what God does for believers when He imputes the six categories of supergrace blessing. God is glorified by what He does, not by what we do.

section: B. The Second and Third Wills: Angelic and Human Volition
text: B. The Second and Third Wills: Angelic and Human Volition

section: B. The Second and Third Wills: Angelic and Human Volition
text: The second and third categories of will in history are the free wills of angelic and human creatures. It is the pleasure of God to permit creature volition in both categories. These two wills form the arena of conflict and choice within which the decrees of God unfold. They are real wills, capable of genuine choice — including choices that violate the desires of God, though never the ultimate purposes of the decrees. The full exposition of these categories will be developed in the continuation of this study.

section: IV. The Will of God and the Believer's Daily Life
text: IV. The Will of God and the Believer's Daily Life

section: IV. The Will of God and the Believer's Daily Life
text: A practical implication of the doctrine emerges from the foregoing analysis. The mature believer does not approach every situation with a formal act of inquiry or petition. The will of God, once resident in the soul through maximum doctrine intake, becomes the operating reflex of the spiritually mature person. There are areas of life — beginning with the daily intake of Bible doctrine — where no deliberation is required, because the principle is already settled. There are other areas where discernment is needed, and that discernment comes not from impressions or emotions but from the application of resident doctrine.

section: IV. The Will of God and the Believer's Daily Life
text: Prayer has its proper place, but it is not a substitute for doctrine. Many questions that believers attempt to resolve through prayer are questions that doctrine has already answered. The habit of replacing doctrine with prayer reflects a deficit of resident truth, not a surplus of piety. Maturity closes that deficit and replaces anxious inquiry with the stable, reflexive application of the Word of God.

section: IV. The Will of God and the Believer's Daily Life
text: Rebound — the naming of known sins to God (1 John 1:9) — is distinct from emotional self-flagellation. God is not satisfied by tears, promises of improvement, or expressions of remorse. He is satisfied by the act for which judicial imputation at the cross has already provided the basis: the naming of the sin, which is a simple act of acknowledgment that the sin has already been judged in Christ. Anything added to that act — vows, penance, emotional demonstrations — reflects a misunderstanding of the justice of God and, practically, tends to perpetuate the very pattern of reversionism it claims to address.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Two
text: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Two

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Two
text: 1. Divine guidance is exclusively doctrinal in the Church Age. God communicates His will through the canon of Scripture alone. No supplementary channels — impressions, voices, signs, or emotional states — constitute legitimate guidance for members of the royal family of God.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Two
text: 2. The justice of God is the believer's point of reference, not the love of God. All blessing flows from the justice of God through the grace pipeline to the righteousness of God carried by the believer. This is the only mechanism by which God can bless without compromising His attributes.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Two
text: 3. Condemnation precedes blessing in the order of the justice of God. No member of the human race is condemned for personal sins; all are condemned solely through the real imputation of Adam's original sin to the genetically formed old sin nature. This singular act of condemnation made possible the imputation of all personal sins to Christ at the cross.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Two
text: 4. Two judicial imputations together produce the real imputation of blessing. The first judicial imputation — sins to Christ at the cross — satisfied divine justice. The second — divine righteousness to the believer at salvation — established the target for all subsequent blessing in time and eternity.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Two
text: 5. Capacity must precede the imputation of supergrace blessing. The justice of God will not impute the six categories of blessing to the believer's divine righteousness until capacity has been established through maximum doctrine intake. Blessing without capacity produces misery, not gratitude or growth.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Two
text: 6. The decree of God and the foreknowledge of God are not equivalent. Foreknowledge is a subset of omniscience that perceives what the decrees have made certain. The decree precedes the foreknowledge in the logical order of eternity past. Foreknowledge makes nothing certain; it confirms what the decrees have already established.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Two
text: 7. The decrees of God and the desires of God must be distinguished. Sin, suffering, good and evil, and death are in the decrees — God knew they would occur and incorporated them into His eternal plan — but they are not His desires. Divine guidance aims at convergence with the desires of God, not merely existence within the decrees.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Two
text: 8. Good and evil as a system of self-determination violates the original divine prohibition. From the beginning, God prohibited the human race from adopting good and evil as their operating framework. Self-righteousness — the attempt to stand before God on the basis of one's own goodness — is therefore not a marginal defect but a direct violation of the first divine instruction to the human race.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Two
text: 9. The mature believer operates by doctrinal reflex, not anxious inquiry. Maximum doctrine resident in the soul transforms the will of God from an external standard to be consulted into an internal operating principle. This is the fullest expression of being led by the Spirit of God.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Two
text: 10. God is glorified by what He does for the believer, not by what the believer does for God. The imputation of the six categories of supergrace blessing to the believer's divine righteousness is the mechanism of divine glorification in time. Works, morality, and human good cannot glorify God because they have no affinity with the justice of God as a source of blessing.

Chapter Three Hundred Three

section: Romans 8:14 — Divine Guidance: The Will of God, Decrees, and Volition
text: Romans 8:14 — Divine Guidance: The Will of God, Decrees, and Volition

section: Romans 8:14 — Divine Guidance: The Will of God, Decrees, and Volition
text: Romans 8:14 “For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God.” (ESV)

section: Romans 8:14 — Divine Guidance: The Will of God, Decrees, and Volition
text: Corrected translation: For as many as are being led by the Spirit of God, these are sons of God.

section: Romans 8:14 — Divine Guidance: The Will of God, Decrees, and Volition
text: Romans 8:14 introduces the principle of divine guidance as the operational expression of the believer's sonship. The present chapter continues an extended study of that principle, focusing on the nature of the divine will — its three categories, its relation to the divine decrees, and its distinction from the divine desires. Understanding these categories is foundational to any correct account of how the believer is guided by God rather than by emotion, personality, or circumstance.

section: I. The Decree of God: Review and Foundation
text: I. The Decree of God: Review and Foundation

section: I. The Decree of God: Review and Foundation
text: The doctrine of divine guidance cannot be correctly understood apart from the doctrine of the decree of God. The decree provides the framework within which all categories of will — divine and creaturely — are defined and distinguished.

section: A. Definition and Characteristics of the Divine Decree
text: A. Definition and Characteristics of the Divine Decree

section: A. Definition and Characteristics of the Divine Decree
text: The decree of God is His eternal, holy, wise, and sovereign purpose, comprehending at once all things that ever were, are, or will be — in their courses, conditions, successions, and relations — and determining their certain future. The several contents of this one eternal purpose are, because of the limitations of creaturely mentality, necessarily perceived by us in partial aspects and in both logical and revealed relations.

section: A. Definition and Characteristics of the Divine Decree
text: The decrees of God are His eternal and immutable will regarding the future existence of events that occur in time and in the precise manner and order of their occurrence. The decrees therefore express the eternal plan and will of God by which He has rendered certain all events of history — past, present, and future. The will of God is the sovereign choice of the divine mentality, inherent in the essence of God, by which all things are brought into being, controlled, and made subject to His pleasure and to His glorification.

section: A. Definition and Characteristics of the Divine Decree
text: It is the pleasure of God to permit creaturely volition in both angelic and human beings. This permission forms the basis for the two remaining categories of volition in history beyond the divine will itself.

section: B. The One Will and Purpose of God
text: B. The One Will and Purpose of God

section: B. The One Will and Purpose of God
text: There is one all-inclusive will and purpose of God concerning all that ever was, is, or will be. This will and purpose originates entirely within the being of God, for there never was a time when God did not exist and there never will be a time when He will not exist. Therefore the plan and will of God were objectively designed for His glory, His pleasure, and His satisfaction. This constitutes the purpose and meaning of creaturely existence. That purpose is achieved not through works or human production but exclusively through the intake of Bible doctrine under the filling of the Holy Spirit.

section: B. The One Will and Purpose of God
text: All creatures have been placed into space and time, and all events related to space and time were simultaneously decreed. These simultaneous decrees of God result in divine action — not human action. Human action is of no ultimate consequence in the plan of God; divine action is of total consequence.

section: C. Two Categories of Divine Action
text: C. Two Categories of Divine Action

section: C. Two Categories of Divine Action
text: Divine action falls into two categories. The first is action within the Godhead: actions that are immanent, intrinsic, and subjective, relating to the members of the Trinity. Divine love in its strict theological sense belongs here. In its absolute sense, divine love is perfect and therefore can only have a perfect object — the other members of the Godhead. The Father loves the Son, the Son loves the Spirit, and so forth. There is also a subjective dimension in which God loves His own integrity. The believer comes within the scope of divine love only because, at salvation, the judicial imputation of divine righteousness gives the believer a portion of divine integrity as the target for blessing.

section: C. Two Categories of Divine Action
text: The second category is action related to creation: divine actions that are extrinsic, outside the Godhead. These include the cognizance of angelic and human volition in eternity past; the transient function of human history chronologically; and the objective function of divine justice.

section: C. Two Categories of Divine Action
text: A critical point: God did not decree Himself into existence. God pre-exists eternally and infinitely pre-exists the divine decrees. This is the most basic statement about divine self-existence and must never be confused with the decrees themselves.

section: D. Efficacious, Permissive, and Overruling Will
text: D. Efficacious, Permissive, and Overruling Will

section: D. Efficacious, Permissive, and Overruling Will
text: The decrees of God are efficacious — they determine all that ever was, is, or will be. The term efficacious is used here in its technical sense: that which is the direct work of God, as distinguished from the permissive will of God, which is accomplished through the free will and action of creatures. Within the will of God there are three categories: directive, permissive, and overruling.

section: D. Efficacious, Permissive, and Overruling Will
text: A distinction must also be made between the decree of God in eternity past and the action of God in time. The action of God in time is the execution of the decree; the execution is not the decree itself but logically follows from it. A further distinction separates God's decrees from God's laws. Decrees are the action and plan of God, while laws regulate human conduct. The laws of God are completely revealed in Scripture; the decrees of God are only partially revealed. The laws of God can be broken by human volition; the decrees of God cannot be broken or frustrated by human volition.

section: E. Omniscience, Foreknowledge, and the Source of the Decrees
text: E. Omniscience, Foreknowledge, and the Source of the Decrees

section: E. Omniscience, Foreknowledge, and the Source of the Decrees
text: The decrees of God do not originate from His foreknowledge. A critical distinction must be maintained between foreknowledge and omniscience. Omniscience is the total wisdom of God — God has always known everything that ever would exist in all its alternatives. Foreknowledge is a subdivision of omniscience, not its equivalent.

section: E. Omniscience, Foreknowledge, and the Source of the Decrees
text: In the logical order of function, the foreknowledge of God makes absolutely nothing certain. Foreknowledge merely perceives what is already certain; it does not establish certainty. The decrees of God make everything certain. The decrees come from omniscience, not from foreknowledge. This distinction is essential for the correct exegesis of Romans 8:29, which reads, οὓς προέγνω καὶ προώρισεν (hous proegnō kai proōrisen), 'whom He foreknew He also predestinated.' This verse has been widely misinterpreted to make foreknowledge the basis of predestination. It does not teach that. Foreknowledge recognizes what is in the decrees; omniscience is the source of the decrees themselves. All things depend on God's will, and nothing is certain apart from God's will.

section: II. The Distinction Between the Decrees and the Desires of God
text: II. The Distinction Between the Decrees and the Desires of God

section: II. The Distinction Between the Decrees and the Desires of God
text: One of the most significant distinctions in the correct understanding of divine guidance is the difference between the decrees of God and the desires of God. These two categories are not identical, and confusing them produces serious theological error.

section: II. The Distinction Between the Decrees and the Desires of God
text: Sin, suffering, death, good, and evil are not the desires of God, but they are decreed. The eating of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil in the garden of Eden provides the clearest illustration: it was decreed that there would be sin, but sin was not desired by God. It was decreed that there would be spiritual death, but spiritual death was not desired by God.

section: II. The Distinction Between the Decrees and the Desires of God
text: God desires only His perfect will. Both angels and men use their God-given free wills to violate the desires of God. God said, in effect: I do not desire you to eat of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. You do not need a knowledge of good and evil. You are perfect persons in perfect environment under a perfect age; I have provided everything for you from My love. And yet both Adam and the woman proceeded to partake of the forbidden fruit. The tree therefore illustrates perfectly the difference between divine desire and divine decree.

section: II. The Distinction Between the Decrees and the Desires of God
text: As born-again believers, our objective is to follow the desires of God — that is, the directive will — rather than to fall into the category of those things that are merely in the decrees by reason of creaturely failure. This distinction is especially critical with respect to human good: the most pervasive damage in Christianity is accomplished not by outright evil but by sincere practitioners of human good who substitute works, sentiment, and morality for the intake of doctrine.

section: II. The Distinction Between the Decrees and the Desires of God
text: God does not desire to cast creatures into the lake of fire, but it is decreed for all who reject Christ as Savior. God does not desire to discipline believers, but divine discipline is decreed for all believers who persist in reversionism and carnality. These are further instances of the difference between divine decree and divine desire.

section: III. Characteristics of the Will of God
text: III. Characteristics of the Will of God

section: III. Characteristics of the Will of God
text: Having established the distinction between decrees and desires, the characteristics of the will of God may be enumerated as follows.

section: III. Characteristics of the Will of God
text: The will of God is all-comprehensive: not the slightest uncertainty could exist as to even the smallest event without confusion to all. All events of history are interwoven and interdependent. The will of God is eternal: God has always known what He knows at any given time; there was never a time when He did not know. The will of God is absolutely perfect: a perfect person can only possess a perfect will. Since nothing can occur unknown to God in eternity past, His will is unchangeable and certain.

section: III. Characteristics of the Will of God
text: The free will of God — divine sovereignty — as reflected in the decrees will be absolutely complemented with regard to His creatures. The attainment of spiritual maturity constitutes the complete complementing of the will of God for the individual believer's life — the execution, within the limitations of a fallen nature and a fallen world, of exactly what God desires.

section: III. Characteristics of the Will of God
text: God is bound by His justice, His truth, and His infinite faithfulness to complete what He has begun. Salvation is not the completion; it is the beginning. God intends for every believer to advance to maturity. His infinite faithfulness sustains the believer in time and provides the conditions necessary to complete what was begun at the moment of faith in Christ.

section: IV. Judicial and Real Imputations: Completion and Blessing
text: IV. Judicial and Real Imputations: Completion and Blessing

section: IV. Judicial and Real Imputations: Completion and Blessing
text: The faithfulness of God to complete what He has begun is illustrated by the structure of the two judicial imputations and the real imputations that follow them.

section: IV. Judicial and Real Imputations: Completion and Blessing
text: Judicial imputation number one: at the cross, all personal sins of the human race were imputed to Christ. These sins had no antecedent relationship to Christ — there was no affinity, no prior ownership. He was impeccable in His humanity. The imputation was therefore abnormal, incomplete in itself, and demanded continuation. Note that personal sin is not the issue in condemnation — condemnation rests on Adam's original sin. Neither is personal sin the issue at the moment of salvation — Christ is the issue. Personal sin is only an issue at the cross, where it was judged in the person of Christ.

section: IV. Judicial and Real Imputations: Completion and Blessing
text: Judicial imputation number two: at the moment of faith in Christ, God's righteousness — one half of divine integrity — is imputed to the believer. Again, there is no antecedent relationship and no natural affinity. This imputation also demands implementation and completion. That is why the believer continues to exist on earth after salvation: the imputed divine righteousness becomes the target for real imputations of blessing in time.

section: IV. Judicial and Real Imputations: Completion and Blessing
text: Real imputations are the completion of what judicial imputations began. When divine blessing in time is imputed to divine righteousness already resident in the believer, that is a true completion. The objective for every believer is to develop the capacity to receive those real imputations — and that capacity is produced by the maximum intake of Bible doctrine over time, which is the definition of maturity.

section: IV. Judicial and Real Imputations: Completion and Blessing
text: The security of these blessings follows from their source. Since the blessing flows from the justice of God to the righteousness of God — and the believer did nothing meritorious to receive it — the believer can do nothing to lose it. The analogy to eternal security is exact: just as salvation cannot be lost because it was never earned, the blessings imputed at maturity cannot be forfeited because the believer's performance played no role in their acquisition. David's blessings under the Bathsheba episode, and Abraham's blessings during and after the Hagar episode, both demonstrate this principle: discipline was severe and real, but not one blessing imputed through the grace pipeline was removed.

section: IV. Judicial and Real Imputations: Completion and Blessing
text: The principle of the will of God is therefore grace. Grace excludes even legitimate talent and legitimate function. God does all the work; the believer's role is to maintain the conditions — positive volition toward doctrine, filling of the Spirit, advancement toward maturity — under which God's action can be executed. The pipeline is encapsulated by divine integrity: righteousness is the principle and justice is the function. Nothing penetrates that encapsulation from the human side.

section: V. Four Defining Characteristics of the Will of God
text: V. Four Defining Characteristics of the Will of God

section: V. Four Defining Characteristics of the Will of God
text: The will of God as it relates to divine guidance may be defined by four terms: directive, determinative, permissive, and preventative.

section: A. Directive
text: A. Directive

section: A. Directive
text: The will of God is directive: God has a plan for the believer's life. God's desire is that the believer receive blessings in time that glorify Christ, and that those blessings be parlayed into blessings in eternity at the judgment seat of Christ. That is the directive will. What actually occurs in a given life is the decree — and the decree reflects what God, from omniscience in eternity past, knew the believer's free will would produce. The decrees came before the events; the events do not determine the decrees.

section: B. Determinative
text: B. Determinative

section: B. Determinative
text: The will of God is determinative: God has permitted non-meritorious volition to bring the believer to the place of blessing or the place of discipline. The believer's free will takes him to one or the other. God has structured everything for whichever direction the believer chooses.

section: B. Determinative
text: Positive volition toward doctrine leads to the fulfillment of the formula: primary potential + capacity = the reality of blessing in time. Primary potential is the judicial imputation of divine righteousness at salvation. Capacity is maximum doctrine resident in the soul — the maturity adjustment to the justice of God. The reality of blessing in time is the six categories of temporal blessing that will be examined in detail at Romans 8:32.

section: B. Determinative
text: Negative volition toward doctrine is also provided for in the structure of the determinative will: warning discipline, intensive discipline, and ultimately the sin unto death. Those in reversionism are also used instrumentally — as a testing mechanism for those who are positive toward doctrine, placing before them the choice between relationship and doctrine. The consistent biblical pattern is that the forces of opposition in any period of testing are drawn from believers in reversionism.

section: C. Permissive
text: C. Permissive

section: C. Permissive
text: The will of God is permissive: negative volition toward doctrine is permitted by God. Free will was created to be free, and God permits it to function. But divine justice always relates to that function. Adjustment to the justice of God results in blessing; maladjustment to the justice of God results in cursing. The present dispensation does not operate under the love of God as its point of reference but under the justice of God. From the moment of the fall, the justice of God has been man's point of reference — and it will remain so.

section: C. Permissive
text: The contrast between the love of God as point of reference and the justice of God as point of reference may be illustrated by the pre-fall condition. Under the love of God, two perfect persons were given perfect environment, perfect provision, and a renewable daily contract with God. The condition was one simple restriction. That condition was violated. The love of God as point of reference can provide only a day-at-a-time existence; it cannot produce eternal life. The justice of God, by contrast, can provide something greater than the garden — for a believer who cracks the maturity barrier attains a quality of blessing that exceeds what was available in the perfect environment of Eden.

section: C. Permissive
text: The mechanics of the permissive will at the three adjustment points are as follows. At salvation, rejection of Christ as Savior is maladjustment at the first point; the justice of God responds with judgment at the great white throne. For the believer, failure to adjust at rebound — the second adjustment point — by the simple naming of known sins to God (1 John 1:9) keeps the believer out of fellowship and prevents the filling of the Spirit. No tears, guilt, promises, or penance constitute rebound; only the citation of the specific sin to God. The third adjustment is the progressive intake of doctrine leading to the maturity barrier.

section: D. Preventative
text: D. Preventative

section: D. Preventative
text: The will of God is preventative: it provides doctrine, establishment laws, and divine discipline to keep human volition inside the will of God. Doctrine is the primary preventative mechanism after salvation. The old sin nature is resident in every cell of the physical body; the Holy Spirit indwells the body. As long as the believer is positive toward doctrine, the soul is controlled by doctrine. That is the great issue of the entire Christian way of life.

section: D. Preventative
text: Establishment laws function as the second preventative mechanism. Divine laws of establishment provide the freedom necessary for evangelism and the teaching of doctrine to occur. These laws operate regardless of the form of government — absolute monarchy, republic, or otherwise — as long as the government upholds the principles of authority, free enterprise, military service, and the rule of law. Establishment laws take cognizance of divinely ordered authority structures: husband over wife, parents over children, teacher over student, management over labor, senior officer over junior officer. Violations of establishment law constitute crime, and the divine establishment response to crime includes capital punishment — the forfeiture of life for murder, rape, and other capital offenses as defined in Scripture.

section: D. Preventative
text: Divine discipline is the third preventative mechanism. When the believer fails to respond to doctrine and to establishment, God's justice intervenes with discipline at the warning, intensive, and terminal levels. The preventative will of God thus operates at every level — through positive instruction, through structural law, and through corrective judgment.

section: VI. Summary: The Will of God and the Three Categories of Volition
text: VI. Summary: The Will of God and the Three Categories of Volition

section: VI. Summary: The Will of God and the Three Categories of Volition
text: The doctrine of divine guidance is grounded in the correct understanding of the will of God as expressed in the divine decrees and as distinguished from the divine desires. Three categories of volition operate in history: the sovereign will of God, the free will of angels, and the free will of man. The sovereign will of God is the foundation; the free wills of creatures operate within the space defined by the permissive will.

section: VI. Summary: The Will of God and the Three Categories of Volition
text: The divine outline of human history is the dispensations — the programming of the ages — all of which were decreed. The divine objective in each dispensation is the preservation and deliverance of believers. The work of God comprehends all events into the fulfillment of His eternal purpose — what theology has called providence. Whether a believer advances to maturity or falls into reversionism, the plan of God moves forward. But the believer who advances participates in the fullness of the blessings God desires for him; the believer in reversionism is only an instrument in the hands of the plan he has refused to embrace.

section: VI. Summary: The Will of God and the Three Categories of Volition
text: The whole point of divine guidance, then, is the execution of the divine will. The believer who does not understand the will of God will be guided by emotion, by personalities he admires, by circumstantial feelings, by spiritual pressure, or by impressions with no divine origin. Only the believer who has maximum doctrine in the soul, who understands the characteristics and categories of the divine will, and who is filled with the Spirit, is positioned to be guided by the Spirit of God in the sense intended by Romans 8:14.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Three
text: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Three

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Three
text: 1. The decree of God is the foundation of divine guidance. God's decree is His eternal, holy, wise, and sovereign purpose comprehending all things that ever were, are, or will be. All events of history are rendered certain by the decree, not by human action or creaturely volition.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Three
text: 2. Omniscience, not foreknowledge, is the source of the decrees. Foreknowledge is a subdivision of omniscience. Foreknowledge perceives what the decrees establish; it does not itself make anything certain. This distinction is essential for correctly interpreting Romans 8:29 and the doctrine of predestination.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Three
text: 3. The decrees and the desires of God are not the same. Sin, suffering, death, and human good are in the decrees but are not God's desires. The believer's objective is to follow the desires of God — which are expressed in the directive will — not merely to be carried along by what the decrees record.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Three
text: 4. Judicial imputations are incomplete and demand real imputations. The judicial imputation of sins to Christ and the judicial imputation of righteousness to the believer are both abnormal in the sense that there is no natural antecedent affinity. Both demand completion through the real imputation of blessing in time to the divine righteousness resident in the mature believer.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Three
text: 5. The security of blessing parallels the security of salvation. Since blessings in time are imputed by divine justice to divine righteousness, the believer contributes nothing to their acquisition and therefore can do nothing to forfeit them. Discipline for sin does not remove these blessings — the examples of David and Abraham demonstrate this principle.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Three
text: 6. The will of God is directive, determinative, permissive, and preventative. These four characteristics define how the divine will relates to creaturely volition. The directive will expresses God's desire for the believer; the determinative will structures the consequences of free will choices; the permissive will allows negative volition while maintaining justice; the preventative will provides doctrine, establishment laws, and discipline to keep creaturely volition within the sphere of the divine purpose.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Three
text: 7. The justice of God, not the love of God, is the present point of reference. From the moment of the fall, the justice of God has been man's point of reference. The justice of God can provide greater blessings than were available in the garden of Eden under the love of God, because the justice of God can fulfill the real imputations of blessing in time and eternity that the love of God, as a day-at-a-time provision, could never have produced.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Three
text: 8. Divine guidance is the execution of the divine will, not the response to impressions or emotion. The believer who lacks maximum doctrine will be guided by emotion, by admired personalities, by circumstantial feelings, or by spiritual pressure — not by the Spirit of God. Only the doctrine-filled believer, operating under the filling of the Spirit, can be guided in the sense of Romans 8:14.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Three
text: 9. Establishment laws are a preventative mechanism of the divine will. The divine laws of establishment — authority structures, rule of law, free enterprise, military service, capital punishment — provide the freedom necessary for evangelism and doctrine to function. Their erosion is a form of maladjustment to the justice of God at the national level.

section: Glossary
