section: Glossary
text: Definition

section: Glossary
text: Decree of God

section: Glossary
text: The eternal, holy, wise, and sovereign purpose of God comprehending at once all things that ever were, are, or will be — in their courses, conditions, successions, and relations — determining their certain future. Distinguished from the laws of God, which regulate human conduct, and from the desires of God, which express what God wants rather than what He has rendered certain.

section: Glossary
text: Omniscience

section: Glossary
text: πρόγνωσις prognōsis — foreknowledge (as a subdivision of omniscience)

section: Glossary
text: The total wisdom of God by which He has always known everything that ever would exist in all its alternatives. Distinguished from foreknowledge (prognōsis), which is a subdivision of omniscience and merely perceives what is already certain in the decrees. Omniscience is the source of the decrees; foreknowledge is not.

section: Glossary
text: Directive Will

section: Glossary
text: The first of four characteristics of the will of God. God has a plan and desire for each believer's life — the attainment of maturity, the reception of real imputations of blessing in time, and the glorification of Christ. The directive will expresses what God desires, as distinguished from what the decrees record as actually occurring.

section: Glossary
text: Determinative Will

section: Glossary
text: The second characteristic of the will of God. God has permitted non-meritorious volition to bring the believer to the place of blessing or the place of discipline. All outcomes — positive and negative — are structured and anticipated by the divine decree.

section: Glossary
text: Permissive Will

section: Glossary
text: The third characteristic of the will of God. God permits the free will of creatures to function, including negative volition toward doctrine and toward God's desires. The permissive will does not imply divine approval of the creature's choices but only that God has created free will and allows it to function within the framework of the decrees.

section: Glossary
text: Preventative Will

section: Glossary
text: The fourth characteristic of the will of God. God provides doctrine, establishment laws, and divine discipline to keep human volition within the sphere of His purpose. These three mechanisms — positive instruction, structural law, and corrective judgment — function together to preserve the conditions under which believers can advance to maturity.

section: Glossary
text: Real Imputation

section: Glossary
text: A genuine imputation in which there is natural antecedent affinity between the thing imputed and its recipient. Distinguished from judicial imputations, which have no such affinity and therefore demand completion. Blessing in time is a real imputation: it is imputed by the justice of God to the divine righteousness already resident in the mature believer, for which there is full affinity.

section: Glossary
text: Judicial Imputation

section: Glossary
text: An imputation in which there is no natural antecedent affinity between the thing imputed and its recipient. Two judicial imputations are foundational: (1) the imputation of all human sin to Christ on the cross, and (2) the imputation of divine righteousness to the believer at salvation. Both are incomplete in themselves and demand the real imputations of blessing in time and eternity as their completion.

section: Glossary
text: Adjustment to the Justice of God

section: Glossary
text: δικαιοσύνη θεοῦ dikaiosynē theou — righteousness of God

section: Glossary
text: The mechanism by which all divine blessing is received. Three categories: (1) salvation adjustment — faith in Christ; (2) rebound adjustment — naming known sins to God (1 John 1:9); (3) maturity adjustment — progressive doctrine intake leading to the cracking of the maturity barrier. Maladjustment to the justice of God results in judgment or discipline proportionate to the category of failure.

section: Glossary
text: Maturity Adjustment

section: Glossary
text: The third and progressive category of adjustment to the justice of God. Achieved through the sustained daily intake of Bible doctrine under the filling of the Holy Spirit. Culminates in the cracking of the maturity barrier and the reception of real imputations of blessing in time. The formula: primary potential (imputed righteousness) + capacity (maximum doctrine) = the reality of blessing in time.

section: Glossary
text: Anthropopathism

section: Glossary
text: ἀνθρωποπάθεια anthrōpopatheia — attribution of human emotion to God

section: Glossary
text: A figure of speech in which human characteristics — love, hate, repentance, jealousy — are attributed to God for the purpose of explaining divine policy in terms of the human frame of reference. Anthropopathisms do not describe actual divine attributes. The phrase 'God so loved the world' is an anthropopathism expressing divine policy toward a fallen world, not the attribute of divine love proper, which can only have a perfect object.

section: Glossary
text: Reversionism

section: Glossary
text: Retroactive spiritual regression — the sustained return of a believer to the thinking, values, and modus operandi of the old sin nature. Results in warning discipline, intensive discipline, and ultimately the sin unto death. Reversionist believers are also used instrumentally by God as a testing mechanism for those who are positive toward doctrine.

section: Glossary
text: Establishment Laws

section: Glossary
text: Divine laws governing the social and political structures necessary for human life to function in a fallen world. Applicable to all members of the human race regardless of spiritual status. Include the authority of government, military service, free enterprise, capital punishment, and the authority structures of family, workplace, and society. Their function is to provide the freedom within which evangelism and doctrine can operate.
Chapter Three Hundred Four

section: Romans 8:14 — Divine Guidance and the Mature Son of God
text: Romans 8:14 — Divine Guidance and the Mature Son of God

section: Romans 8:14 — Divine Guidance and the Mature Son of God
text: Romans 8:14 “For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God.” (ESV)

section: Romans 8:14 — Divine Guidance and the Mature Son of God
text: Corrected translation: For as many as are being led by the Spirit of God, these are mature sons of God.

section: Romans 8:14 — Divine Guidance and the Mature Son of God
text: Romans 8:14 continues the exposition of life in the Spirit that has dominated chapter 8 from its opening verse. The exegesis of verse 14 is now complete with respect to its grammatical structure, and the verse yields two connected affirmations: a description of those who are led by the Spirit of God, and a declaration of what they are. Both the subject and the predicate nominative carry precise theological weight that the standard translations do not fully render. This chapter works through the doctrine of divine guidance in its full scope — its axioms, its categories, its mechanics, and its ultimate objective — before returning to the verse itself to draw out its conclusion.

section: I. The Axiom of Divine Guidance (1 John 3:23)
text: I. The Axiom of Divine Guidance (1 John 3:23)

section: I. The Axiom of Divine Guidance (1 John 3:23)
text: Point three in the doctrine of divine guidance is an axiom applicable to the entire human race. The human race divides into two categories — believers and unbelievers — and the axiom addresses both.

section: I. The Axiom of Divine Guidance (1 John 3:23)
text: 1 John 3:23 “And this is his commandment, that we believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ and love one another, just as he has commanded us.” (ESV)

section: I. The Axiom of Divine Guidance (1 John 3:23)
text: Corrected translation: And this is his commandment: that we believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ, and love one another just as he has given us commandment.

section: I. The Axiom of Divine Guidance (1 John 3:23)
text: The word 'commandment' appears twice in this verse. The repetition is not accidental; it exposes the distinction between God's desire and God's decree. The divine decrees encompass all that actually occurs in history — including both those who believe and those who do not. God's desire, by contrast, is that all members of the human race believe in Christ. The decrees record the actuality; the desire expresses what God wants. Not all people believe, which is precisely why the divine decrees and the divine desire are not identical.

section: I. The Axiom of Divine Guidance (1 John 3:23)
text: For the unbeliever, then, the will of God is faith in the Lord Jesus Christ — the salvation adjustment to the justice of God. Believing in Christ is the only means of salvation. Human life was imputed to the soul at birth and is therefore permanent. Adam's original sin was imputed to the old sin nature at birth, and that imputation is the basis of universal condemnation — not personal sins. Personal sins were collected, not individually imputed to man, and were instead imputed to Christ on the cross. When a person believes in Jesus Christ, God's righteousness is imputed to carry out the subsequent plan.

section: I. The Axiom of Divine Guidance (1 John 3:23)
text: For the believer, the second commandment — 'love one another' — is explained by Romans 5:5 as the filling of the Spirit. It is not an emotional effort or a program of charitable activity. The Christian way of life is a supernatural way of life and demands supernatural execution. Anything an unbeliever can do is not the Christian way of life. The supernatural execution is the filling of the Holy Spirit, and the only way to be filled with the Spirit is to rebound when necessary.

section: I. The Axiom of Divine Guidance (1 John 3:23)
text: The axiom, therefore, reduces to two statements. For the unbeliever: believe in Christ. For the believer: be filled with the Spirit. These are the irreducible expressions of God's will for each category of the human race.

section: II. Rebound: The Mechanics of the Filling of the Spirit
text: II. Rebound: The Mechanics of the Filling of the Spirit

section: II. Rebound: The Mechanics of the Filling of the Spirit
text: The filling of the Spirit is obtained through rebound — the adjustment to the justice of God by which fellowship with God is restored. The mechanics of rebound are straightforward: the believer cites, names, or specifies known sins to God alone (1 John 1:9). Those sins were already imputed to Christ on the cross and judged there. They are not judged again. The believer is simply citing the case in the courtroom where the judgment was actually rendered.

section: II. Rebound: The Mechanics of the Filling of the Spirit
text: What must not be added to this: apology, penance, promises of future improvement, emotional expression of remorse, or any system of self-mortification. Adding any of these to the act of naming sin constitutes a form of arrogance — it inserts the believer's own merit into a transaction that was completed entirely by Christ. More seriously, it implicitly denies the sufficiency of what Christ accomplished on the cross, which is blasphemy against His finished work. The cross is the basis of rebound. Grace is the policy. Forgiveness and restoration of the filling of the Spirit are immediate and unconditional upon naming the sin.

section: II. Rebound: The Mechanics of the Filling of the Spirit
text: The filling of the Spirit is not obtained by yielding, by feeling, by giving up something, or by any experiential state. All systems of grace emanate from the justice of God. Grace is the policy of divine justice in blessing mankind. No personal sacrifice, no emotional intensity, no righteous living can produce the filling of the Spirit. Rebound alone restores it.

section: II. Rebound: The Mechanics of the Filling of the Spirit
text: Because personal sins were judged at the cross, they are not raised at the Last Judgment. The unbeliever at the Last Judgment is not condemned for personal sins — those were judged at the cross — but for the absence of imputed divine righteousness, which comes only through faith in Christ.

section: III. Three Categories of God's Will in Phase Two
text: III. Three Categories of God's Will in Phase Two

section: III. Three Categories of God's Will in Phase Two
text: Phase two is the interval between the cross and the Rapture, or between the cross and the believer's physical death — whichever occurs first. Phase one is salvation; phase three is eternity. Within phase two, the will of God for the believer operates in three categories:

section: III. Three Categories of God's Will in Phase Two
text: First, the viewpoint will of God: what does God want the believer to think? Second, the operational will of God: what does God want the believer to do? Third, the geographical will of God: where does God want the believer to be? These three categories must converge. The point at which all three intersect is the will of God for the believer's life in any given situation.

section: IV. Three Classifications of the Will of God (Numbers 22)
text: IV. Three Classifications of the Will of God (Numbers 22)

section: IV. Three Classifications of the Will of God (Numbers 22)
text: Point five in the doctrine distinguishes three classifications of divine will, most clearly illustrated by the account of Balaam in Numbers 22–23.

section: A. The Directive Will of God
text: A. The Directive Will of God

section: A. The Directive Will of God
text: Numbers 22:12 — God told Balaam directly: 'Do not go with them.' This is the directive will of God, equivalent to what God desires. It is the sovereign will of God stated as a directive command. It is what God actually wants to happen.

section: B. The Permissive Will of God
text: B. The Permissive Will of God

section: B. The Permissive Will of God
text: Numbers 22:20 — God subsequently said: 'If the men have come to call you, rise and go with them; but only do what I tell you.' This is the permissive will of God — what actually happens even when it is not God's directive will. God permits it within the framework of His decrees. The permissive will encompasses sin, human good, evil, the function of Satan as ruler of this world, and the function of the old sin nature. God does not desire these things, but He permits them.

section: C. The Overruling Will of God
text: C. The Overruling Will of God

section: C. The Overruling Will of God
text: Numbers 23:5, 8, 23, 25–26 — God would not permit Israel to be cursed. Despite Balaam's attempts, the overruling will of God intervened. This is the expression of divine sovereignty in the principle that Jesus Christ controls history. The overruling will of God supersedes both the directive and permissive will when necessary for the fulfillment of the divine decrees.

section: V. The Academic Concept of Divine Guidance
text: V. The Academic Concept of Divine Guidance

section: V. The Academic Concept of Divine Guidance
text: Point six develops the academic concept of divine guidance — the specifics God wants all believers to accomplish. Since the battleground of the angelic conflict is the soul, the primary objective is Bible doctrine resident in the soul.

section: V. The Academic Concept of Divine Guidance
text: The soul is saved. The body contains the old sin nature in every cell except the female ovum, which by means of meiosis and polar body formation is completely cleansed of the old sin nature's genetic corruption — a fact which explains the virgin birth. The indwelling of the Holy Spirit and the indwelling of Christ are in the soul. The controlling question is: who controls the soul — the old sin nature or the Holy Spirit? That battle is resolved only when doctrine becomes resident in the soul.

section: V. The Academic Concept of Divine Guidance
text: Three passages state this principle directly. Psalm 32:8: 'I will instruct you and teach you in the way which you should go; I will counsel you with my eye upon you.' Isaiah 58:11: 'The Lord will continually guide you and satisfy your soul in scorched places and give strength to your bones; you will be like a watered garden, and like a spring of water whose waters do not fail.' Proverbs 3:1–6: 'My son, do not forget my doctrine, but let your heart keep my commandments, for length of days and years of life and prosperity they will add to you... Trust in the Lord with all your heart; do not lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge Him, and He will direct your paths.'

section: V. The Academic Concept of Divine Guidance
text: Romans 12:2 anticipates the same principle: 'Stop being conformed to this age, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind' — the renewing of the mind being the daily intake of Bible doctrine — 'so that you may prove what the will of God is, namely, that which is good and well-pleasing and perfect.' The will of God is perfect. Believers are not. Therefore the will of God demands maximum doctrine intake in order to receive the one thing that glorifies God in the angelic conflict: the real imputation of blessing in time to the mature believer.

section: V. The Academic Concept of Divine Guidance
text: A second academic principle is the filling of the Spirit, referenced in Ephesians 5:14–18. The passage builds from a command to awakeness — 'Wake up, you sleeping ones' (the reversionist, those who have rejected doctrine) — through the admonition to 'walk accurately, not as unwise but as wise ones, constantly purchasing time, because the days are evil,' to its culmination: 'Stop becoming intoxicated by means of wine, which is dissipation, but be filled — be fully possessed in the soul — by means of the Spirit.'

section: V. The Academic Concept of Divine Guidance
text: A third academic principle is the combination: filling of the Holy Spirit plus the daily function of the Grace Apparatus for Perception (GAP) equals spiritual growth and eventually maturity adjustment to the justice of God. Second Peter 3:18 states it in the instrumental case: 'But grow by grace and by knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. To Him be glory both now and to the day of eternity.' The two temporal markers — 'now' and 'the day of eternity' — identify the two moments at which God is glorified above and beyond the baseline given to every believer: when the mature believer receives the real imputation of blessing in time, and when the resurrection body is received minus the old sin nature.

section: V. The Academic Concept of Divine Guidance
text: Hebrews 11:7 illustrates the ultimate result: 'By means of doctrine resident in the soul, Noah was warned about things not yet seen, and having been motivated by reverence and occupation with Christ, he constructed an ark for the deliverance of his family. Through this he condemned the world and became an heir of righteousness pertaining to doctrine.' The phrase 'heir of righteousness pertaining to doctrine' refers to the justice of God sending as a real imputation through the grace pipeline the blessings appropriate to a mature believer. The grace pipeline runs from the justice of God on one end to the righteousness of God on the other, encapsulated entirely within divine integrity. It cannot be broken by human failure, and it cannot be shortcut by human achievement.

section: VI. The Mechanics of Guidance (Acts 11)
text: VI. The Mechanics of Guidance (Acts 11)

section: VI. The Mechanics of Guidance (Acts 11)
text: Point seven identifies the specific mechanical devices by which God guides the believer, drawn from Acts 11. Seven mechanics are identified:

section: VI. The Mechanics of Guidance (Acts 11)
text: 1. Prayer (Acts 11:5) — effective only when the believer is filled with the Spirit and operating with doctrine. 2. Thinking (Acts 11:6) — reasoning from doctrine resident in the soul. 3. Divine revelation through Bible teaching and the recall of doctrine (Acts 11:7–10). 4. Providential circumstances (Acts 11:11) — the expression of Jesus Christ controlling history. 5. The Holy Spirit (Acts 11:12). 6. Christian fellowship and comparison of spiritual data (Acts 11:13–14). 7. The recalling of doctrine (Acts 11:16). Nearly every one of these mechanics depends upon either the filling of the Spirit, the intake of doctrine, or both.

section: VII. Free Will as the Basis of Divine Guidance
text: VII. Free Will as the Basis of Divine Guidance

section: VII. Free Will as the Basis of Divine Guidance
text: Point eight addresses the person of Christ as the foundation for the doctrine of free will. As the God-Man in hypostatic union, the Lord Jesus Christ possessed both divine sovereignty and human volition. The relevant passages are Matthew 20:22; 26:42; Hebrews 10:7, 9. The implication is decisive: if Christ did not have free will in His humanity, there is no free will in mankind. Without free will in mankind, there is no free will in the humanity of Christ. Without free will in the humanity of Christ, there is no genuine issue in the angelic conflict. Divine guidance is therefore predicated upon the existence of free will — a free will created by God and designed to function within His plan for the resolution of the angelic conflict.

section: VIII. The Ultimate in the Will of God: Maturity Adjustment
text: VIII. The Ultimate in the Will of God: Maturity Adjustment

section: VIII. The Ultimate in the Will of God: Maturity Adjustment
text: Point nine: the ultimate expression of the will of God for the believer is maturity adjustment to the justice of God. Second Peter 3:18 states both the means and the goal: growth by grace and by knowledge of Christ. That is the purpose for which the believer remains in phase two. Everything else relates to it as a function of the real and judicial imputations described throughout Romans.

section: VIII. The Ultimate in the Will of God: Maturity Adjustment
text: The structure of the imputations is as follows. At salvation, the justice of God imputed divine righteousness to the believer as a judicial imputation. This forms the basis and potential for all subsequent blessing. The believer carries this imputed righteousness at all times. Capacity, however, must be developed. Maximum doctrine resident in the soul produces that capacity. Primary potential (imputed divine righteousness) plus capacity (from maximum doctrine) equals the reality of blessing in time as a real imputation.

section: VIII. The Ultimate in the Will of God: Maturity Adjustment
text: A secondary potential also exists. The baptism of the Holy Spirit — positional truth — plus capacity equals the reality of encapsulated environment. This means that when the believer cracks the maturity barrier, the resulting prosperity is encapsulated so that historical circumstances — adversity or prosperity — cannot alter it. This exceeds what Adam possessed in the garden, where environment was controlled externally. The mature believer's prosperity is internal and therefore inviolable.

section: VIII. The Ultimate in the Will of God: Maturity Adjustment
text: By the argument from the greater to the lesser (a fortiori, as developed in Romans 5:17): if God provided the greater — the judicial imputation of divine righteousness at salvation — it follows a fortiori that He can provide the less, which is the real imputation of blessing in time to the mature believer. And if God can provide the real imputation of blessing in time, it follows a fortiori that He can provide the less — blessing and reward in eternity as a real imputation to the resurrection body, minus the old sin nature.

section: VIII. The Ultimate in the Will of God: Maturity Adjustment
text: God is glorified only when blessings flow through the grace pipeline — from the justice of God to the righteousness of God — with no human merit intruding. No talent, no ability, no sacrifice, no achievement — whether commanded or uncommanded — can produce or accelerate this flow. The believer never receives the credit. The glory belongs to God. This is the point of the doxology in 2 Peter 3:18: 'To Him be glory both now and to the day of eternity.'

section: VIII. The Ultimate in the Will of God: Maturity Adjustment
text: Six categories of blessing flow through this grace pipeline to the mature believer: (1) spiritual blessings — occupation with the person of Christ, capacity for life, capacity for happiness, capacity for blessing, and the ability to interpret current events in light of Scripture; (2) material blessings — wealth, promotion, success, and various forms of prosperity including social, professional, and establishment prosperity; (3) blessing by association — a mature believer connected with a company, military unit, school, marriage, or family brings blessing to that association, wholly apart from its own functional merits; (4) historical impact — the pivot of mature believers in a national entity whose adjustment sustains divine blessing on the nation; (5) undeserved suffering as a blessing — the subject of Romans 8:18–30; and (6) dying blessing.

section: VIII. The Ultimate in the Will of God: Maturity Adjustment
text: Blessing by association also explains the prosperity of the wicked. When the wicked prosper, it is because somewhere in their network of relationships they have had contact with a mature believer whose blessing radiates outward. Prosperity without capacity is not a blessing; it is a liability. But the mechanism of blessing by association is real.

section: IX. Exegesis of Romans 8:14b — 'These Are Mature Sons of God'
text: IX. Exegesis of Romans 8:14b — 'These Are Mature Sons of God'

section: IX. Exegesis of Romans 8:14b — 'These Are Mature Sons of God'
text: The second clause of verse 14 now comes into focus. The standard translations render it 'they are sons of God' or 'these are the sons of God.' Neither is precise.

section: The Demonstrative Pronoun
text: The Demonstrative Pronoun

section: The Demonstrative Pronoun
text: The subject of the clause is the nominative plural demonstrative pronoun houtos (οὗτοι). When a demonstrative pronoun is used in place of a personal pronoun, it signals special emphasis on the designated object. The correct translation is these, not they. The demonstrative restricts the reference to a specific category within the larger class of all believers — namely, the mature believer who is being led by the Holy Spirit through the application of resident doctrine.

section: The Present Active Indicative of eimi
text: The Present Active Indicative of eimi

section: The Present Active Indicative of eimi
text: The verb is the present active indicative of eimi (εἰμί), to be. The present tense here is a perfective present, denoting the continuation of existing results. It describes a fact that came to be in the past — specifically, the combination of the filling of the Holy Spirit plus the daily function of GAP that produced maturity adjustment — and is now a present, ongoing reality. The indicative mood is declarative, making a dogmatic statement of fact.

section: The Anarthrous Predicate Nominative
text: The Anarthrous Predicate Nominative

section: The Anarthrous Predicate Nominative
text: The predicate nominative is the plural of huios (υἱός), son. Critically, it appears in an anarthrous construction — there is no definite article of any kind. In Greek grammar, the absence of the definite article does not weaken the noun; it emphasizes the qualitative character of the noun. The anarthrous construction therefore highlights not merely that these are sons, but the high quality of the sonship involved. In Koine Greek and throughout the patristic literature, huios in this quality-emphasizing use denotes mature sons — sons who have grown to full development. This is in deliberate contrast to the word teknon (τέκνον), which will appear later in Romans 8 and refers to immature children. All believers are children of God by faith in Christ (teknon), but only mature believers are designated here by the anarthrous huios. The corrected translation is therefore: 'For as many as are being led by the Spirit of God, these are mature sons of God.'

section: The Contextual Implications for Romans 8:18–30
text: The Contextual Implications for Romans 8:18–30

section: The Contextual Implications for Romans 8:18–30
text: This conclusion — that verse 14b refers to the mature believer specifically — controls the interpretation of the rest of Romans 8. Verses 18 through 30 deal with undeserved suffering and its transformation into blessing. That transformation is possible only for the mature believer. Verse 28 ('all things work together for good') is not a universal promise to all believers. The qualifying phrase is 'to those who love God' — a technical term for maximum category one love, that is, occupation with the person of Christ, which characterizes maturity adjustment. Throughout verses 18–30, the frame of reference is the mature believer unless the context explicitly indicates otherwise.

section: X. Principles from Romans 8:14b
text: X. Principles from Romans 8:14b

section: X. Principles from Romans 8:14b
text: Several governing principles emerge from the completed exegesis of verse 14:

section: X. Principles from Romans 8:14b
text: 1. God guides all members of the royal family of God in this dispensation. Maximum guidance, however, is the prerogative and the blessing of the mature believer.

section: X. Principles from Romans 8:14b
text: 2. Guidance through the filling of the Spirit, making application of doctrine resident in the soul, begins when the believer is consistently positive toward doctrine. It reaches its full expression in the mature believer.

section: X. Principles from Romans 8:14b
text: 3. For the immature or carnal believer, guidance comes through divine discipline as a warning to return to Bible doctrine. The pain of discipline motivates the reversionist toward rebound and reversion recovery through positive volition.

section: X. Principles from Romans 8:14b
text: 4. One of the results of maturity adjustment is that the believer becomes spiritually self-sustaining. As a royal priest, the mature believer has direct access to God and direct access to doctrine. The privacy of the royal priesthood demands that guidance come through doctrine resident in the soul, not through dependence on the counsel of other believers.

section: X. Principles from Romans 8:14b
text: 5. Seeking guidance from other believers is a mark of spiritual immaturity. The mature believer does not use other believers as a crutch. He makes his own correct decisions from his own doctrine and possesses total confidence about the will of God in any situation.

section: X. Principles from Romans 8:14b
text: 6. The mature believer does not seek guidance or counsel from others; he frequently provides it.

section: X. Principles from Romans 8:14b
text: Verse 15 introduces a second result of maturity: confidence. The first result is divine guidance; the second is the quality of confidence that characterizes the mature believer who is not operating in a spirit of slavery but in the full assurance of his standing before God.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Four
text: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Four

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Four
text: 1. The axiom for divine guidance is twofold: for unbelievers, believe in Christ; for believers, be filled with the Spirit. These two imperatives correspond to the two commandments of 1 John 3:23 and to the two fundamental adjustments to the justice of God — salvation adjustment and rebound adjustment.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Four
text: 2. Rebound is strictly a matter of naming known sins to God alone. Adding apology, penance, promises, or emotional expression to the act of naming sin destroys the grace concept and constitutes blasphemy against the finished work of Christ on the cross. Forgiveness and restoration of the filling of the Spirit are immediate upon naming the sin.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Four
text: 3. The will of God in phase two operates in three intersecting categories: viewpoint (what God wants the believer to think), operational (what God wants the believer to do), and geographical (where God wants the believer to be). All three must converge; the point of convergence is God's will for the believer in any given situation.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Four
text: 4. The will of God is classified in three types, illustrated by Balaam: the directive will (what God desires — Numbers 22:12), the permissive will (what God allows even when it is not His directive will — Numbers 22:20), and the overruling will (when God intervenes to ensure the fulfillment of His decrees — Numbers 23:5ff). The permissive will encompasses sin, human good, evil, and the function of the old sin nature and Satan.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Four
text: 5. The academic concept of divine guidance has three components: Bible doctrine resident in the soul (Psalm 32:8; Isaiah 58:11; Proverbs 3:1–6; Romans 12:2), the filling of the Holy Spirit (Ephesians 5:14–18), and the daily function of GAP combined with the filling of the Spirit to produce maturity adjustment (2 Peter 3:18).

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Four
text: 6. Seven mechanical devices for divine guidance are identified in Acts 11: prayer, thinking from doctrine, recalled doctrine through Bible teaching, providential circumstances, the Holy Spirit, Christian fellowship and comparison of spiritual data, and recall of doctrine. Nearly all depend on the filling of the Spirit, the intake of doctrine, or both.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Four
text: 7. Divine guidance presupposes free will. If the humanity of Christ did not possess genuine free will — as demonstrated in Matthew 20:22; 26:42; Hebrews 10:7, 9 — there is no free will in mankind and no genuine issue in the angelic conflict. The existence of free will is the precondition for divine guidance to have meaning.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Four
text: 8. The ultimate in the will of God for the believer is maturity adjustment to the justice of God. The judicial imputation of divine righteousness at salvation forms the potential. Capacity from maximum doctrine resident in the soul activates that potential. The result is a real imputation of blessing in time — six categories — followed by a real imputation of blessing in eternity to the resurrection body minus the old sin nature. The believer receives no credit; all glory belongs to God.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Four
text: 9. The demonstrative pronoun houtos in Romans 8:14b and the anarthrous predicate nominative huios together establish that only mature believers are in view. The anarthrous construction emphasizes the qualitative character of the sonship — mature sons, not merely children (teknon). This controls the interpretation of Romans 8:18–30, which deals exclusively with the mature believer's experience of undeserved suffering as a category of blessing.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Four
text: 10. Romans 8:28 ('all things work together for good') is restricted to mature believers. 'Those who love God' is a technical designation for maximum category one love — occupation with the person of Christ — which characterizes maturity adjustment to the justice of God. The promise does not apply universally to all believers.

Chapter Three Hundred Five

section: Romans 8:15 — Slavery, Fear, and Adoption (Huiothesia)
text: Romans 8:15 — Slavery, Fear, and Adoption (Huiothesia)

section: Romans 8:15 — Slavery, Fear, and Adoption (Huiothesia)
text: Romans 8:15 “For you did not receive the spirit of slavery to fall back into fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, 'Abba! Father!'” (ESV)

section: Romans 8:15 — Slavery, Fear, and Adoption (Huiothesia)
text: Corrected translation: For you have not received again a life of slavery for the purpose of fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption.

section: Romans 8:15 — Slavery, Fear, and Adoption (Huiothesia)
text: Romans 8:15 stands at a pivotal point in the apostle Paul's argument concerning the believer's new life in union with Christ. Having established in the preceding verses that those who are indwelt by the Holy Spirit are not under obligation to the old sin nature, Paul now draws a contrast between two fundamentally different states of existence: a life of slavery characterized by fear, and a life of adoption characterized by the Spirit's work at salvation. This chapter examines the grammar of the verse, the doctrine of fear in both its negative and positive biblical senses, and introduces the doctrine of adoption as it was understood in the Roman world Paul inhabited.

section: I. Grammatical Analysis of Romans 8:15a
text: I. Grammatical Analysis of Romans 8:15a

section: I. Grammatical Analysis of Romans 8:15a
text: The verse opens with the explanatory conjunctive particle γάρ (gar), rendered 'for,' which is characteristic of Paul's method of connecting each thought to what precedes it. Paul does not permit a doctrinal statement to float in isolation; every clause is linked to the unfolding argument. This particle signals that what follows explains why those who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God (v. 14).

section: I. Grammatical Analysis of Romans 8:15a
text: The verb is the constative aorist active indicative of lambanō (λαμβάνω), meaning to receive. The constative aorist gathers into one entirety all of the action indicated — in this instance the negative: the believer has not received this thing. The active voice indicates the believer as the subject who produces or in this case does not produce the action. The indicative mood is declarative, representing the verbal action from the viewpoint of reality.

section: I. Grammatical Analysis of Romans 8:15a
text: The direct object is the accusative singular of pneuma (πνεύμα), which in this context carries the meaning of a state of mind, a disposition, or a manner of life — not the Holy Spirit as a person, though the same word is used for both. The corrected translation of this phrase is therefore: you have not received a life.

section: I. Grammatical Analysis of Romans 8:15a
text: Modifying pneuma is the descriptive genitive singular of douleia (δουλεία), meaning slavery or bondage. This specifies the character of the life in view: a life of slavery. There are many forms of slavery, and not all are negative in every respect. The form indicated here is clearly negative, as the following modifier confirms.

section: I. Grammatical Analysis of Romans 8:15a
text: The adverb palin (πάλιν) means again or back, specifically in the sense of returning to a previous state or former manner of life. The implication is that the slavery in view was at one time the believer's condition before salvation and could potentially be reverted to in practice, though not in legal standing.

section: I. Grammatical Analysis of Romans 8:15a
text: The prepositional phrase eis phobon (εἰς φόβον), accusative of purpose, means for the purpose of fear. The noun phobos (φόβος) is the standard Greek word for fear, from which the English suffix -phobia derives. Here it denotes fear as a mental attitude sin, not fear as reverence.

section: I. Grammatical Analysis of Romans 8:15a
text: Working translation of the first clause: For you have not received again a life of slavery for the purpose of fear.

section: II. Doctrinal Observations on Romans 8:15a
text: II. Doctrinal Observations on Romans 8:15a

section: II. Doctrinal Observations on Romans 8:15a
text: 1. The new life in Christ Jesus is not designed by God to be a life of slavery to fear. God has not provided the blessings of salvation and the indwelling Holy Spirit in order to produce frightened, anxious believers. Fear is incompatible with the life the Protocol Plan of God designs for those in union with Christ.

section: II. Doctrinal Observations on Romans 8:15a
text: 2. Believers were not born again to become driven by anxiety. The purpose of regeneration is not to produce timid, fearful people but rather believers advancing toward spiritual maturity and the glorification of God.

section: II. Doctrinal Observations on Romans 8:15a
text: 3. Assurance and confidence are the characteristics of the normal Christian way of life. This is not self-confidence but confidence in the integrity of God — assurance based on doctrine resident in the soul. There is a critical distinction between self-reliance and trust grounded in the Word.

section: II. Doctrinal Observations on Romans 8:15a
text: 4. The life of the unbeliever is characterized by instability proportional to historical instability. The more turbulent the historical environment, the more destabilizing that environment becomes for those without doctrinal orientation. By contrast, the believer's life was designed for courage and integrity in any historical atmosphere.

section: II. Doctrinal Observations on Romans 8:15a
text: 5. The life of slavery described here is marriage to the old sin nature. Retroactive positional truth — the believer's identification with Christ in His death and burial — provides the legal basis for divorce from the old sin nature. This divorce frees the believer from the life-pattern of fear, arrogance, jealousy, bitterness, vindictiveness, and instability that characterizes the sin nature's mental attitude trends.

section: II. Doctrinal Observations on Romans 8:15a
text: 6. The purpose of the believer's life has been fundamentally altered at salvation. Whether or not the believer is aware of it, the purpose of his life is the glorification of the Lord Jesus Christ as a member of the royal family of God. This purpose can only be accomplished by advancing to maturity and receiving the real imputation of maximum blessing from the justice of God, imputed to the righteousness of God.

section: II. Doctrinal Observations on Romans 8:15a
text: 7. Fear is therefore incompatible with the purpose of the royal family of God. It is not required of nor appropriate for believers who understand their standing before God.

section: II. Doctrinal Observations on Romans 8:15a
text: 8. Fear and instability in the believer indicate failure of the filling of the Spirit. They indicate failure to assimilate Bible doctrine on a consistent basis, and, as will become clear from the second half of this verse, failure to understand the doctrine of adoption.

section: III. The Doctrine of Fear
text: III. The Doctrine of Fear

section: A. Definition
text: A. Definition

section: A. Definition
text: Fear is used in Scripture in two antithetical senses. First, fear functions as a mental attitude sin. Second, fear is used to describe one of the highest aspects of love: reverence, respect, and awe — particularly when directed toward God. These two uses are not unrelated; the difference lies entirely in the object and orientation of the attitude.

section: A. Definition
text: As a mental attitude sin, fear is characterized by mental failure, panic, instability of mentality, emotional irrationality, and divorce from reality. Fear in this sense is a passion excited by the expectation of harm or evil, accompanied by a strong desire to escape, or by an imagination that generates anticipation of horrible consequences. It manifests in varying degrees: apprehension, consternation, dread, fright, terror.

section: A. Definition
text: As an expression of love, fear denotes reverence, respect, and awe directed toward a legitimate authority — supremely toward God. Reverence in this sense is not terror but rather love and honor expressed through recognition of authority, obedience to authority, and deference to the one in authority.

section: B. Fear as an Expression of Reverence and Love
text: B. Fear as an Expression of Reverence and Love

section: B. Fear as an Expression of Reverence and Love
text: The following passages illustrate the positive use of fear as reverence:

section: B. Fear as an Expression of Reverence and Love
text: 2 Samuel 23:2–3 records David's last words, in which he attributes just and righteous rule to the fear of the Lord. The principle is that no one can exercise authority properly until he has been formed by respect for authority. David became a great ruler because he first learned about authority from the Lord. This principle applies equally to military command, business leadership, pastoral ministry, and any other context in which authority is exercised. The one who rules in fear of the Lord — that is, in genuine reverence for divine authority — rules justly and protects those under his care.

section: B. Fear as an Expression of Reverence and Love
text: Nehemiah 5:9 records Nehemiah's rebuke of the people of Israel for social disorder: "Should you not walk in the fear of our God?" The absence of reverence for divine authority produces confusion and the collapse of legitimate social order.

section: B. Fear as an Expression of Reverence and Love
text: Job 28:28 — "the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom." Reverence for God's authority, which comes from maximum doctrine resident in the soul, produces wisdom. Respect for authority automatically generates sound judgment.

section: B. Fear as an Expression of Reverence and Love
text: Psalm 19:9 — "the fear of the Lord is clean, enduring forever." Where genuine reverence for divine authority exists, righteous function follows: the protection of the individual, the preservation of privacy, and the maintenance of personal freedom within a society.

section: B. Fear as an Expression of Reverence and Love
text: Psalm 34:11–14 — "Come, you sons, listen to me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord." The fear of the Lord is here connected with the capacity for life and the daily pursuit of divine good. The negative command to keep the tongue from evil includes not only slander and maligning but also the espousal of causes that erode freedom and destroy legitimate social function.

section: B. Fear as an Expression of Reverence and Love
text: Psalm 111:10; Proverbs 9:10 — "The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom." Wisdom begins with genuine reverence for God. Without it, doctrine cannot be properly received or applied.

section: B. Fear as an Expression of Reverence and Love
text: Proverbs 10:27 — "The fear of the Lord prolongs life." The self-discipline that accompanies genuine reverence for God extends physical life through ordered, controlled habits of living.

section: B. Fear as an Expression of Reverence and Love
text: Proverbs 22:4 — "The reward of grace orientation and the fear of the Lord are riches, honor, and capacity for life."

section: B. Fear as an Expression of Reverence and Love
text: Malachi 3:16 — "Then those who feared the Lord spoke with one another, and the Lord paid attention and heard them, and a book of remembrance was written before him for those who feared the Lord and esteemed his name."

section: B. Fear as an Expression of Reverence and Love
text: Ephesians 5:21 — "submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ." Here the revealed Lord Jesus Christ is the object of the believer's reverential fear, which grounds the mutual submission of believer-priests to one another in appropriate authority structures.

section: C. Fear as a Mental Attitude Sin
text: C. Fear as a Mental Attitude Sin

section: C. Fear as a Mental Attitude Sin
text: 1 Samuel 17:11, 24 — The entire army of Israel was immobilized and then routed by fear of Goliath. Fear as a mental attitude sin produces first paralysis, then movement in the wrong direction — the opposite of the courage that doctrine resident in the soul produces.

section: C. Fear as a Mental Attitude Sin
text: Proverbs 29:25 — "The fear of man lays a snare, but whoever trusts in the Lord is safe." Fear of man functions as a snare because it prevents the individual from orienting to the plan of God. Divine blessing can only be received through adjustment to the justice of God, not through navigating the approval or disapproval of other people.

section: D. Fear as a Sign of Reversionism
text: D. Fear as a Sign of Reversionism

section: D. Fear as a Sign of Reversionism
text: 1 Samuel 18:12, 29 — Saul's persistent and irrational fear of David is the biblical portrait of a reversionistic believer. Saul had departed from the Lord while David walked in alignment with Him. The result was a pattern of fear and hostility that had no basis in David's behavior but was entirely a product of Saul's spiritual condition. Fear is a diagnostic indicator of reversionism.

section: E. Fear Is Prohibited in the Grace Plan
text: E. Fear Is Prohibited in the Grace Plan

section: E. Fear Is Prohibited in the Grace Plan
text: Scripture repeatedly commands the believer against fear, directly linking the prohibition to the presence and sufficiency of God:

section: E. Fear Is Prohibited in the Grace Plan
text: Exodus 14:13–14 — Moses: "Do not fear, stand firm, and see the salvation of the Lord."

section: E. Fear Is Prohibited in the Grace Plan
text: Deuteronomy 31:6, 8 — "Be strong and courageous. Do not be afraid or dismayed... The Lord is the one who goes before you. He will be with you; he will not leave you or forsake you. Do not fear or be dismayed."

section: E. Fear Is Prohibited in the Grace Plan
text: Joshua 8:1 — "Do not fear or be dismayed. Take all the fighting men with you... I have given the king of Ai into your hand."

section: E. Fear Is Prohibited in the Grace Plan
text: 1 Chronicles 28:20 — David to Solomon: "Be strong and courageous and do it. Do not be afraid and do not be dismayed, for the Lord God, even my God, is with you. He will not leave you or forsake you."

section: E. Fear Is Prohibited in the Grace Plan
text: 2 Timothy 1:7 — "For God gave us a spirit not of fear but of power and love and self-discipline."

section: F. Spiritual Maturity Is Characterized by Courage
text: F. Spiritual Maturity Is Characterized by Courage

section: F. Spiritual Maturity Is Characterized by Courage
text: Psalm 3:6 — "I will not be afraid of many thousands of people who have set themselves against me all around." The psalmist surrounded and isolated, yet unafraid — a portrait of the mature believer who is oriented to the plan of God regardless of historical circumstances.

section: F. Spiritual Maturity Is Characterized by Courage
text: Psalm 56:11 — "In God I trust; I shall not be afraid. What can man do to me?"

section: F. Spiritual Maturity Is Characterized by Courage
text: Hebrews 11:27 — Moses left the throne of Egypt "not being afraid of the anger of the king, for he endured as seeing him who is invisible." Occupation with Christ — maintaining focus on the invisible God through doctrine resident in the soul — is what sustained Moses under pressure.

section: G. Perfect Love Excludes Fear as a Mental Attitude Sin
text: G. Perfect Love Excludes Fear as a Mental Attitude Sin

section: G. Perfect Love Excludes Fear as a Mental Attitude Sin
text: 1 John 4:18 — "There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear. For fear has to do with punishment, and whoever fears has not been perfected in love." Mental attitude love, when developed to its fullest capacity, excludes not only fear but all mental attitude sins — arrogance, jealousy, bitterness, vindictiveness, instability, and guilt. The growth of love as a mental attitude displaces the entire complex of mental attitude sins.

section: G. Perfect Love Excludes Fear as a Mental Attitude Sin
text: Hebrews 4:1 — There is a legitimate application of fear: the fear of missing God's grace provision through failure to advance spiritually. This is the one context in which an element of fear functions as a motivating force within the grace plan, not as a sin.

section: IV. Romans 8:15b — The Spirit of Adoption
text: IV. Romans 8:15b — The Spirit of Adoption

section: IV. Romans 8:15b — The Spirit of Adoption
text: The second clause of verse 15 opens with the adversative conjunction ἀλλά (alla), setting up a sharp contrast between the two clauses and the two conditions they describe: a first marriage to the old sin nature characterized by a life of slavery and fear, and a second marriage to Christ characterized by the Spirit of adoption.

section: IV. Romans 8:15b — The Spirit of Adoption
text: The verb is again the constative aorist active indicative of lambanō (λαμβάνω), this time positive: you have received. This refers to the instantaneous action occurring at salvation — specifically the baptism of the Spirit by which the believer is entered into union with Christ (current positional truth). The active voice again identifies the believer as the one who receives; the declarative indicative represents the action from the standpoint of absolute reality.

section: IV. Romans 8:15b — The Spirit of Adoption
text: The direct object is again the accusative singular of pneuma (πνεύμα), but now with a different referent: God the Holy Spirit as the author of the baptism of the Spirit at salvation.

section: IV. Romans 8:15b — The Spirit of Adoption
text: The descriptive genitive singular is huiothesia (υἱοθεσία), translated adoption. This compound word derives from huios (υἱός), meaning adult son, and tithēmi (τίθημι), meaning to place or put. The compound therefore means to place as an adult son. The corrected translation of the clause: but you have received the Spirit of adoption.

section: V. The Doctrine of Adoption (Huiothesia)
text: V. The Doctrine of Adoption (Huiothesia)

section: A. Definition and Historical Background
text: A. Definition and Historical Background

section: A. Definition and Historical Background
text: The biblical connotation of adoption is not the 20th-century practice whereby a family receives into its home a child born of other parents. In Scripture, adoption carries the meaning of being recognized by God as an adult son, positionally, at the moment of salvation. The word υἱοθεσία (huiothesia) is compounded from the noun for adult son and the verb meaning to place, yielding the sense of recognition as an adult son.

section: A. Definition and Historical Background
text: God does not impute adverse things to infants — He makes only the one adverse imputation at physical birth, the imputation of Adam's original sin to the genetically formed old sin nature. But at the new birth, He cannot make an adverse imputation. Instead, the believer is entered into union with Christ as an adult son. The ceremony of adoption therefore represents recognition that the believer now has a plan and a purpose in life — he is under the Protocol Plan of God permanently.

section: B. The Roman Custom of Adoption
text: B. The Roman Custom of Adoption

section: B. The Roman Custom of Adoption
text: Paul writes within a Roman cultural context, and the Bible must be interpreted in the time and culture in which it was written. In Roman law, adoption — called adoptio — was a public and legal ceremony practiced within the aristocracy. It was not primarily the reception of an infant from another family but the formal recognition of one's heir as a legal adult son. The ceremony could apply to a natural-born son, a nephew, a grandnephew, or anyone chosen as heir by the paterfamilias.

section: B. The Roman Custom of Adoption
text: In the ceremony, the son appeared before the assembled family wearing the toga of childhood. The father removed that toga and presented the son with the toga virilis — a formal adult robe, the style and border of which varied according to the family's station. The father then formally declared the son's new name and legal status, conferring upon him all the rights of citizenship: military service, marriage, business, political participation, and the right of inheritance. From that moment, the adopted son was the legal adult heir, regardless of whether he had been born to the family or brought into it.

section: B. The Roman Custom of Adoption
text: The importance of this ceremony to the continuity of Roman imperial rule is illustrated by the Julio-Claudian dynasty. Julius Caesar, lacking a living legitimate male heir at his death, had already conducted the adoption ceremony with his grandnephew Octavius, conferring on him the name Gaius Julius Caesar Octavianus. Octavius subsequently became the first emperor, taking the title Augustus. When Augustus in turn had outlived his own sons, he adopted his stepson Tiberius under the name Tiberius Claudius Nero Caesar. Tiberius similarly outlived his son Germanicus and adopted his grandnephew under the name Gaius Caesar Augustus Germanicus — known to history as Caligula. When Caligula failed to conduct the adoption ceremony and died without an heir, the Praetorian Guard stepped into the succession vacuum and elevated his uncle Claudius — a departure from the aristocratic principle of adoption that permanently altered the Roman imperial system. Claudius, learning the lesson, adopted his stepson Lucius Domitius Ahenobarbus of the ancient Ahenobarbus family, giving him the name Nero Claudius Caesar — the emperor who later had Paul executed. The word adoption, therefore, carried enormous legal and historical weight in the world Paul addressed.

section: C. The Theological Application
text: C. The Theological Application

section: C. The Theological Application
text: Adoption in the biblical sense is defined as the fulfillment of the Father's plan for the believer as a legal adult son. The ceremony of adoption was the exclusive prerogative of the aristocracy in the Roman Empire. Paul's use of this term is deliberate: it identifies every believer in the Church Age as spiritual aristocracy — royal family of God.

section: C. The Theological Application
text: At the moment of the new birth, the believer is spiritually a baby. But at that same moment, he is legally an adult son of God. This paradox is intentional: the legal standing confers all the rights and privileges of sonship immediately and permanently, while the experiential reality of maturity is developed progressively through the intake of doctrine. The adoption ceremony establishes the purpose; spiritual advance fulfills it.

section: C. The Theological Application
text: Adoption therefore anticipates great blessing and great responsibility flowing from the integrity of God. The believer's objective is to advance to spiritual maturity — through the maturity barrier to supergrace and ultra-supergrace — and to receive the maximum imputations of blessing from the justice of God. This is what glorifies God. This is why the royal family was placed here.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Five
text: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Five

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Five
text: 1. Romans 8:15 presents two antithetical conditions defined by their characteristic spirits. The first is a life of slavery for the purpose of fear, which characterized the believer's pre-salvation condition and remains the condition of the unbeliever. The second is the Spirit of adoption, received at salvation, which defines the believer's new legal and positional standing before God.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Five
text: 2. The grammatical structure emphasizes both negative and positive absolutes. The constative aorist gathers the entirety of the action into one summary statement: the believer did not receive — and does not have — a life of slavery to fear. He did receive — and permanently possesses — the Spirit of adoption. Both are facts of equal certainty grounded in what occurred at the moment of salvation.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Five
text: 3. Fear as a mental attitude sin is a diagnostic indicator of spiritual failure. It signals failure of the filling of the Spirit, failure to assimilate doctrine consistently, and in its chronic form, a pattern of reversionism. Fear is incompatible with the purpose of the royal family of God and is never required of the believer under the Protocol Plan.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Five
text: 4. Fear as reverence and respect for divine authority is a mark of spiritual maturity. The fear of the Lord in the positive biblical sense is inseparable from wisdom, justice in the exercise of authority, the prolonging of life, and the capacity for blessing. Maximum doctrine resident in the soul produces the mental attitude of genuine reverence — which is love and honor expressed toward God and toward those in legitimate authority.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Five
text: 5. The doctrine of adoption must be interpreted in its Roman cultural and legal context. Huiothesia does not describe the reception of an infant from another family but the formal public ceremony by which the aristocratic Roman father recognized his heir as a legal adult son with full rights of inheritance and citizenship. Paul uses this word to identify every Church Age believer as spiritual aristocracy — royal family of God — with a permanent legal standing and a defined purpose under the Protocol Plan.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Five
text: 6. At salvation, the believer simultaneously becomes a spiritual infant and a legal adult son. The adoption is instantaneous and permanent, conferred at the moment of the new birth through the baptism of the Holy Spirit and entrance into union with Christ. The legal standing is complete from the first moment; the experiential maturity is the goal toward which the entire life of doctrine intake and spiritual advance is directed.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Five
text: 7. The contrast between the two marriages underlies the structure of verse 15. The first marriage — to the old sin nature — is characterized by slavery and fear. The second marriage — to Christ through current positional truth — is characterized by the Spirit of adoption. Retroactive positional truth provides the legal divorce from the first marriage; current positional truth provides the legal basis for the second. The believer's entire freedom from fear rests on the reality of what occurred at the moment of salvation.
