section: Romans 8:20 — The Rapture of the Church: Definition, Imminency, Resurrection, and Ultimate Sanctification
text: Romans 8:20 — The Rapture of the Church: Definition, Imminency, Resurrection, and Ultimate Sanctification

section: Romans 8:20 — The Rapture of the Church: Definition, Imminency, Resurrection, and Ultimate Sanctification
text: Romans 8:19 “For the creation waits with eager longing for the revealing of the sons of God.” (ESV)

section: Romans 8:20 — The Rapture of the Church: Definition, Imminency, Resurrection, and Ultimate Sanctification
text: Corrected translation: For the confident expectation of the creation — that is, the material universe — stands in eager anticipation for the revealing of the sons of God.

section: Romans 8:20 — The Rapture of the Church: Definition, Imminency, Resurrection, and Ultimate Sanctification
text: Romans 8:19 establishes that the entire material creation stands in eager anticipation for the revealing of the sons of God. That revealing is inextricably bound to the resurrection of the royal family of God — the event known as the rapture of the church. Before proceeding to verse 20, this chapter develops the doctrine of the rapture in systematic form, organized around its definition, promise, imminency, exclusive character, resurrection provisions, and its role in ultimate sanctification.

section: I. Definition of the Rapture
text: I. Definition of the Rapture

section: I. Definition of the Rapture
text: In its ordinary sense, the word rapture denotes the act or condition of being transported, a state of being carried out of oneself. In its technical theological sense, however, rapture refers specifically to the resurrection of the royal family of God — that is, the body of church age believers — at the close of the present dispensation. The rapture is the second stage of the first resurrection, following immediately upon the resurrection of the Lord Jesus Christ Himself.

section: I. Definition of the Rapture
text: Christ's resurrection, ascension, and session at the right hand of the Father constitute His battlefield royalty — the royalty He possesses uniquely as the victorious commander in the angelic conflict. This is the one royalty for which Christ has no royal family at the moment of its conferral. The church age is therefore the dispensation inserted into the age of Israel — what may be called intercalation — for the specific purpose of forming that royal family. Once the royal family of God is complete, the rapture occurs. The church age is, by definition, the age of history during which Christ's royal family is being assembled.

section: I. Definition of the Rapture
text: This doctrine is developed extensively in Ephesians 1:22–23; 2:16; 4:4–5, and in Colossians 1 and 2. Ephesians and Colossians together may be understood as the briefing documents of the royal family of God.

section: II. The Promise of the Rapture
text: II. The Promise of the Rapture

section: II. The Promise of the Rapture
text: The Lord Jesus Christ gave the foundational promise of the rapture in John 14:1–3:

section: II. The Promise of the Rapture
text: John 14:1–3 “Let not your hearts be troubled. Believe in God; believe also in me. In my Father's house are many rooms. If it were not so, would I have told you that I go to prepare a place for you? And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and will take you to myself, that where I am you may be also.” (ESV)

section: II. The Promise of the Rapture
text: Corrected translation: Do not let your heart be troubled. You believe in God — believe also in me. In my Father's house are many dwelling places. If it were not so, I would have told you. For you see, I go to prepare a place for you. And if I go to prepare a place for you, I will come again and receive you to myself, that where I am, there you also may be.

section: II. The Promise of the Rapture
text: The Greek term translated 'rooms' or 'mansions' simply denotes a dwelling place without specification of scale or grandeur. The doctrinal weight falls on the promise itself: 'I will come again.' This coming is the rapture — a movement from heaven to the atmosphere above the earth, where the resurrected royal family meets the Lord. The passage uses the Greek word for 'air' or 'atmosphere,' indicating a rendezvous within the atmospheric envelope of the earth, not in deep space. This was a promise and a prophecy at the time of its utterance, since the church age had not yet begun.

section: III. The Imminency of the Rapture
text: III. The Imminency of the Rapture

section: III. The Imminency of the Rapture
text: Imminency, in its theological sense, refers to a prophesied event for which no other prophecy must first be fulfilled. It does not mean immediacy. Once the church age began — ten days after the ascension of Christ, on the day of Pentecost — there has been no unfulfilled prophecy that must precede the rapture. By contrast, the second advent cannot be said to be imminent because all the events of the tribulation period must first occur. The rapture has been imminent for two thousand years. Imminency is therefore entirely independent of any time calculation.

section: III. The Imminency of the Rapture
text: Several passages illustrate the imminent character of the rapture. Paul's treatment in 1 Corinthians 1:4–9 communicates that the rapture could have occurred the day after he wrote those words. Two thousand years have since elapsed, and it has not yet occurred — which confirms that imminency carries no predictive force about timing. The rapture may occur tonight; it may occur a thousand years from tonight. No human calculation can determine the moment. As our Lord stated plainly, no one knows the day or the hour (Matthew 24:36).

section: III. The Imminency of the Rapture
text: Paul reinforces this in Titus 2:13:

section: III. The Imminency of the Rapture
text: Titus 2:13 “waiting for our blessed hope, the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ,” (ESV)

section: III. The Imminency of the Rapture
text: Corrected translation: Waiting with keen anticipation for that happy guarantee — even the appearance of the glory of the great God, even our Savior Jesus Christ.

section: III. The Imminency of the Rapture
text: The phrase 'keen anticipation' reflects the imminency of the event. Nothing must occur first. Similarly, James 5:7–8 applies this to the patience of the mature believer:

section: III. The Imminency of the Rapture
text: James 5:7–8 “Be patient, therefore, brothers, until the coming of the Lord. See how the farmer waits for the precious fruit of the earth, being patient about it, until it receives the early and the late rains. You also, be patient. Establish your hearts, for the coming of the Lord is at hand.” (ESV)

section: III. The Imminency of the Rapture
text: Corrected translation: Have patience, therefore, members of the royal family, until the coming of our Lord. The farmer waits with anticipation for the valuable production of the soil, constantly being patient over it until he has received the early and the latter rains. Have patience also — all of you, become stabilized in your right lobes — because the coming of the Lord has approached with the result that it is constantly drawing nearer.

section: III. The Imminency of the Rapture
text: The rapture has been drawing nearer since these passages were written. It remains imminent. Speculation about its timing based on current events is without exegetical warrant and historically has always been falsified by subsequent history. The timing of the rapture belongs to the sovereign determination of God; it is not contingent upon any human action or any unfulfilled evangelical task.

section: IV. The Rapture as Exclusive Resurrection
text: IV. The Rapture as Exclusive Resurrection

section: IV. The Rapture as Exclusive Resurrection
text: The rapture is an exclusive event. It includes only church age believers — the royal family of God. No Old Testament saint will be raised at the rapture. Abraham, Moses, Elijah, and even John the Baptist — who died before the church age began — are not part of this resurrection. The rapture belongs to the unique dispensation of the royal family and is as exclusive as the church itself.

section: IV. The Rapture as Exclusive Resurrection
text: This exclusivity is grounded in 1 Corinthians 15:50–53:

section: IV. The Rapture as Exclusive Resurrection
text: 1 Corinthians 15:50–53 “I tell you this, brothers: flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does the perishable inherit the imperishable. Behold! I tell you a mystery. We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will be raised imperishable, and we shall be changed. For this perishable body must put on the imperishable, and this mortal body must put on immortality.” (ESV)

section: IV. The Rapture as Exclusive Resurrection
text: Corrected translation: Now I communicate this to you, royal family: flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, neither does corruption inherit incorruption. Behold, I tell you a mystery: we shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed — in a moment, in the blinking of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, and the dead shall be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed. For this corruptible must put on the incorruptible, and this mortal must put on immortality.

section: IV. The Rapture as Exclusive Resurrection
text: The term mystērion (μυστήριον) is a technical term derived from the secret fraternities of the ancient world. It denotes a body of doctrine that is inaccessible to the uninitiated. Entry into the mystery — the point of initiation — is the baptism of the Holy Spirit at salvation, which is exclusive to the church age. The first mystērion doctrine for all initiates is the baptism of the Holy Spirit; the last is the rapture of the church. This body of doctrine was not revealed in the Old Testament, though the cross, resurrection, ascension, and session of Christ were anticipated there (cf. Psalm 110:1). The royal family status of church age believers, the baptism of the Spirit, and all the distinctive provisions of this dispensation were withheld until the day of Pentecost.

section: IV. The Rapture as Exclusive Resurrection
text: In verse 51, 'we shall not all sleep' refers to the physical body, not the soul. Christian death is described as sleep because the body ceases its biological functions and awaits resurrection — analogous to sleep from which one awakens. The soul, however, never sleeps. Human life is imputed to the soul at physical birth, and that soul never ceases to exist. At physical death, the soul and spirit depart the body and are immediately in the presence of the Lord. The body sleeps; the soul does not. There is no such doctrine as soul sleep in the New Testament.

section: IV. The Rapture as Exclusive Resurrection
text: Verse 51 also establishes the basis of imminency from a different angle: 'we shall not all sleep' means there will be one generation of royal family who do not die. Which generation that will be remains unknown. Every generation of church age believers is a candidate. The generation alive at the rapture will be changed without passing through physical death; every other generation will be changed through the resurrection of the body that died. In either case, both receive the identical resurrection body.

section: IV. The Rapture as Exclusive Resurrection
text: Verse 52 provides the mechanics: instantaneous transformation — 'in a moment, in the blinking of an eye' — accompanied by the military trumpet of God. Those who died in Christ receive incorruptible bodies; those alive at the rapture receive immortal bodies. The distinction is terminological, not ontological. Both are the resurrection body of glory described in Philippians 3:20–21:

section: IV. The Rapture as Exclusive Resurrection
text: Philippians 3:20–21 “But our citizenship is in heaven, and from it we await a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform our lowly body to be like his glorious body, by the power that enables him even to subject all things to himself.” (ESV)

section: IV. The Rapture as Exclusive Resurrection
text: Corrected translation: For the seat of our citizenship exists in heaven, even from which place we eagerly anticipate the Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, who shall change the form of the body of our humble station into conformity with the body of his glory, according to the operational power by which he also keeps on being able to bring into subjection all things to himself.

section: IV. The Rapture as Exclusive Resurrection
text: The trumpet is not incidental. It is a military command-signal — a bugle call, a reveille — sounding the assembly of the royal family into resurrection bodies. The initiative belongs entirely to Christ. The rapture occurs on His timetable, by His authority, according to His attributes, and in expression of His integrity and grace. No human action precipitates it or delays it.

section: IV. The Rapture as Exclusive Resurrection
text: First John 3:1–2 supplies a further dimension:

section: IV. The Rapture as Exclusive Resurrection
text: 1 John 3:1–2 “See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God; and so we are. The reason why the world does not know us is that it did not know him. Beloved, we are God's children now, and what we will be has not yet appeared; but we know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is.” (ESV)

section: IV. The Rapture as Exclusive Resurrection
text: Corrected translation: Concentrate on how great a love the Father has given us, that we should be called the children of God — and we are. Therefore the world does not recognize us, because it did not recognize him. Beloved, now we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be; but we know that if he should appear — the rapture — we shall be an exact copy of him, because we shall see him just as he is.

section: IV. The Rapture as Exclusive Resurrection
text: The love of God is dispensed through the justice of God. At salvation, the justice of God imputed divine righteousness to the believer. Wherever divine righteousness resides, the love of God is directed toward it. Because the justice of God has always loved divine righteousness — in eternity past, in the hypostatic union, and in every church age believer — the gift of that love follows the imputation of that righteousness. At the rapture, the believer sees Christ as He is and becomes an exact copy of Him in resurrection body.

section: V. The Rapture and the Great Genuflection
text: V. The Rapture and the Great Genuflection

section: V. The Rapture and the Great Genuflection
text: Immediately following the rapture, before the judgment seat of Christ, an event occurs which may be described as the great genuflection — the corporate kneeling of the entire royal family before the Lord Jesus Christ in their resurrection bodies. This is the subject of Philippians 2:9–11:

section: V. The Rapture and the Great Genuflection
text: Philippians 2:9–11 “Therefore God has highly exalted him and bestowed on him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.” (ESV)

section: V. The Rapture and the Great Genuflection
text: Corrected translation: Therefore also, God the Father has exalted him to the maximum, and has bestowed on him Jesus Christ the rank which is above every rank — his battlefield royalty — in order that in the presence of the person of Jesus, at the rapture of the church, every knee of heaven shall bow: both those on earth, the believers alive at the rapture, and those under the earth, the church age believers who died before the rapture. And every tongue shall acknowledge that Jesus Christ is Lord, resulting in the glory of God the Father.

section: V. The Rapture and the Great Genuflection
text: The kneeling manifests the emotional capacity of the resurrection body responding to what has been resident in the soul as doctrine. Emotion is designed to appreciate and express what the believer has apprehended in the right lobe. When emotion precedes intellect, it is unstable and unproductive. When emotion follows the content of the soul — responding to truth already resident — it constitutes genuine capacity for life and worship. In the resurrection body, with full cognitive and emotional capacity perfected, the sight of Christ will produce an overwhelming response of adoration expressed in the genuflection.

section: V. The Rapture and the Great Genuflection
text: Every tongue acknowledging Christ as Lord simultaneously means the entire royal family singing in unison. This is the ultimate expression of worship — not a select choir, not a soloist, but the entirety of the royal family, in resurrection bodies, united in the acknowledgment of the battlefield royalty of their King. Singing in corporate worship is the emotional response to doctrine held in common, expressed through music with which that doctrine is identified. The great genuflection is the eschatological fulfillment of that principle.

section: V. The Rapture and the Great Genuflection
text: The chronological sequence in the atmosphere is therefore: (1) the rapture — resurrection bodies received; (2) the great genuflection — corporate worship of Christ in the sky; (3) the judgment seat of Christ — the evaluation of each believer's production in time.

section: VI. Characteristics of the Rapture
text: VI. Characteristics of the Rapture

section: 1. Cognizance of the Rapture Produces Stability
text: 1. Cognizance of the Rapture Produces Stability

section: 1. Cognizance of the Rapture Produces Stability
text: The practical application of the doctrine of the rapture is stability under pressure. First Corinthians 15:58 connects resurrection truth directly to steadfastness in the present:

section: 1. Cognizance of the Rapture Produces Stability
text: 1 Corinthians 15:58 “Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that in the Lord your labor is not in vain.” (ESV)

section: 1. Cognizance of the Rapture Produces Stability
text: Corrected translation: Therefore, am I beloved brethren: be stabilized, immovable — always abounding in the production of the Lord, knowing that your labor in the advance to maturity is not empty in the Lord.

section: 1. Cognizance of the Rapture Produces Stability
text: Immovability here is not stubbornness. Stubbornness is rigidity rooted in the old sin nature. Immovability is stability rooted in doctrine resident in the soul. The believer who has internalized resurrection truth has a frame of reference that remains fixed regardless of historical pressure, personal adversity, or the instability of the culture.

section: 2. The Rapture Removes the Sting of Death
text: 2. The Rapture Removes the Sting of Death

section: 2. The Rapture Removes the Sting of Death
text: First Corinthians 15:54–57 declares that death is 'swallowed up in victory.' For the believer who understands the rapture, death is not a terminus but a transition. The body sleeps; the soul is immediately in the presence of the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8). The resurrection body awaits in the rapture. Death therefore loses its terror. The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law — but the justice of God has been satisfied through Christ, and victory has been given to the believer. Death is palatable; it can be accepted without fear.

section: 3. The Rapture Removes Hysteria and Hopelessness in Bereavement
text: 3. The Rapture Removes Hysteria and Hopelessness in Bereavement

section: 3. The Rapture Removes Hysteria and Hopelessness in Bereavement
text: First Thessalonians 4:13 addresses believers concerning those who have died: 'in order that you might not grieve as the rest of the world who has no hope.' Grief at the loss of a fellow believer is not forbidden — it is a normal human response. What the doctrine of the rapture removes is hopelessness and hysteria. The body is sleeping; the soul is with the Lord. At the rapture, the entire royal family will be reunited in resurrection bodies. Bereavement informed by this doctrine maintains its emotional authenticity while being anchored in eschatological certainty.

section: 4. The Rapture Is the Source of Comfort in Bereavement
text: 4. The Rapture Is the Source of Comfort in Bereavement

section: 4. The Rapture Is the Source of Comfort in Bereavement
text: 1 Thessalonians 4:15–18 “For this we declare to you by a word from the Lord, that we who are alive, who are left until the coming of the Lord, will not precede those who have fallen asleep. For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a cry of command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the sound of the trumpet of God. And the dead in Christ will rise first. Then we who are alive, who are left, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so we will always be with the Lord. Therefore encourage one another with these words.” (ESV)

section: 4. The Rapture Is the Source of Comfort in Bereavement
text: Corrected translation: For this doctrine in the Word of the Lord we communicate to you: that we who are alive, who remain until the coming of the Lord — the rapture — shall not precede those who are asleep. For the Lord Himself will descend from heaven with a command; with the voice of the archangel; and also with the bugle of God — and the dead in Christ shall rise first. Then we who are alive, who remain, shall be caught up together with them in the clouds, in the atmosphere, for the purpose of meeting the Lord above the earth. And so we shall always be with the Lord. Therefore comfort one another with these doctrines.

section: 4. The Rapture Is the Source of Comfort in Bereavement
text: The rendezvous occurs within the atmosphere — the clouds are atmospheric clouds. The rapture is not a deep-space event but one proximate to the surface of the earth. The command from Christ, the archangel's voice, and the military trumpet together constitute a coordinated call to assembly. The dead in Christ are raised first; those alive are simultaneously transformed. The entire royal family assembles in the atmosphere under the direct authority of Christ. The concluding exhortation — 'comfort one another with these doctrines' — establishes that the doctrine of the rapture is not speculative theology but the practical source of stability and consolation for the royal family in time.

section: 5. The Rapture Is a Component of Ultimate Sanctification
text: 5. The Rapture Is a Component of Ultimate Sanctification

section: 5. The Rapture Is a Component of Ultimate Sanctification
text: The rapture constitutes the final stage of the sanctification of the believer's physical existence. Positional sanctification occurs at salvation through the baptism of the Holy Spirit. Experiential sanctification advances through the intake of Bible doctrine over the course of the Christian life. Ultimate sanctification is the permanent, irreversible transformation of the body at the rapture — the removal of the old sin nature through the provision of the resurrection body. At that moment, the corruptible puts on incorruption; the mortal puts on immortality. The believer is conformed to the resurrection body of Christ (Philippians 3:21; 1 John 3:2). This aspect of the doctrine will be developed further in the study of Romans 8:20 and the subsequent context.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Fourteen
text: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Fourteen

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Fourteen
text: 1. The rapture defined: The rapture is the resurrection of the royal family of God — church age believers only — constituting the second stage of the first resurrection. It follows the resurrection, ascension, and session of Christ, which established His battlefield royalty and created the need for a royal family.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Fourteen
text: 2. The promise of the rapture: John 14:1–3 records the Lord's personal promise: 'I will come again and receive you to myself.' This promise was given before the church age began and has awaited fulfillment since Pentecost.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Fourteen
text: 3. Imminency defined and defended: Imminency means no prophecy must be fulfilled before the rapture occurs. It does not mean immediacy. The rapture has been imminent for two thousand years. No human calculation, no current event, and no unfulfilled evangelical task either precipitates or delays it. The timing belongs entirely to God.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Fourteen
text: 4. The rapture is exclusive: Only church age believers participate in the rapture. Old Testament saints, including John the Baptist, are not included. The rapture is as unique as the church age and the royal family status that defines it.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Fourteen
text: 5. The resurrection body: Those who die before the rapture receive incorruptible bodies; those alive at the rapture receive immortal bodies. The distinction is terminological — both are the identical resurrection body conformed to the glory of Christ. The transformation is instantaneous, accomplished at the sounding of the military trumpet.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Fourteen
text: 6. The mystery doctrine: The rapture belongs to the body of mystērion — doctrine inaccessible to the uninitiated, revealed exclusively to church age believers through the baptism of the Holy Spirit. The first mystery doctrine is the baptism of the Spirit; the last is the rapture itself.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Fourteen
text: 7. The great genuflection: Immediately following the rapture, in the atmosphere, the entire royal family kneels before Christ in an act of corporate worship. This is the fulfillment of Philippians 2:9–11 — every knee bowing, every tongue acknowledging the battlefield royalty of Christ, to the glory of God the Father.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Fourteen
text: 8. Practical characteristics of the rapture: Cognizance of the rapture produces stability, not fanaticism. It removes the sting of death, eliminates hopelessness in bereavement, provides the ground of comfort for those who grieve, and constitutes the ultimate stage of sanctification — the permanent removal of the old sin nature through the resurrection body.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Fourteen
text: 9. The rapture and the justice of God: The love of God follows the righteousness of God. Because the justice of God imputed divine righteousness to the believer at salvation, the love of God is now directed toward every member of the royal family. The rapture — the transformation into the exact likeness of Christ — is the ultimate expression of that love operating through the integrity of God on behalf of those who have adjusted to His justice.

text: The royalty conferred on the Lord Jesus Christ as a result of His strategic victory in the angelic conflict — His death, resurrection, ascension, and session at the right hand of the Father. The soul of the believer is immediately in the presence of the Lord at physical death (2 Corinthians 5:8; Philippians 1:23).

Chapter Three Hundred Fifteen

section: Romans 8:20 — The Subordination of Creation to Futility; Doctrine of the Rapture, Points 7–10
text: Romans 8:20 — The Subordination of Creation to Futility; Doctrine of the Rapture, Points 7–10

section: Romans 8:20 — The Subordination of Creation to Futility; Doctrine of the Rapture, Points 7–10
text: Romans 8:20 “For the creation was subjected to futility, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it, in hope” (ESV)

section: Romans 8:20 — The Subordination of Creation to Futility; Doctrine of the Rapture, Points 7–10
text: Corrected translation: For the creation, that is the material universe, was subordinated at the fall of man to futility — void of purpose — against its own will, but because of him, God the Father, who has subordinated it in the time of hope, that is, the second advent.

section: Romans 8:20 — The Subordination of Creation to Futility; Doctrine of the Rapture, Points 7–10
text: Romans 8:20 stands within the larger context of the eagerly anticipating creation introduced in verse 19. Having established that the material universe awaits the revealing of the sons of God at the second advent, Paul now provides the reason: creation was placed under a curse at the fall of man, not by its own volition, but by the sovereign act of God, and it remains in that state until the second advent restores it to pristine perfection. This chapter also completes the doctrinal survey of the rapture begun in the preceding study, covering points seven through ten: the rapture as part of ultimate sanctification, the basis for confidence, chronological sequence, and the relationship of the rapture to reward.

section: I. The Doctrine of the Rapture — Points 7–10
text: I. The Doctrine of the Rapture — Points 7–10

section: Point 7: The Rapture as Part of Ultimate Sanctification
text: Point 7: The Rapture as Part of Ultimate Sanctification

section: Point 7: The Rapture as Part of Ultimate Sanctification
text: The rapture belongs to the category of ultimate sanctification — the final and complete purification of the royal family of God. This is the subject of Ephesians 5:26–27, where Christ is described as having purified the church that he might consecrate her by means of the washing of the water with the word, that is, Bible doctrine, and present her to himself as a splendid and glorious church, not having stain or wrinkle or any such thing, but holy and blameless.

section: Point 7: The Rapture as Part of Ultimate Sanctification
text: No purification of this ultimate kind is possible so long as the believer remains in the body of corruption. Prior to the resurrection, the sin capacity inherent in the old sin nature remains operative. The solution to sin in the present age is the rebound technique — naming known sins to God as per 1 John 1:9 — combined with sustained spiritual growth through doctrine intake. These are the present-age provisions within the devil's triangle: the combination of sin, human good, and evil that characterizes life apart from doctrine.

section: Point 7: The Rapture as Part of Ultimate Sanctification
text: The devil's triangle contains three elements: sin, good, and evil. Good and evil are the primary factors in this triangle, and the only means of avoiding their influence is doctrine resident in the soul, inserted between the believer and his circumstances of life. The person who claims to have ceased from sinning in this life contradicts 1 John 1:8, which states that such a claim makes one a liar with no doctrine in him.

section: Point 7: The Rapture as Part of Ultimate Sanctification
text: Ultimate sanctification removes all three elements permanently. The resurrection body is without the old sin nature — no stain, which represents the sin capacity. No wrinkle, which represents the accumulation of human good and evil. Blameless means freedom from the entire range of the devil's triangle. The church at glorification is holy and blameless, entirely beyond the reach of sin, human good, and evil.

section: Point 7: The Rapture as Part of Ultimate Sanctification
text: It is significant that the original transgression in the garden involved not immorality but a single prohibited act. There was no morality involved in the original sin. The tree of the knowledge of good and evil is precisely that: knowledge of good and evil is the one thing unnecessary to a right relationship with God. The Adamic covenant renewed daily at sundown, when the Lord came in the cool of the evening to provide doctrine and fellowship, was a one-day-at-a-time arrangement. The love of God provided perfect persons with perfect environment and perfect conditions, but only for one day at a time. The love of God could not provide eternal life or eternal salvation. When Adam sinned, the love of God was no longer the operative principle. The justice of God became the sole point of reference.

section: Point 7: The Rapture as Part of Ultimate Sanctification
text: This transition is foundational. The justice of God, unlike the love of God, can provide something permanent. All blessing flows from the justice of God to the imputed righteousness of God — and blessings so conveyed are secured. The term for this encapsulated environment of divine blessing is security. Security has three temporal expressions: logistical security, which guarantees the believer's physical provision from salvation to the maturity barrier; prosperity security, conferred at the maturity barrier; and eschatological security, which encompasses the entirety of the rapture doctrine.

section: Point 7: The Rapture as Part of Ultimate Sanctification
text: Logistical grace guarantees that every genuinely positive believer will never lack anything necessary to crack the maturity barrier — food, shelter, clothing, transportation, access to a right pastor and the communication of doctrine. The security provided by the justice of God is not dependent on wealth, status, or material circumstances. It is the undergirding of the entire operation. Prosperity security, illustrated by the career of David, means that the blessings imputed from the justice of God to the imputed righteousness of a mature believer are just as secure as salvation itself. Divine discipline may accompany the mature believer when he steps out of line, but it does not remove those blessings. Confidence — the awareness of security — is the experiential result.

section: Point 8: The Rapture as the Basis for Confidence
text: Point 8: The Rapture as the Basis for Confidence

section: Point 8: The Rapture as the Basis for Confidence
text: Confidence is the awareness of security. The distinction between stubbornness and integrity is parallel: stubbornness is a manifestation of ignorance, while integrity is a manifestation of cognizance. Doctrinal cognizance produces confidence; the absence of doctrine produces the paralysis of insecurity. When a believer lacks the awareness of security, the result is panic, the cessation of thinking, and the desperate reaction of a cornered animal.

section: Point 8: The Rapture as the Basis for Confidence
text: The noun elpis (ἐλπίς) is consistently rendered 'hope' in English translations, but the modern connotation of hope — expressing uncertainty, as in 'I hope so' — is the opposite of its New Testament meaning. Elpis carries the force of total assurance, absolute confidence. Three passages illustrate the confidence associated with the rapture: 1 Peter 1:3 describes a 'living elpis' — a living confidence — grounded in the resurrection of Jesus Christ. Titus 2:13 describes the rapture as a 'blessed elpis' — a happy guarantee — specifically the appearing of the glory of the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ. And 1 John 3:3 speaks of a 'purifying elpis' — a purifying confidence. In every case, the rapture doctrine fills in and confirms the believer's security.

section: Point 8: The Rapture as the Basis for Confidence
text: Philippians 1:6 expresses the same confidence: 'I have confidence in this same doctrine, that he who began a good work in you will accomplish it until the day of Christ Jesus' — the day of Christ Jesus being the rapture of the church. The presence of doctrine precedes confidence from doctrine. Cognizance must come first; then the emotional and experiential reality of confidence follows.

section: Point 9: The Rapture and Reward
text: Point 9: The Rapture and Reward

section: Point 9: The Rapture and Reward
text: Philippians 2:16 provides the basis for this point: 'concentrating on the word of life, that I may have a basis for the spread of glory with reference to the day of Christ.' The phrase 'spread of glory' — better rendered as a 'basis for boasting' in the technical sense of legitimate exultation — refers to the reward ceremony at the judgment seat of Christ. Paul's concern is that his sustained effort in assimilating and communicating the word of life, the crossing of no man's land to ultra-supergrace, should not be in vain. The rapture and the subsequent judgment seat of Christ are the context in which that labor receives its evaluation and reward.

section: Point 10: The Chronology of the Rapture
text: Point 10: The Chronology of the Rapture

section: Point 10: The Chronology of the Rapture
text: The events following the rapture occur in a specific sequence. First is the actual resurrection of the royal family of God, as described in 1 Corinthians 15:51–58 and 1 Thessalonians 4:13–18. Second is what may be called the great genuflection of the sky — the worship of Christ immediately following resurrection, as described in Philippians 2:9–11. Emotion follows doctrine here, not the reverse: the reality of Christ is first, the face-to-face encounter follows, and the emotional response of worship — expressed in the act of genuflection — follows from that reality.

section: Point 10: The Chronology of the Rapture
text: Third is the judgment seat of Christ, at which the royal family receives its efficiency rating for the period between salvation and the rapture — the evaluation of all that was accomplished in the body. This is treated in Romans 14:10 and 2 Corinthians 5:10, and will receive extended treatment later in Romans 8. Fourth is the return of the bride with Christ at the second advent, in resurrection bodies, as per 1 Thessalonians 3:13. Fifth is the manifestation of the bride — which was the subject that initiated this doctrinal survey from Romans 8:19 — as described also in Colossians 3:4: 'On the occasion when Christ our life shall become manifest, also you shall become manifest together with him in glory.'

section: Point 10: The Chronology of the Rapture
text: Sixth is Operation Footstool, as described in Psalm 110:1 and Zechariah 13:2. Colossians 2:15 describes the removal and incarceration of Satan and the fallen angels, clearing the decks for the millennial reign. Seventh is the coronation of the Lord Jesus Christ, Revelation 19:6. Eighth is the great celebration known as the wedding supper of the Lamb, Revelation 19:7–9.

section: The Wedding Supper of the Lamb — Revelation 19:6–9
text: The Wedding Supper of the Lamb — Revelation 19:6–9

section: The Wedding Supper of the Lamb — Revelation 19:6–9
text: Revelation 19:6 records the coronation doxology in three voices: the voice of a great crowd of people — the royal family of God; the voice of many waters — the Old Testament believers and tribulational martyrs who are the friends of the groom; and the voice of mighty thunders — the tribulational believers alive at the second advent, the friends of the bride. All three join in the acclamation: 'Praise the Lord, for the Lord God, the Almighty, has become king.' The structure of ancient wedding celebration illuminates the passage. The groom and his friends celebrate inside; the friends of the bride wait outside to escort the bride in. The ten virgins of Matthew 25:1–13 are friends of the bride, and the parable turns on readiness for that role.

section: The Wedding Supper of the Lamb — Revelation 19:6–9
text: The wedding dress of Revelation 19:8 is the fine linen given to the church — representing the perfection of ultimate sanctification: the meeting of imputed righteousness with the resurrection body, entirely free from human good and evil. The guests at the supper include the friends of the groom — Old Testament believers in resurrection bodies, received at the second advent — and the friends of the bride — tribulational believers still in physical bodies, who survive the tribulation and enter the millennium as its initial population. These become the progenitors of the millennium's civilization. Their physical children and descendants will include the unbelievers who constitute the final revolt at the close of the millennium.

section: The Wedding Supper of the Lamb — Revelation 19:6–9
text: The worship described in Revelation 19 is the model for all worship: doctrinal cognizance first, emotional response from that cognizance, then the expression of the emotion in song and praise. The sequence cannot be reversed. Emotion that precedes doctrine is not worship; it is mere sentiment. The church at the wedding supper, having passed through resurrection, the judgment seat, and the coronation, sings with complete doctrinal cognizance. The emotional response is authentic precisely because it is grounded in reality.

section: II. Romans 8:20 — Exegesis
text: II. Romans 8:20 — Exegesis

section: The Introductory Particle and the Subject
text: The Introductory Particle and the Subject

section: The Introductory Particle and the Subject
text: Verse 20 opens with the post-positive conjunctive particle gar (γάρ), which introduces the reason or cause for creation's eager anticipation described in verse 19. The subject is the nominative singular ktisis (κτίσις) — the creation, specifically the material universe. This is the same term used in verse 19 and carries forward the personification of nature as a subject capable of anticipation and longing.

section: The Verb: hupotassō
text: The Verb: hupotassō

section: The Verb: hupotassō
text: The main verb is the aorist passive indicative of hupotassō (ὑποτάσσω), a military term meaning to be placed in formation under the authority of a commanding officer — to be subordinated. The preposition hupo (ὑπό) carries the sense of being under authority; tassō (τάσσω) means to arrange in military formation. The compound conveys the idea of ordered subordination to superior authority.

section: The Verb: hupotassō
text: The aorist tense is a constative aorist, gathering up the entire period from the fall of man to the second advent into a single action. It refers to the point in time when Adam sinned — Genesis 3:17 — as the moment when the material universe was brought under subordination. The passive voice indicates that creation receives the action: it did not subordinate itself but was subordinated by God the Father. The indicative mood is declarative, representing the verbal action from the standpoint of historical reality.

section: The Indirect Object: mataiotes
text: The Indirect Object: mataiotes

section: The Indirect Object: mataiotes
text: The dative singular indirect object is mataiotēs (ματαιότης) — futility, emptiness, purposelessness. In Attic Greek, mataiotēs anthrōpou designated the nothingness of man. The term has appeared in this study as the technical description of the vacuum opened in the soul through negative volition — the spiritual vacuum of Ephesians 4:17 — but here it carries a distinct though related meaning: the state of futility into which the material universe was placed at the fall, rendering it void of its original grace purpose.

section: The Indirect Object: mataiotes
text: Nature was originally perfectly suited to Adam's rulership. In its original state, it provided sustenance without requiring the labor of cultivation; it had a grace purpose oriented toward man's flourishing. When Adam sinned and the rulership of the world passed to Satan, nature lost that original grace purpose and entered a state of futility — productive only through hard labor, subject to thorns, drought, poison, and disorder. Nature did not sin. Nature had no volition in the matter. The subordination of nature to futility is therefore undeserved suffering — a personification used by Paul to make the parallel with the mature believer in undeserved suffering.

section: The Independent Nominative: Against Its Own Will
text: The Independent Nominative: Against Its Own Will

section: The Independent Nominative: Against Its Own Will
text: The phrase 'not willingly' renders the negative ou (οὐ) plus the independent nominative singular of the adjective hekōn (ἑκών) — against its own will. The independent nominative is a grammatical construction in which a word stands in the nominative case but is not the grammatical subject of the sentence. It expresses an idea independently of any particular verbal relationship. Here it names an idea — the involuntary nature of creation's subordination — rather than naming the subject of the verb. Nature was placed under futility against what Paul personifies as its own will.

section: The Adversative Clause: dia plus the Accusative
text: The Adversative Clause: dia plus the Accusative

section: The Adversative Clause: dia plus the Accusative
text: The adversative conjunction alla (ἀλλά) sets up a contrast between nature's involuntary futility and the sovereign purpose of God the Father. The prepositional phrase dia (διά) plus the accusative is followed by the definite article used as a personal pronoun — an accepted construction in Koine Greek — referring to God the Father as the author of the divine plan for mankind. The phrase is correctly rendered 'but because of him,' God the Father.

section: The Adversative Clause: dia plus the Accusative
text: The following participle is the aorist active participle of hupotassō again — 'who has subordinated' — with the constative aorist contemplating the action in its entirety. The active voice indicates that God the Father produces the action. The circumstantial participle is completed by the supplied word 'it,' referring to the material universe. God the Father subordinated the material universe — against its own will — in accordance with his own sovereign plan.

section: The Final Phrase: epi plus the Locative of Time — elpis
text: The Final Phrase: epi plus the Locative of Time — elpis

section: The Final Phrase: epi plus the Locative of Time — elpis
text: The verse concludes with ep' elpidi (ἐπ' ἐλπίδι), the preposition epi (ἐπί) plus the locative of time from elpis (ἐλπίς) — confidence, assurance. Because it is the locative of time, the correct rendering is 'in the time of hope,' or more precisely, 'in the time of confidence.' This phrase refers to the second advent, the moment at which nature is redeemed as prophesied in Isaiah 35.

section: The Final Phrase: epi plus the Locative of Time — elpis
text: The complete corrected translation of verse 20 reads: For the creation, that is the material universe, was subordinated at the fall of man to futility — void of purpose — against its own will, but because of him, God the Father, who has subordinated it in the time of hope — that is, the second advent.

section: III. Nature Under Undeserved Suffering and the Hope of Restoration
text: III. Nature Under Undeserved Suffering and the Hope of Restoration

section: III. Nature Under Undeserved Suffering and the Hope of Restoration
text: Nature's subordination to futility is not purposeless. Even in its cursed state, the material universe provides food, beauty, and the aesthetic dimension of human experience. The very undeserved suffering of nature in its present condition illustrates and parallels the undeserved suffering of the mature believer: suffering does not negate blessing; it accompanies and at times constitutes the vehicle for blessing. Just as the mature believer under undeserved suffering possesses great happiness and great blessing precisely through that suffering, so nature in its cursed state still manifests the glory and provision of God.

section: III. Nature Under Undeserved Suffering and the Hope of Restoration
text: The restoration of nature at the second advent is the subject of Isaiah 35:1–2. The wilderness and the desert will exult; the Arabah will rejoice and blossom like a crocus. The doubling of the verb for blossoming in verse 2 — the Hebrew infinitive absolute construction with the finite verb — functions as an intensity marker: it will blossom profusely. Isaiah describes the land rejoicing with rejoicing and singing with happiness. This singing of nature at the second advent is concurrent with the great choir of the royal family, the Old Testament believers, and the tribulational saints at the wedding supper of the Lamb. Nature participates in the celebration.

section: III. Nature Under Undeserved Suffering and the Hope of Restoration
text: Nature's subordination to futility was an act of obedience to the integrity of God, who linked the destiny of the material universe to the destiny of man. When Adam ruled, nature was perfect. When Adam fell and the rulership passed to Satan, nature entered undeserved suffering. When the second Adam — the Lord Jesus Christ — assumes his millennial reign, nature is restored to its pristine beauty in keeping with the perfect environment of the millennium. The corruption and disorder in nature at the present time represent and parallel the corruption and disorder in man from the old sin nature and spiritual death. The redemption of the believer's body in resurrection is thus accompanied by the redemption of nature in the restored millennium.

section: III. Nature Under Undeserved Suffering and the Hope of Restoration
text: Nature's eagerly awaiting the revealing of the sons of God, described in verse 19, is therefore grounded in verse 20: creation was subordinated involuntarily, by divine decree, in the time of the fall, with the second advent as the appointed terminus of that subordination. The groaning of nature — which will be treated in verse 21 — continues from the fall to the second advent, the entire span of the present age, and will be the subject of the next study.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Fifteen
text: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Fifteen

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Fifteen
text: 1. Ultimate sanctification requires the rapture. No purification from the old sin nature, human good, and evil is possible while the believer remains in the body of corruption. The resurrection body minus the old sin nature is the precondition for the holy and blameless state described in Ephesians 5:27. This is the final and permanent resolution of the devil's triangle.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Fifteen
text: 2. Security is the product of divine justice, not divine love. The love of God provided perfect environment on a day-at-a-time basis; it could not provide permanent security or eternal life. The justice of God, operating through imputed righteousness, provides three categories of security: logistical, prosperity, and eschatological. These are permanent, secured against both divine discipline and historical catastrophe.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Fifteen
text: 3. Confidence is the experiential awareness of security. The distinction between stubbornness and integrity is the distinction between ignorance and doctrinal cognizance. Doctrinal cognizance of security produces confidence — not the modern sense of wishful hope, but the total assurance conveyed by the Greek

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Fifteen
text: The noun elpis (ἐλπίς) is consistently used in the New Testament for total assurance, not tentative uncertainty. Panic, insecurity, and the cessation of rational thinking are the experiential consequences of the absence of this doctrinal cognizance.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Fifteen
text: 4. The rapture introduces a precise eschatological sequence. Resurrection of the royal family; the great genuflection of worship at the first sight of Christ; the judgment seat for evaluation and reward; the return with Christ at the second advent; the manifestation of the bride; Operation Footstool and the incarceration of fallen angels; the coronation of Christ; the wedding supper of the Lamb. Each event is documented in specific Scripture passages and constitutes a separate point of eschatological security.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Fifteen
text: 5. The Greek verb hupotassō establishes nature's subordination as a military-order act. The material universe was placed in ordered subordination to futility by God the Father — not by its own volition, not by Satan's action, but by divine decree at the fall. The constative aorist gathers the entire period from the fall to the second advent into one verbal action, defining the present age as the duration of nature's undeserved suffering.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Fifteen
text: 6. Mataiotes in verse 20 designates purposelessness, not the soul-vacuum of Ephesians 4:17. Though the same Greek noun appears in both contexts, the referent differs. In Ephesians 4:17, it describes the vacuum in the soul produced by negative volition. Here it describes the objective state of futility — void of original grace purpose — into which the material universe was placed at the fall. The term carries the Attic Greek sense of the nothingness of man, applied here to the nothingness of nature's original design under Satanic rulership.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Fifteen
text: 7. Nature under undeserved suffering parallels the mature believer under undeserved suffering. In both cases, the suffering is involuntary and undeserved. In both cases, the suffering is the vehicle for present blessing — the beauties of nature, agricultural provision, aesthetic experience — and the anticipation of future glory. The parallel is not incidental; it is the point of the personification. Isaiah 35 confirms that nature will share in the glory of the royal family at the second advent, just as it shared in the consequences of Adam's fall.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Fifteen
text: 8. The phrase ep' elpidi places the terminus of nature's subordination at the second advent. The locative of time from elpis — 'in the time of confidence' — refers specifically to the second advent, the appointed moment of redemption for the material universe. Nature's subordination is therefore bounded: it has a beginning (the fall) and an end (the second advent). The believer's eschatological security includes the knowledge that the present disorder of nature, like the present disorder of the sin nature, is temporary and will be resolved at the appointed time.

Chapter Three Hundred Sixteen

section: Romans 8:21 — Nature's Deliverance from Corruption; Undeserved Suffering as Blessing; Laws of Nature and the Faithfulness of Christ
text: Romans 8:21 — Nature's Deliverance from Corruption; Undeserved Suffering as Blessing; Laws of Nature and the Faithfulness of Christ

section: Romans 8:21 — Nature's Deliverance from Corruption; Undeserved Suffering as Blessing; Laws of Nature and the Faithfulness of Christ
text: Romans 8:21 “that the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to corruption and obtain the freedom of the glory of the children of God.” (ESV)

section: Romans 8:21 — Nature's Deliverance from Corruption; Undeserved Suffering as Blessing; Laws of Nature and the Faithfulness of Christ
text: Corrected translation: Therefore, the material universe itself also shall be set free from the slavery to corruption, into the freedom of the glory of the sons of God.

section: Romans 8:21 — Nature's Deliverance from Corruption; Undeserved Suffering as Blessing; Laws of Nature and the Faithfulness of Christ
text: Romans 8 continues its treatment of undeserved suffering as a category of divine blessing. Having established in verse 20 that the material universe was subordinated to futility against its own will at the fall of man, verse 21 completes the thought: nature, which shares man's curse, will also share in man's glorification at the second advent. The analogy between nature's undeserved suffering and the mature believer's undeserved suffering governs this paragraph. This chapter also addresses the theological significance of what science calls laws of nature, and concludes with an orientation toward the coming code of the royal family of God beginning in Romans 12.

section: I. The Royal Family of God and the Code That Will Follow
text: I. The Royal Family of God and the Code That Will Follow

section: I. The Royal Family of God and the Code That Will Follow
text: The material covered in Romans 1 through 8 establishes the doctrinal foundation for what Paul will present beginning in Romans 12: the code of the royal family of God. Romans 9, 10, and 11 constitute a parenthesis addressing Israel's relationship to the covenants. The code itself — the operational standard for Church Age believers as royal family — runs from Romans 12 through Romans 15. Romans 16 is a distinct closing chapter.

section: I. The Royal Family of God and the Code That Will Follow
text: The royal family of God is constituted at regeneration, not at physical birth. The believer enters royalty at the moment of saving faith. The thinking of the believer must therefore be transformed — Romans 8 is part of that transformation. Everything in Romans 1 through 8 is designed to change the believer's frame of reference so that the code of Romans 12 through 15 is meaningful and operational.

section: I. The Royal Family of God and the Code That Will Follow
text: The contrast is with what may be called a peasant mentality — the absence of an internalized code of honor, integrity, and personal responsibility. Aristocracy in the historical sense has always represented the rise of those who practice authority responsibly, police themselves by volition, and take the long view of consequence. The code of the royal family of God is infinitely superior to any historical aristocracy because it includes the spiritual factor: Bible doctrine in the soul, the filling of the Holy Spirit, and the adjustments to the justice of God. This code will be examined in detail beginning at Romans 12.

section: II. Verse 21: Grammatical Analysis and Corrected Translation
text: II. Verse 21: Grammatical Analysis and Corrected Translation

section: A. The Conjunction
text: A. The Conjunction

section: A. The Conjunction
text: The verse opens with the compound conjunction dioti (διότι), which introduces an inferential clause. This is distinct from the simple inferential conjunction oun (οὖν), which draws a straightforward conclusion from preceding data. Dioti is used here because the conclusion being drawn is also setting up an analogy — the analogy between nature's undeserved suffering and the undeserved suffering of the mature believer. The correct rendering is therefore 'therefore' or 'because of this.'

section: B. The Subject
text: B. The Subject

section: B. The Subject
text: The nominative singular subject is ktisis (κτίσις), 'creation' or 'the material universe.' This is the same subject that has governed the paragraph since verse 19. The intensive pronoun autos (αὐτός) is used attributively, yielding 'itself.' The conjunctive kai (καί) adds the force of 'also.' Combined: 'the material universe itself also.'

section: C. The Verb
text: C. The Verb

section: C. The Verb
text: The main verb is the future passive indicative of eleutheroo (ἐλευθερόω), 'to set free.' In the future passive: 'shall be set free.' The predictive future tense points to the second advent and the inauguration of the millennium. The passive voice indicates that the material universe receives the action — it does not liberate itself. The declarative indicative mood presents the verbal action as future historical reality.

section: D. The Prepositional Phrase
text: D. The Prepositional Phrase

section: D. The Prepositional Phrase
text: The preposition apo (ἀπό) governs the ablative of douleia (δουλεία), 'slavery' or 'bondage.' This is followed by a genitive of reference from phthora (φθορά), 'corruption.' The full phrase: 'from the slavery to corruption.' The King James rendering 'bondage of corruption' is acceptable but less precise. The ablative construction emphasizes separation from a state of enslavement.

section: E. Corrected Translation of Verse 21
text: E. Corrected Translation of Verse 21

section: E. Corrected Translation of Verse 21
text: Therefore, the material universe itself also shall be set free from the slavery to corruption, into the freedom of the glory of the sons of God.

section: III. Doctrinal Principles from Verse 21
text: III. Doctrinal Principles from Verse 21

section: 1. The Basis of Corruption: Adam's Original Sin
text: 1. The Basis of Corruption: Adam's Original Sin

section: 1. The Basis of Corruption: Adam's Original Sin
text: The corruption from which nature shall be set free is grounded in Adam's original sin. The old sin nature did not originate with God but with Adam's volitional act of disobedience. The old sin nature carries three trends: a trend toward sin, a trend toward human good, and a trend toward evil. All three are expressions of corruption. The trend toward human good and the trend toward evil are as spiritually destructive as the trend toward sin, though they are less often recognized as such.

section: 2. Nature Shared Adam's Bondage
text: 2. Nature Shared Adam's Bondage

section: 2. Nature Shared Adam's Bondage
text: At the fall of man, the material universe was brought under the curse along with mankind. This is the teaching of Genesis 3:17–18. Nature did not choose corruption — it was subjected to it because of Adam's sin. This is precisely what verse 20 stated: the creation was subordinated to futility not by its own will, but by the will of God who subjected it in hope.

section: 3. Nature in Undeserved Suffering Still Points to God
text: 3. Nature in Undeserved Suffering Still Points to God

section: 3. Nature in Undeserved Suffering Still Points to God
text: Even under the curse and in slavery to corruption, the material universe continues to bear witness to the existence and character of God. This was established in Romans 1:20: 'For since the creation of the world His invisible attributes, His eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly perceived through what has been made, so that they are without excuse.' Nature suffers undeservedly, yet in that suffering it remains a vehicle of general revelation.

section: 4. Nature's Slavery to Corruption Requires Man to Work
text: 4. Nature's Slavery to Corruption Requires Man to Work

section: 4. Nature's Slavery to Corruption Requires Man to Work
text: One of the immediate consequences of nature's corruption is that man must now labor to sustain himself. The ground yields thorns and thistles; food must be obtained by effort. The material universe shares man's condemnation through Adam's original sin, and the practical result is that the effortless provision of the garden of Eden is no longer available in the present age.

section: 5. The Crown of Thorns as a Theological Sign
text: 5. The Crown of Thorns as a Theological Sign

section: 5. The Crown of Thorns as a Theological Sign
text: The thorns that are a product of the curse upon nature became the instrument of our Lord's humiliation at the crucifixion. The crown of thorns placed on Christ at His trial was an expression of the very curse that His death was designed to reverse. This is not incidental — it is a deliberate theological connection between the curse of the fall and the work of the cross.

section: 6. Laws of Nature as Laws of God
text: 6. Laws of Nature as Laws of God

section: 6. Laws of Nature as Laws of God
text: Because the material universe is in a corrupted state, God has provided laws for its governance just as He has provided laws of establishment for corrupt humanity. What are commonly called scientific laws are more accurately understood as divine laws — expressions of the omnipotence and immutability of the Lord Jesus Christ.

section: 6. Laws of Nature as Laws of God
text: Colossians 1:17 teaches that in Christ 'all things hold together.' Hebrews 1:3 adds that He upholds 'all things by the word of His power.' The consistency of natural phenomena — the repeatability of chemical reactions, the regularity of celestial mechanics, the predictability of physical processes — is not a self-sustaining property of matter. It is the ongoing work of the immutable Christ. The reaction HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H2O proceeds consistently not because of an abstract law inherent in chemistry, but because Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever (Hebrews 13:8).

section: 6. Laws of Nature as Laws of God
text: Science can observe these patterns and formulate descriptions of them, but science neither originated these regularities nor can it guarantee their continuation. Every discovery of a consistent pattern in the universe is a treatise on the faithfulness of the Lord Jesus Christ. These laws demonstrate His perfect character — His omnipotence, His immutability, and His veracity. They can be overridden by divine sovereignty at any time, and they will be fundamentally altered in the future, as taught in 2 Peter 3:10–12.

section: 6. Laws of Nature as Laws of God
text: The purpose for maintaining the present order of the universe is covenantal and soteriological: to allow grace to run its full course, to resolve the angelic conflict in human history, and to bring many sons to glory (Hebrews 2:10). The stability of the universe is God's provision for the continuation of human history under the plan of salvation. In contrast to the temporary physical universe, the believer will remain forever, surviving even the dissolution of the present creation, as Hebrews 12:26–28 makes clear.

section: IV. The Millennium: Nature's Future Deliverance
text: IV. The Millennium: Nature's Future Deliverance

section: IV. The Millennium: Nature's Future Deliverance
text: The deliverance of nature from slavery to corruption is an event of the millennium. The millennium is the 'time of hope' referenced in verse 20. A review of its key characteristics illuminates what nature's liberation will entail.

section: A. Biblical Basis for the Millennium
text: A. Biblical Basis for the Millennium

section: A. Biblical Basis for the Millennium
text: The millennium is promised in 2 Samuel 7:8–17 (the Davidic covenant). It is prophesied extensively in Isaiah: Isaiah 2, Isaiah 11, and Isaiah 35 are primary texts. It is presented in the Gospels, postponed in the New Testament epistles, plagiarized by the tribulation's counterfeit world system under the beast and the false prophet, proclaimed by the angelic heralds of Revelation 10 and the human heralds of Revelation 11, and perfected as described in Revelation 19 and following.

section: B. Characteristics of the Millennium
text: B. Characteristics of the Millennium

section: B. Characteristics of the Millennium
text: First: perfect environment exists because Satan is bound and demons are removed from the earth. The absence of satanic influence eliminates religion — the system by which human effort seeks to gain divine approval. Christianity is not a religion; religion is man's work attempting to satisfy God. Perfect environment requires the removal of the entire apparatus of satanic deception.

section: B. Characteristics of the Millennium
text: Second: optimum spirituality among believers. In that day, believers will function as the true aristocracy they were always intended to be. The filling of the Spirit will operate differently from its present Church Age mode. Isaiah 65:24, Joel 2:28–29, and Zechariah 14:16–17 address this characteristic.

section: B. Characteristics of the Millennium
text: Third: Israel is restored as a nation. Romans 9, 10, and 11 address why the Davidic, Palestinian, and Abrahamic covenants are not being fulfilled in the present age and whether God has abandoned Israel. The answer is definitively negative. The restoration of Israel is taught in Isaiah 5:26–30; 10:19–23; 11:11–16; 65:19; Joel 2:16 and following; and Zechariah 8:20–23, among many other passages.

section: B. Characteristics of the Millennium
text: Fourth: all unconditional covenants are fulfilled in the millennium. Daniel 9:24 addresses this comprehensively.

section: B. Characteristics of the Millennium
text: Fifth: the nations of the earth enjoy perfect environment under the universal reign of Jesus Christ. Universal peace — the imagery of the lion lying down with the lamb, swords beaten into plowshares, spears into pruning hooks — is taught in Psalm 46:9, Isaiah 2:4, Isaiah 24, and Micah 4:3. Universal prosperity is taught in Psalm 72:7, 16, operating on the principles of free enterprise, competition, and the honorable principle of profit. A perfect world government under Christ will exist for the first time — Isaiah 11:1–2, Zechariah 14:9. Universal knowledge of God will characterize the age — Isaiah 11:9. Longevity and health will remove the capacity limitations that disease and premature death impose in the present age.

section: B. Characteristics of the Millennium
text: Sixth: perfect objectivity in the administration of justice. The last period of perfect environment prior to the millennium was the garden of Eden, and even there, justice was perfectly administered — which is precisely why Adam and Eve were removed from the garden. There will be no perfect administration of justice again until Christ Himself rules the earth. Isaiah 11:3–4 and Psalm 72:12–14 address this characteristic.

section: B. Characteristics of the Millennium
text: Seventh: perfect environment in nature. This is the characteristic directly relevant to Romans 8:21. Creation is released from the body of corruption — Romans 8:19–22. Plant life will abound — Isaiah 35. Animals will lose their ferocity — Isaiah 11:6–9; 65:25.

section: B. Characteristics of the Millennium
text: Eighth: a great human population explosion. The baptism of fire at the end of the tribulation removes all unbelievers from the earth's population. The millennial age therefore begins with an entirely believing population in a state of perfect environment. This creates the conditions for population growth on an unprecedented scale. Ezekiel 20:34–38 and Matthew 25:31–46 address the initial composition of the millennial population.

section: B. Characteristics of the Millennium
text: Ninth: the Gog Revolution terminates perfect environment. As at the garden of Eden, perfect environment ends with a revolt against God. Revolution is not a mechanism for improving the human condition. It is always a seizure of legitimate authority by those who have no right to it — the theft of power. Revelation 20:7–10 and related passages in Ezekiel describe this final rebellion. Its occurrence in the context of absolute perfection demonstrates that environmental conditions do not determine human volition. The problem of the human race is spiritual and volitional, not circumstantial.

section: V. The Analogy: Nature and the Mature Believer
text: V. The Analogy: Nature and the Mature Believer

section: V. The Analogy: Nature and the Mature Believer
text: The controlling analogy of Romans 8:18–22 is between the undeserved suffering of nature and the undeserved suffering of the mature believer. Nature is in undeserved suffering — it did not choose corruption. The mature believer in the advanced stages of spiritual growth will also experience undeserved suffering. Neither the suffering of nature nor the suffering of the mature believer is to be interpreted as evidence of divine disfavor. Both are categories of blessing.

section: V. The Analogy: Nature and the Mature Believer
text: Nature in its corrupted state continues to produce food, aesthetic beauty, and the witness of general revelation. It suffers, and yet it blesses. The mature believer under undeserved suffering is not in a state of divine discipline but in a state of divine blessing. The capacity to receive that blessing comes from Bible doctrine resident in the soul.

section: V. The Analogy: Nature and the Mature Believer
text: The common assumption is that blessing is associated with pleasant circumstances — prosperity, success, promotion, comfort. The royal family of God operates on a different principle: no circumstance of life is greater than the plan of God. The believer who is inside the plan of God is in the highest possible state of blessing, regardless of outward circumstances. Undeserved suffering, when received with capacity built by sustained doctrine intake, is not an interruption of blessing — it is an intensified form of blessing and a guarantee of future glorification.

section: V. The Analogy: Nature and the Mature Believer
text: The remainder of verse 21 — the phrase 'into the freedom of the glory of the sons of God' — will be examined in the next study, where the direct analogy to the believer's undeserved suffering becomes explicit. The paragraph that follows verse 21 develops this into one of the most important doctrinal statements in the epistle.

section: VI. The Imputation of Martyrdom
text: VI. The Imputation of Martyrdom

section: VI. The Imputation of Martyrdom
text: In preparation for the analogy between nature's suffering and the believer's undeserved suffering, it is necessary to clarify what constitutes true martyrdom. The subject is among the most widely misunderstood in church history.

section: VI. The Imputation of Martyrdom
text: True martyrdom is not simply dying for one's faith under persecution. The imputation of martyrdom — the divine act of assigning this category of death — is restricted to ultra-supergrace believers. It is the highest honor God can bestow on a believer in time, and it is given to very few. In the nearly two thousand years of Church Age history, the number of genuine martyrs — measured by the divine standard — is estimated in the low hundreds at most.

section: VI. The Imputation of Martyrdom
text: The death of Job is the Old Testament paradigm for the imputation of martyrdom to an ultra-supergrace believer. When Isaiah was executed by being sawed in two under Manasseh, this was not a theological disaster — it was the highest honor God could confer on a believer of that standing. Among Church Age believers, Peter, Paul, and James are among those to whom true martyrdom was imputed.

section: VI. The Imputation of Martyrdom
text: The vast majority of deaths recorded as martyrdoms in church history — including the thousands documented in historical accounts of persecution — were not imputed martyrdom in the technical sense. Most represent the sin unto death administered to reversionistic believers. The sin unto death is the final stage of maximum divine discipline applied to a believer in sustained reversionism. It produces physical death, but it is a judgment, not an honor. The two categories — imputed martyrdom and the sin unto death — must not be conflated.

section: VI. The Imputation of Martyrdom
text: The demand for martyrdom, or the seeking of persecution as a spiritual credential, does not constitute martyrdom. Martyrdom is imputed by the justice of God to a specific category of believer at a specific stage of spiritual maturity. It cannot be pursued, manufactured, or assumed.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Sixteen
text: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Sixteen

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Sixteen
text: 1. Verse 21 uses dioti rather than oun: because the conclusion it draws is not merely inferential but sets up an analogy — the analogy between nature's undeserved suffering and the undeserved suffering of the mature believer. Paul's selection of this compound conjunction reflects precise theological intent.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Sixteen
text: 2. The verb eleutheroo in the future passive indicative: 'shall be set free' — confirms that nature's liberation is not self-generated but divinely enacted at the second advent. The passive voice is theologically significant: as nature was subjected against its will, so it will be freed by the same divine act.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Sixteen
text: 3. The slavery to corruption originates in Adam's original sin: not in any deficiency of the material universe itself. Nature suffers undeservedly. The old sin nature carries three trends — toward sin, toward human good, and toward evil — all of which constitute the corruption from which the creation waits to be freed.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Sixteen
text: 4. Nature in its corrupted state still functions as a vehicle of general revelation: Romans 1:20 establishes that the invisible attributes of God are clearly perceived through creation. Undeserved suffering does not eliminate the capacity to bless and witness.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Sixteen
text: 5. What are called scientific laws are more accurately called divine laws: they are expressions of the omnipotence and immutability of Jesus Christ, who holds the universe together (Colossians 1:17; Hebrews 1:3). Science can observe these patterns but did not originate them and cannot guarantee their continuation. Every consistent pattern in the natural order is a testimony to the faithfulness of Christ.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Sixteen
text: 6. The universe is maintained in its present state for a covenantal purpose: to allow grace to run its course, to resolve the angelic conflict, and to bring many sons to glory (Hebrews 2:10). The believer, by contrast, will survive the dissolution of the present universe (Hebrews 12:26–28).

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Sixteen
text: 7. The millennium is the time of hope referenced in verse 20: the period when nature's liberation from corruption will be fully realized. Its characteristics — perfect environment, universal peace, universal prosperity, perfect justice, restored Israel, fulfilled covenants, and the transformation of nature — are extensively documented in the prophetic literature.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Sixteen
text: 8. The Gog Revolution terminates the millennium: demonstrating that perfect environment does not solve the problem of human volition. Revolution is always the seizure of legitimate authority by illegitimate means. No environmental condition can substitute for the spiritual transformation that comes through adjustment to the justice of God.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Sixteen
text: 9. The analogy between nature's suffering and the mature believer's suffering is the key to Romans 8:18–22: both are undeserved; both are accompanied by capacity to bless; both point forward to a glorification that far exceeds the suffering. The principle is that no circumstance of life is greater than the plan of God.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Sixteen
text: 10. True martyrdom is imputed by the justice of God to ultra-supergrace believers only: it is the highest honor God can bestow in time, given to a very small number in all of church history. It must be distinguished from the sin unto death, which is maximum divine discipline terminating in physical death for reversionistic believers. The two categories are frequently and seriously confused in popular accounts.
