section: Romans 8:32 — The Doctrine of Imputation, Part 2: Real Imputations at Birth and Judicial Imputations at the Cross
text: Romans 8:32 — The Doctrine of Imputation, Part 2: Real Imputations at Birth and Judicial Imputations at the Cross

section: Romans 8:32 — The Doctrine of Imputation, Part 2: Real Imputations at Birth and Judicial Imputations at the Cross
text: Romans 8:32 “He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?” (ESV)

section: Romans 8:32 — The Doctrine of Imputation, Part 2: Real Imputations at Birth and Judicial Imputations at the Cross
text: Corrected translation: He who indeed did not spare His own Son, but delivered Him over on behalf of us all, how shall He not also with Him graciously give to us all things?

section: Romans 8:32 — The Doctrine of Imputation, Part 2: Real Imputations at Birth and Judicial Imputations at the Cross
text: Romans 8:32 stands at the apex of the apostle Paul's exposition of divine provision within the Protocol Plan of God. The verse presupposes the entire mechanism of imputation — the means by which God both condemns and blesses within the framework of His justice. This chapter continues the doctrine of imputation at point two, examining the two real imputations that occur at physical birth, the exception to those imputations at the birth of Jesus Christ, and the first judicial imputation accomplished at the cross.

section: I. The Equation of Divine Purpose: x + y + z = the Glory of God
text: I. The Equation of Divine Purpose: x + y + z = the Glory of God

section: I. The Equation of Divine Purpose: x + y + z = the Glory of God
text: Before treating the real imputations in detail, it is necessary to locate them within the larger framework introduced in connection with Romans 8:28 — the good and the glory of God as the telos of all divine imputations. The full equation may be summarized as follows.

section: I. The Equation of Divine Purpose: x + y + z = the Glory of God
text: The x-radical includes the two real imputations at birth: human life imputed to the soul, and Adam's original sin imputed to the genetically formed old sin nature. This produces the first potential — the possibility of salvation. Added to pertinent doctrine (the gospel), this yields the first hope: confident assurance of salvation. The reality that replaces this hope is the moment of faith in Christ — eternal salvation.

section: I. The Equation of Divine Purpose: x + y + z = the Glory of God
text: The y-radical includes two judicial imputations: first, the imputation of all personal sins of the human race to Christ at the cross; second, the imputation of divine righteousness to the believer at salvation. These together constitute the second potential — the basis for blessing in time. Added to pertinent doctrine, this yields the second hope: confident assurance of all blessing in time. That hope is replaced by the reality of the maturity adjustment to the justice of God, at which point the sixth imputation occurs.

section: I. The Equation of Divine Purpose: x + y + z = the Glory of God
text: The z-radical includes eternal life and blessing in time already imputed, producing the third potential — blessing and reward at the Judgment Seat of Christ. Added to pertinent doctrine and undeserved suffering, this yields the third hope: confident assurance of blessing and reward in eternity. The entire equation terminates in the glory of God — the seventh imputation.

section: II. The Two Real Imputations at Physical Birth
text: II. The Two Real Imputations at Physical Birth

section: II. The Two Real Imputations at Physical Birth
text: A real imputation is distinguished by having two factors: what is imputed and the divinely prepared target or home for that imputation. Between these two factors there exists affinity — an inherent correspondence that makes the imputation coherent and permanent. All real imputations are permanent; divine imputations cannot be revoked.

section: A. The Real Imputation of Human Life to the Soul
text: A. The Real Imputation of Human Life to the Soul

section: A. The Real Imputation of Human Life to the Soul
text: Physical birth — not gestation — is the moment at which God imputes human life to mankind. This is the consistent testimony of Scripture and the necessary implication of the doctrine of real imputation. Several points follow from this.

section: A. The Real Imputation of Human Life to the Soul
text: There is no human life in the blastocyst, embryo, or fetus. Human life does not exist in the womb. Life is not imputed until the fetus emerges from the womb. At that moment, the justice of God imputes human life — designated in Hebrew by the word

section: A. The Real Imputation of Human Life to the Soul
text: At that moment, the justice of God imputes human life — designated in Hebrew by the word nᵊšāmāh (נְשָׁמָה), meaning the spark of life — to its divinely prepared home, the human soul. Factor one is human life; factor two is the soul. Between the two there is affinity, and that affinity ensures that the human life placed in the soul remains there permanently.

section: A. The Real Imputation of Human Life to the Soul
text: What is often mistaken for human life in the womb is reflex motility — the involuntary movement of the embryo or fetus. This is a physiological phenomenon, not the presence of human life in the theological sense.

section: A. The Real Imputation of Human Life to the Soul
text: Death does not destroy human life. Physical death separates the soul from the body, but human life — as distinct from eternal life — remains in the soul perpetually. Whether the soul resides in heaven or in the lake of fire, the human life imputed at birth is never extinguished. This is not eternal life in the redemptive sense; it is the perpetuation of human existence into eternity.

section: B. The Real Imputation of Adam's Original Sin to the Old Sin Nature
text: B. The Real Imputation of Adam's Original Sin to the Old Sin Nature

section: B. The Real Imputation of Adam's Original Sin to the Old Sin Nature
text: Simultaneously with the imputation of human life to the soul, the justice of God imputes Adam's original sin to the genetically formed old sin nature. Factor one is Adam's original sin; factor two is the old sin nature. The affinity between the two derives from the fact that the old sin nature originated from Adam's original transgression.

section: B. The Real Imputation of Adam's Original Sin to the Old Sin Nature
text: The old sin nature is transmitted through the twenty-three male chromosomes that fertilize the female ovum. Every cell of the human body — excepting one class addressed below — is contaminated by the old sin nature with its trends toward personal sin, toward human good, and toward evil.

section: B. The Real Imputation of Adam's Original Sin to the Old Sin Nature
text: The consequence of this dual imputation is that every member of the human race is born as a facsimile of Adam immediately after the fall: physically alive, bearing human life in the soul, but spiritually dead by virtue of Adam's original sin imputed to the old sin nature. We are born dichotomous — body and soul and old sin nature — having lost the human spirit that Adam possessed before the fall.

section: III. Adam's Original Sin: The One Basis of Universal Condemnation
text: III. Adam's Original Sin: The One Basis of Universal Condemnation

section: III. Adam's Original Sin: The One Basis of Universal Condemnation
text: A critical principle follows from the structure of the real imputations: spiritual death at birth is not caused by personal sins. It is caused by one sin only — Adam's original sin, imputed to the old sin nature at birth. Personal sin is not the basis of condemnation; it is a manifestation of the spiritual death that already exists.

section: III. Adam's Original Sin: The One Basis of Universal Condemnation
text: Three manifestations of spiritual death may be identified: the function of personal sin, the function of human good, and the function of evil. None of these three constitutes the ground of condemnation; all three are expressions of the spiritually dead condition that results from the imputation of Adam's sin.

section: III. Adam's Original Sin: The One Basis of Universal Condemnation
text: In the garden prior to the fall, the point of reference for the divine attribute governing man's relationship with God was divine love. God created perfect persons in perfect environment. The single prohibition — the tree of the knowledge of good and evil — was not a moral test in the ordinary sense. It was a test of volition: obedience or disobedience to the expressed will of God. No mental attitude sin, no verbal sin, no overt moral sin was possible in the garden. The only issue was the exercise of free will.

section: III. Adam's Original Sin: The One Basis of Universal Condemnation
text: The woman was the first to partake of the forbidden fruit, but she did so in ignorance, having been deceived. The man, by contrast, received the fruit from the woman with full knowledge of its significance. For this reason, it is Adam's sin — not Eve's — that serves as the basis for the imputation. The woman was guilty, but her guilt was the guilt of deception; the man's transgression was deliberate disobedience.

section: III. Adam's Original Sin: The One Basis of Universal Condemnation
text: At the fall, the point of reference for the operative divine attribute shifted permanently from divine love to the justice of God. The justice of God condemned Adam's original sin and the old sin nature that emerged from it. From that point forward, all divine dealing with mankind — both condemnation and blessing — flows through the justice of God. Condemnation must precede salvation; this is a fixed principle of the divine economy.

section: III. Adam's Original Sin: The One Basis of Universal Condemnation
text: Because the entire human race is condemned by one sin at birth — and not by an accumulation of personal sins — the justice of God is free to save those who die before reaching the age of accountability. Having already been condemned, such individuals have already satisfied the requirement that condemnation precede salvation. The justice of God therefore saves them at the point of death. Furthermore, whatever personal sins may have been committed by those who die before accountability were included in the judicial imputation of all sins to Christ at the cross.

section: III. Adam's Original Sin: The One Basis of Universal Condemnation
text: Personal sin is not imputed to the individual for condemnation. Personal sins are preserved — reserved — for their own imputation at the cross as a judicial imputation. This distinction between real imputation (at birth) and judicial imputation (at the cross) is essential to the structure of the doctrine.

section: IV. The Exception: The Virgin Pregnancy and the Birth of Jesus Christ
text: IV. The Exception: The Virgin Pregnancy and the Birth of Jesus Christ

section: IV. The Exception: The Virgin Pregnancy and the Birth of Jesus Christ
text: There is one exception to the pattern of the two real imputations at birth, and that exception is the birth of Jesus Christ. This exception is the means by which the humanity of Christ entered the world to form the hypostatic union — true humanity and eternal deity in one person forever.

section: A. The Mechanism: Meiosis and the Uncontaminated Ovum
text: A. The Mechanism: Meiosis and the Uncontaminated Ovum

section: A. The Mechanism: Meiosis and the Uncontaminated Ovum
text: All cells of the human body are contaminated by the old sin nature. There is one exception. Through the process of meiosis and the function of polar body, twenty-three chromosomes are expelled from the ovum, leaving twenty-three uncontaminated chromosomes. These twenty-three chromosomes constitute the female ovum, which passes through the Fallopian tubes on a roughly monthly cycle. The ovum itself — one half of a cell — is entirely free from contamination by the old sin nature.

section: A. The Mechanism: Meiosis and the Uncontaminated Ovum
text: While both man and woman are carriers of the old sin nature, only the man can transmit it, and transmission occurs through copulation. The male contribution of twenty-three chromosomes introduces the old sin nature into every conception accomplished by ordinary generation.

section: B. Mary's Own Birth and Spiritual Condition
text: B. Mary's Own Birth and Spiritual Condition

section: B. Mary's Own Birth and Spiritual Condition
text: The Virgin Mary was born under the same conditions as every other member of the human race. Her father provided twenty-three male chromosomes, which transmitted the old sin nature. When she emerged from the womb, human life was imputed to her soul, and simultaneously Adam's original sin was imputed to her genetically formed old sin nature. Mary was born spiritually dead, as all humans are born spiritually dead. At the time of her virgin pregnancy, however, she was a believer — a member of the royal family of God in her own right.

section: C. The Virgin Pregnancy: The Decisive Doctrine
text: C. The Virgin Pregnancy: The Decisive Doctrine

section: C. The Virgin Pregnancy: The Decisive Doctrine
text: The doctrinally decisive event is not the virgin birth but the virgin pregnancy. The virgin birth is the necessary consequence of the virgin pregnancy, but the theological weight rests entirely on what occurred at conception.

section: C. The Virgin Pregnancy: The Decisive Doctrine
text: God the Holy Spirit provided twenty-three perfect chromosomes — free from any contamination by the old sin nature — and fertilized the prepared ovum of Mary. No copulation occurred. No artificial insemination occurred. There was no human male agency in the transmission of genetic material to the developing embryo. Therefore, no old sin nature was genetically formed in the blastocyst, embryo, or fetus.

section: C. The Virgin Pregnancy: The Decisive Doctrine
text: Whether Mary was a virgin at the time is, from the standpoint of the doctrine of imputation, a secondary consideration. The determining factor is the absence of copulation — not the virginal state of the mother. What made the virgin pregnancy theologically necessary was that it was the only mechanism by which a human fetus could develop without a genetically formed old sin nature. Without the virgin pregnancy there could be no virgin birth in the theologically significant sense; without the virgin pregnancy the entire saving work of Christ would have been impossible.

section: D. The Birth of Christ: Only One Real Imputation
text: D. The Birth of Christ: Only One Real Imputation

section: D. The Birth of Christ: Only One Real Imputation
text: At the birth of Christ, only one real imputation could occur. The justice of God the Father imputed human life to the divinely prepared soul of the Lord Jesus Christ. This imputation proceeded normally: factor one (human life) was imputed to its prepared home (the human soul), with full affinity between the two.

section: D. The Birth of Christ: Only One Real Imputation
text: The imputation of Adam's original sin, however, could not occur. Being a real imputation, it can only move toward its target by affinity — and the target is the genetically formed old sin nature. Since no such nature had been formed, there was no target, no home, no affinity, and no antecedent basis for the imputation. The imputation of Adam's original sin was completely excluded.

section: D. The Birth of Christ: Only One Real Imputation
text: The result is that Christ was born as a facsimile of Adam before the fall. Adam before the fall was trichotomous — body, soul, and spirit. Christ was born trichotomous — body, soul, and spirit. We are born as a facsimile of Adam after the fall: dichotomous — body, soul, and old sin nature, the human spirit absent. At regeneration we acquire the human spirit and become trichotomous once again, though the old sin nature remains.

section: D. The Birth of Christ: Only One Real Imputation
text: Christ lived thirty-three years under sustained temptation without ever committing a personal sin. He arrived at the cross free from Adam's original sin, free from any old sin nature, and free from any personal sin. He was impeccable — and His impeccability was the prerequisite for His qualification as the substitute for every member of the human race.

section: V. The First Judicial Imputation: All Personal Sins to Christ at the Cross
text: V. The First Judicial Imputation: All Personal Sins to Christ at the Cross

section: V. The First Judicial Imputation: All Personal Sins to Christ at the Cross
text: A judicial imputation, unlike a real imputation, has only one factor: what is being imputed. There is no divinely prepared home, no affinity, no natural target. What is judicially imputed is not inherently the property of the one who receives it; it does not belong to the recipient by nature or by desert. Judicial imputations are therefore either entirely gracious (as in the imputation of righteousness to the believer) or entirely substitutionary (as in the imputation of sins to Christ).

section: V. The First Judicial Imputation: All Personal Sins to Christ at the Cross
text: Because personal sins were not imputed to individuals at birth for condemnation — condemnation resting solely on Adam's one sin — all personal sins of the entire human race were preserved for imputation to Christ at the cross. This includes sins committed before the crucifixion, sins committed at the time of the crucifixion, and sins that would be committed at any future point in history. Only God, existing outside of time, could accomplish such a comprehensive imputation.

section: V. The First Judicial Imputation: All Personal Sins to Christ at the Cross
text: There was no affinity between the impeccable Son of God and the personal sins of the human race. Those sins were not His own. He did not commit them. He had no capacity for them. They were judicially laid upon Him by the justice of God the Father. Once imputed, the justice of God judged every one of those sins in the person of Christ. This is the saving work of the cross — not the physical death of Christ, but the spiritual death that occurred when the sins of the world were imputed to Him and judged.

section: V. The First Judicial Imputation: All Personal Sins to Christ at the Cross
text: The distinction between Christ's two deaths on the cross is essential. His spiritual death — bearing the judgment of all human sin — is the saving work. His physical death followed as the completion of His completed work; He dismissed His spirit voluntarily. The physical death has significance for resurrection but not for atonement. The wages of sin is spiritual death, and it was spiritual death that Christ bore as our substitute.

section: V. The First Judicial Imputation: All Personal Sins to Christ at the Cross
text: The preposition huper (ὑπέρ) with the genitive in Romans 5:8 — "Christ died on behalf of us" — is substitutionary. He died in our place, as our substitute. The phrase "God demonstrated His love toward us in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us" points to the judicial imputation of our sins and their judgment as the expression of divine love mediated through divine justice.

section: V. The First Judicial Imputation: All Personal Sins to Christ at the Cross
text: Several passages from Isaiah 53 illuminate this judicial imputation with precision.

section: V. The First Judicial Imputation: All Personal Sins to Christ at the Cross
text: Isaiah 53:4 “Surely he has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows; yet we esteemed him stricken, smitten by God, and afflicted.” (ESV)

section: V. The First Judicial Imputation: All Personal Sins to Christ at the Cross
text: Corrected translation: Therefore He Himself carried the guilt of our sinful afflictions — we evaluated Him as the one being struck down in judgment, the one being judged by God, the one being degraded.

section: V. The First Judicial Imputation: All Personal Sins to Christ at the Cross
text: Isaiah 53:5 “But he was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his wounds we are healed.” (ESV)

section: V. The First Judicial Imputation: All Personal Sins to Christ at the Cross
text: Corrected translation: For He was the one being pierced by our transgressions, the one being crushed by our punishment for sin; the punishment which produced our peace fell on Him.

section: V. The First Judicial Imputation: All Personal Sins to Christ at the Cross
text: Isaiah 53:6 “All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned — every one — to his own way; and the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all.” (ESV)

section: V. The First Judicial Imputation: All Personal Sins to Christ at the Cross
text: Corrected translation: Therefore the LORD — God the Father — caused to fall on Him the punishment for sin for all of us.

section: V. The First Judicial Imputation: All Personal Sins to Christ at the Cross
text: Isaiah 53:11–12 “Out of the anguish of his soul he shall see and be satisfied; by his knowledge shall the righteous one, my servant, make many to be accounted righteous, and he shall bear their iniquities. Therefore I will divide him a portion with the many, and he shall divide the spoil with the strong, because he poured out his soul to death and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and makes intercession for the transgressors.” (ESV)

section: V. The First Judicial Imputation: All Personal Sins to Christ at the Cross
text: Corrected translation: He and only He will bear the punishment for sin; prior to His physical death He was identified with the sin offerings, for He carried the sin of many and the whole of the sin offering was caused to fall on Him.

section: V. The First Judicial Imputation: All Personal Sins to Christ at the Cross
text: 1 Peter 2:24 “He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, that we might die to sin and live to righteousness. By his wounds you have been healed.” (ESV)

section: V. The First Judicial Imputation: All Personal Sins to Christ at the Cross
text: Corrected translation: And He Himself carried our sins in His own body on the cross.

section: V. The First Judicial Imputation: All Personal Sins to Christ at the Cross
text: The blood of Christ in the sacrificial system and in New Testament usage refers to this first death on the cross — the spiritual death in which sins were received and judged. In the Levitical offerings, the priest gripped the animal's muzzle, drew the blade across the throat, and the animal bled to death. That blood — the life of the animal poured out — portrayed the imputation of sins and their judgment. Christ is the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world. The phrase 'the blood of Christ' identifies the saving work of the cross; 'the Lamb of God' identifies the person doing that work. Physical blood did not cause the saving work; the spiritual death under judgment accomplished it. The Roman soldier who pierced Christ's side after death found blood and serum — Christ had not bled to death; His blood remained in His body, already beginning its post-mortem chemical transformation.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Thirty-One
text: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Thirty-One

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Thirty-One
text: 1. Real imputation requires two factors and affinity. A real imputation consists of what is imputed (factor one) and its divinely prepared home or target (factor two). Affinity — an inherent correspondence between the two factors — is what makes the imputation coherent, permanent, and irreversible. All real imputations are eternal in their effect.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Thirty-One
text: 2. Two real imputations occur simultaneously at physical birth. Human life is imputed to the soul, and Adam's original sin is imputed to the genetically formed old sin nature. The result is that every human being is born physically alive and spiritually dead — a facsimile of Adam immediately after the fall.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Thirty-One
text: 3. Human life is imputed at birth, not during gestation. There is no human life in the blastocyst, embryo, or fetus. The moment of imputation is when the fetus emerges from the womb. What is observable during gestation as movement is reflex motility — a physiological phenomenon, not the presence of divine imputation.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Thirty-One
text: 4. Human life, once imputed, is perpetual. Death separates the soul from the body but does not destroy the human life residing in the soul. Whether in heaven or in eternal judgment, human life continues. This is distinct from eternal life in the redemptive sense.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Thirty-One
text: 5. Spiritual death at birth results from one sin only — Adam's original sin. Personal sins are not imputed to individuals for condemnation. They are preserved for judicial imputation to Christ at the cross. Condemnation is based on one sin, and this single-sin basis enables the justice of God to save all who die before reaching the age of accountability.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Thirty-One
text: 6. The virgin pregnancy — not merely the virgin birth — is the doctrinally decisive event. The Holy Spirit provided twenty-three perfect, uncontaminated chromosomes to fertilize the prepared ovum of Mary. Because no copulation occurred, no old sin nature was genetically formed in the developing fetus. Without the virgin pregnancy there can be no virgin birth in the theologically significant sense.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Thirty-One
text: 7. At the birth of Christ, only one real imputation occurred. Human life was imputed to the soul of Christ normally. The imputation of Adam's original sin was completely excluded because there was no genetically formed old sin nature to serve as its target. Christ was therefore born as a facsimile of Adam before the fall — trichotomous, spiritually alive, impeccable.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Thirty-One
text: 8. A judicial imputation has one factor only and operates without affinity. What is judicially imputed is not the inherent property of the recipient. It is neither earned nor deserved, and there is no natural correspondence between the two parties. Judicial imputations are either wholly substitutionary or wholly gracious.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Thirty-One
text: 9. All personal sins of the entire human race were judicially imputed to Christ at the cross. Past, present, and future sins — every sin ever committed in human history — were laid on Christ by the justice of God the Father. Once imputed, they were judged in His person. There was no sin committed in the human race that was not imputed to Christ and judged on the cross.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Thirty-One
text: 10. The saving work of Christ at the cross was His spiritual death, not His physical death. When sins were imputed to Christ and judged, He underwent spiritual death as our substitute. His physical death followed as the completion of a finished work. The wages of sin is spiritual death; it was spiritual death that Christ bore. The physical death is significant for resurrection, not for atonement.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Thirty-One
text: 11. The blood of Christ refers to His saving work in bearing and bearing the judgment of sin. The Levitical offerings portrayed this: the slaughter of the animal and the shedding of its blood represented imputation and judgment. 'The Lamb of God' identifies the person; 'the blood of Christ' identifies the work. Physical blood loss did not accomplish salvation; the judicial imputation of sins and their judgment did.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Thirty-One
text: 12. Condemnation must precede salvation — this is a fixed principle of divine justice. The justice of God must condemn before the justice of God can bless. Both condemnation and blessing have the same source: the justice of God. Adjustment to the justice of God — at salvation and subsequently — is the mechanism by which all divine blessing reaches the human race.

section: Glossary
text: nᵊšāmāh

section: Glossary
text: נְשָׁמָה nᵊšāmāh — the spark of life

section: Glossary
text: Hebrew noun referring to the divinely imparted spark of life. Used in Genesis 2:7 of God breathing life into Adam. In the doctrine of imputation, designates the human life imputed by the justice of God to the soul at physical birth.

section: Glossary
text: Old sin nature (OSN)

section: Glossary
text: The sin capacity inherited at physical birth, transmitted through the twenty-three male chromosomes. Originated in Adam's original transgression in the garden. Characterized by three trends: toward personal sin, toward human good, and toward evil. Present in every member of the human race except Jesus Christ.

section: Glossary
text: Hypostatic union

section: Glossary
text: The union of full deity and true humanity in the one person of Jesus Christ. Neither nature is diminished or confused; both are permanent. The hypostatic union was made possible by the virgin pregnancy, which allowed a fully human nature to develop without a genetically formed old sin nature.

section: Glossary
text: Virgin pregnancy

section: Glossary
text: The doctrinally precise designation for the conception of Jesus Christ. God the Holy Spirit provided twenty-three perfect, uncontaminated chromosomes that fertilized the prepared ovum of Mary apart from any copulation. The absence of male genetic contribution prevented the formation of a genetically constituted old sin nature in the developing fetus. The virgin birth is the necessary consequence of the virgin pregnancy.

section: Glossary
text: Meiosis / polar body

section: Glossary
text: The biological process by which the female ovum is prepared. During meiosis, twenty-three chromosomes are expelled via polar body, leaving twenty-three uncontaminated chromosomes in the ovum. These chromosomes are free from the old sin nature, since the old sin nature is transmitted only through the male genetic contribution.

section: Glossary
text: Impeccability

section: Glossary
text: The sinless condition of Jesus Christ. Having no old sin nature, no imputation of Adam's original sin, and no personal sin, Christ arrived at the cross entirely free from all categories of sin. Impeccability was the prerequisite for His qualification as the substitute for the human race in the judicial imputation of sins.

section: Glossary
text: Greek preposition used with the genitive to express substitution. In Romans 5:8 and related passages, designates Christ's death as substitutionary — He died in the place of, and on behalf of, the entire human race.

section: Glossary
text: The condition of separation from God caused by the imputation of Adam's original sin to the old sin nature at birth. Not caused by personal sins. Personal sin, human good, and evil are manifestations of spiritual death, not its cause. Spiritual death is also what Christ experienced on the cross when the sins of the world were imputed to Him and judged — this is the saving work of atonement.

section: Glossary
text: Adjustment to the justice of God

section: Glossary
text: The mechanism by which all divine blessing reaches the human race. Condemnation and blessing both originate from the justice of God. Three categories: salvation adjustment (faith in Christ), rebound adjustment (naming known sins to God; 1 John 1:9), and maturity adjustment (progressive doctrine intake culminating in supergrace).

section: Romans 8:32 — The Doctrine of Imputation, Points 5–6: The Second Judicial Imputation and the Real Imputation at Salvation
text: Romans 8:32 — The Doctrine of Imputation, Points 5–6: The Second Judicial Imputation and the Real Imputation at Salvation

section: Romans 8:32 — The Doctrine of Imputation, Points 5–6: The Second Judicial Imputation and the Real Imputation at Salvation
text: Romans 8:32 “He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?” (ESV)

section: Romans 8:32 — The Doctrine of Imputation, Points 5–6: The Second Judicial Imputation and the Real Imputation at Salvation
text: Corrected translation: He who did not even spare his own Son, but on behalf of all of us delivered him over to judgment — how shall he not with him also in grace give to us the all things?

section: Romans 8:32 — The Doctrine of Imputation, Points 5–6: The Second Judicial Imputation and the Real Imputation at Salvation
text: Romans 8:32 is the anchor verse for an extended study of the doctrine of imputation. The phrase 'the all things' points back to the 'all things' of Romans 8:28, where Paul declares that all things work together for the purpose of good for those who love God — that is, for mature believers — according to a predetermined plan. The preceding verses (8:29–30) set out the logical sequence of foreknowledge, predestination, calling, justification, and glorification. Verse 32 then grounds the certainty of 'all things' in the two judicial imputations accomplished at the cross and at salvation. This chapter continues the verse-by-verse exposition of Romans 8:28–32 and advances the doctrine of imputation through points five and six: the second judicial imputation at salvation and the real imputation of eternal life at the new birth.

section: I. The Equation of All Things: X + Y + Z = Good (Review)
text: I. The Equation of All Things: X + Y + Z = Good (Review)

section: I. The Equation of All Things: X + Y + Z = Good (Review)
text: Romans 8:28 states the governing principle: all things work together for the purpose of good for mature believers, according to God's predetermined plan. The three radicals of the equation summarize the entire course of divine blessing from physical birth to eternity.

section: I. The Equation of All Things: X + Y + Z = Good (Review)
text: The X radical begins with the real imputation of human life to the divinely prepared home — the human soul — at physical birth. Simultaneously, Adam's original sin is imputed to the genetically formed old sin nature. These two imputations at birth produce the first potential: condemnation, which in turn creates the occasion for salvation. The presentation of the gospel to anyone who pauses at the point of God-consciousness — regardless of geography or language — yields the first hope: confident assurance that faith in Christ secures eternal life. When that faith is exercised, the first hope is replaced by reality, and the X radical closes with salvation adjustment to the justice of God.

section: I. The Equation of All Things: X + Y + Z = Good (Review)
text: The Y radical opens with the two judicial imputations: first, all personal sins of the human race imputed to Christ on the cross and judged; second, divine righteousness imputed to the believer at salvation. These two judicial imputations produce the second potential — the potential for blessing in time at maturity — and through sustained intake of Bible doctrine via the Grace Apparatus for Perception (GAP), yield the second hope: confident assurance that the maturity barrier will be cracked and that divine blessing will flow through the grace pipeline as a real imputation from the justice of God to the righteousness of God. When the maturity barrier is cracked, the Y radical closes with maturity adjustment to the justice of God.

section: I. The Equation of All Things: X + Y + Z = Good (Review)
text: The Z radical begins with the real imputation of eternal life to regeneration at salvation and continues with the real imputation of blessing in time at maturity. Together these produce the third potential — blessing and reward at the judgment seat of Christ — which, combined with pertinent doctrine and undeserved suffering, yields the third hope: confident assurance of the seventh imputation, the real imputation of eternal blessing and resurrection reward. This equals the good of Romans 8:28 and the glorification of God.

section: II. Omniscience and Foreknowledge Distinguished
text: II. Omniscience and Foreknowledge Distinguished

section: II. Omniscience and Foreknowledge Distinguished
text: A necessary clarification precedes the exposition of Romans 8:29–30. Omniscience and foreknowledge are not synonymous, and conflating them produces a fundamental theological error.

section: II. Omniscience and Foreknowledge Distinguished
text: Omniscience is the divine attribute by which God knows all the knowable — every reality, every alternative, every contingency, down to the remotest possibility across every generation. God knows what would have happened had Adam never sinned, had the fall never occurred, had any person made any different decision at any point in history. All alternatives are present to omniscience. Omniscience is logically and chronologically prior to the divine decrees.

section: II. Omniscience and Foreknowledge Distinguished
text: The decrees of God represent the insertion into the divine plan of what actually occurs in history — only reality, not alternatives. Foreknowledge, election, and predestination are then descriptions of the content of the decrees. Foreknowledge is not omniscience; it deals only with what is real in the decrees. Omniscience and foreknowledge intersect at exactly one point: the point of reality. Omniscience encompasses all the knowable; foreknowledge encompasses only what is decreed.

section: II. Omniscience and Foreknowledge Distinguished
text: Romans 8:29–30 does not present a chronological sequence among foreknowledge, predestination, calling, justification, and glorification. These are simultaneous descriptions of the content of the divine decrees. Acts 2:23, by contrast, does present a chronological order: omniscience, then decrees, then foreknowledge as a description of the decreed reality. The logical order applies only after the decrees are established. This distinction must be maintained precisely.

section: III. Point Five — The Second Judicial Imputation at Salvation
text: III. Point Five — The Second Judicial Imputation at Salvation

section: III. Point Five — The Second Judicial Imputation at Salvation
text: We are now at point five of the doctrine of imputation, located within the Y radical of the equation. The Y radical contains two judicial imputations: the imputation of all personal sins to Christ on the cross (judicial imputation one) and the imputation of divine righteousness to the believer at salvation (judicial imputation two). Point five addresses the second judicial imputation.

section: A. The Imputation of Divine Righteousness at Salvation
text: A. The Imputation of Divine Righteousness at Salvation

section: A. The Imputation of Divine Righteousness at Salvation
text: At the moment of faith in Christ, the justice of God imputes to the new believer the perfect righteousness of God. This is the second judicial imputation. It is designated judicial because divine righteousness is not antecedently the believer's own — it has no prior home or target in the believer. The believer possesses various forms of human righteousness, all of which are as filthy rags before God (Isaiah 64:6); none of these constitutes the infinite and perfect righteousness of God that is imputed. The imputation is thus entirely a work of divine justice, with no human merit involved.

section: A. The Imputation of Divine Righteousness at Salvation
text: Abraham is the pattern. Genesis 15:6 records: 'He had believed in the Lord, and He imputed it to him for righteousness.' The verb translated 'believed' employs the

section: A. The Imputation of Divine Righteousness at Salvation
text: Hiphil stem of the Hebrew ʾāman (אמן), indicating causative action — Abraham was caused to believe. This corresponds to the distinction between common grace and efficacious grace studied earlier in Romans: common grace presents the gospel to the spiritually dead; efficacious grace enables the positive response. God the Father then imputed Abraham's faith in Christ to him for righteousness. This is the pattern of the second judicial imputation for every believer in every dispensation where salvation is by faith.

section: B. The Grace Pipeline
text: B. The Grace Pipeline

section: B. The Grace Pipeline
text: The judicial imputation of divine righteousness at salvation results in the establishment of a grace pipeline encapsulated by the integrity of God. The pipeline has two ends: the justice of God on the giving end, and the righteousness of God on the receiving end. These two attributes together constitute the integrity of God — righteousness is the principle of divine integrity, justice is the function of divine integrity. What righteousness demands, justice executes.

section: B. The Grace Pipeline
text: The encapsulation of the pipeline by divine integrity means that no human work, no Christian service, no act of sacrifice or giving, no personality change, no moral performance of any kind can penetrate the pipeline from the outside. Legitimate forms of Christian service — witnessing, prayer, giving, functioning within one's spiritual gift, serving within the local church — are valid expressions of the believer's royal ambassadorship. But they are not mechanisms for receiving blessing from God or for glorifying God directly. They are the operational expression of ambassadorship, not the basis of divine blessing.

section: B. The Grace Pipeline
text: Legalistic systems are equally excluded. Tithing, in the age of Israel, functioned as a form of civil taxation — ten percent across the board. It had no application as a spiritual giving system in the Church Age and carries no capacity to generate divine blessing. No amount of sacrificial giving, self-denial, asceticism, or moral discipline can introduce blessing into the pipeline from the human side. The encapsulation is perfect and absolute.

section: B. The Grace Pipeline
text: Furthermore, no blessing flows through the pipeline until the believer cracks the maturity barrier. Between salvation and maturity, the believer operates under logistical grace: God provides everything necessary to sustain physical life and spiritual advance — food, shelter, clothing, transportation, a right pastor, access to the Word of God in the original languages through the science of lower criticism. These provisions are genuine expressions of divine faithfulness, and appropriate gratitude is their proper response. But they are not the same as the real imputation of divine blessing from the justice of God to the righteousness of God. That blessing does not flow until maturity is attained.

section: B. The Grace Pipeline
text: Gratitude does not require the accourtments of blessing. Capacity for gratitude is itself a product of doctrine, and a believer with maximum doctrine resident in the soul can give thanks in all circumstances (1 Thessalonians 5:18) — not because all circumstances constitute blessing, but because doctrine provides the capacity to recognize and appreciate logistical support as the faithful provision of a just God.

section: C. Blessing by Association
text: C. Blessing by Association

section: C. Blessing by Association
text: A distinction must be observed between genuine blessing from the justice of God and blessing by association. A reversionist may receive what appears externally to be divine blessing — wealth, favorable circumstances, material prosperity — not because of his own spiritual advance, but because of his association with a believer who has cracked the maturity barrier. The mature believer's real imputation of divine blessing extends outward, and those in proximity may share in its temporal expression.

section: C. Blessing by Association
text: However, blessing received without the capacity for blessing produces misery, not joy. Capacity is the prerequisite. The justice of God does not impute blessing for which the recipient has no capacity, because blessing without capacity becomes a source of divine discipline rather than divine favor. Blessing by association is a real phenomenon, but it is categorically distinct from the real imputation of divine blessing to the mature believer himself.

section: D. The Love of God and the Integrity of God
text: D. The Love of God and the Integrity of God

section: D. The Love of God and the Integrity of God
text: The second judicial imputation is also the basis by which the believer becomes the recipient of the divine attribute of love — in contrast to the anthropopathism of love ascribed to God in certain passages.

section: D. The Love of God and the Integrity of God
text: An anthropopathism is a human characteristic ascribed to God in order to explain divine policy in terms of the human frame of reference. Because God is perfect righteousness and perfect justice, He cannot love the world in the same sense that a human being loves another. God is omniscient: He knows every thought of every person who has ever lived, and His perfect righteousness cannot be reconciled with approbation of the world, which is under Satan's rulership and composed of sinful creatures. When Scripture says 'God so loved the world' (John 3:16), the term 'love' functions as an anthropopathism explaining the universal offer of salvation — not as a description of the divine attribute of love directed toward fallen humanity as such.

section: D. The Love of God and the Integrity of God
text: The divine attribute of love — love one, the objective love of God — has as its eternal object the other persons of the Trinity. God the Father loves God the Son and God the Holy Spirit, and vice versa, in eternal and perfect inter-Trinitarian love. Because God is perfect, His love requires a perfect object. Additionally, God's subjective love is directed toward His own integrity — His own righteousness and justice.

section: D. The Love of God and the Integrity of God
text: When divine righteousness is imputed to the believer at salvation, the love of God follows that righteousness. The divine love that was directed toward divine righteousness in eternity is now directed toward divine righteousness as it resides in the believer. This is the only basis on which the believer can be the recipient of the divine attribute of love. The love of God does not itself supply blessing; all blessing flows from the justice of God through the grace pipeline. But the believer who has been given divine righteousness has also become the object of divine love directed toward that righteousness.

section: E. The A Fortiori of Blessing
text: E. The A Fortiori of Blessing

section: E. The A Fortiori of Blessing
text: The relationship between the two judicial imputations and the real imputation of divine blessing constitutes the first a fortiori argument of Romans 8. The a fortiori principle — 'how much more' — reasons from the greater to the less on the basis of degree of effort rather than quality or quantity.

section: E. The A Fortiori of Blessing
text: The greater is the two judicial imputations: the justice of God imputing all personal sins of the human race to Christ on the cross and judging them, and then imputing divine righteousness to the believer at salvation. In both cases there was no antecedent affinity, no pre-existing home. The personal sins imputed to Christ were not intrinsically His own — Christ is God, perfect in both His divine and human natures in hypostatic union, and had no personal sin. The divine righteousness imputed to the believer was not intrinsically the believer's own — the believer possesses only forms of human righteousness that fall entirely short of the perfect righteousness of God. Both imputations therefore required the greater effort: imputation without antecedent affinity.

section: E. The A Fortiori of Blessing
text: The less is the real imputation of divine blessing in time at maturity. In this case, there is an antecedent affinity: divine righteousness already resides in the believer as the result of the second judicial imputation. The grace pipeline is already in place. Blessing flows to divine righteousness because there is an affinity between the blessing designed for the believer in eternity past and the righteousness of God that now resides in the believer.

section: E. The A Fortiori of Blessing
text: The a fortiori argument of Romans 8:32 is therefore: if the justice of God accomplished the greater — the two judicial imputations with no antecedent affinity — it follows with certainty that the justice of God will not withhold the less — the real imputation of divine blessing at maturity, for which the affinity already exists. Imputed righteousness is the basis for the real imputation of divine blessing from the justice of God at maturity.

section: E. The A Fortiori of Blessing
text: This principle is summarized in Matthew 6:33: 'But seek first the kingdom and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you.' Seeking the kingdom corresponds to positive volition at the point of God-consciousness and salvation adjustment. His righteousness is the judicial imputation of divine righteousness at salvation. And all these things — blessing in time and blessing in eternity — are the real imputations that follow. The verse encompasses the entire equation: X + Y + Z = good.

section: E. The A Fortiori of Blessing
text: Summary of the subpoints of the second judicial imputation in relation to blessing:

section: E. The A Fortiori of Blessing
text: It takes two judicial imputations to provide the real imputation of divine blessing. The first judicial imputation provides the basis for the second by clearing the sin account. The second judicial imputation establishes the grace pipeline. Together they create the a fortiori basis for the real imputation at maturity. There is no divine blessing until the believer has the capacity for that blessing — capacity built through maximum doctrine resident in the soul via the daily function of GAP. And what appears to be blessing before maturity is logistical grace: the divine support that sustains the believer between salvation and the crack of the maturity barrier.

section: IV. Point Six — The Real Imputation at Salvation: Eternal Life
text: IV. Point Six — The Real Imputation at Salvation: Eternal Life

section: IV. Point Six — The Real Imputation at Salvation: Eternal Life
text: Point six of the doctrine of imputation addresses the real imputation of eternal life at salvation — a distinct imputation from the judicial imputation of divine righteousness, though both occur at the same moment.

section: A. The Structure of a Real Imputation
text: A. The Structure of a Real Imputation

section: A. The Structure of a Real Imputation
text: A judicial imputation has one factor: what is imputed. There is no antecedent affinity; the imputed content has no prior home in the recipient. A real imputation has two factors: what is imputed, and the target or home — the point of antecedent affinity. The imputed content belongs with the target; there is a prior relationship of fitness between them.

section: A. The Structure of a Real Imputation
text: In the real imputation of eternal life at salvation: factor one is what is imputed — eternal life; factor two is the target or home — regeneration. Just as human life at physical birth is imputed to its divinely prepared home, the human soul, so eternal life at the new birth is imputed to its home, the regenerate human spirit created by the Holy Spirit at salvation. Life is always a real imputation. It is never imputed without a home.

section: B. The Agent and the Pattern
text: B. The Agent and the Pattern

section: B. The Agent and the Pattern
text: God the Holy Spirit is the agent of regeneration. At the moment of faith in Christ, the Holy Spirit creates the human spirit — regeneration — which becomes the home for the imputation of eternal life. This is the new birth of John 3:3–7. The believer is born again — not of physical generation, but of the Spirit.

section: B. The Agent and the Pattern
text: Most salvation passages explicitly link believing with eternal life, thereby describing the affinity that characterizes a real imputation. John 6:47: 'Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever believes has eternal life.' John 3:36: 'Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; whoever does not obey the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains on him.' The connection between faith and eternal life in these texts describes the real imputation: believing establishes the affinity, and eternal life is imputed to regeneration as its home.

section: C. The Double Portion of the Royal Family
text: C. The Double Portion of the Royal Family

section: C. The Double Portion of the Royal Family
text: In the Church Age, believers receive a double portion of eternal life. First John 5:11–12 states: 'God has given us eternal life, and this life is in his Son. Whoever has the Son has life; whoever does not have the Son of God does not have life.' The first statement describes the real imputation: the justice of God imputes eternal life to regeneration at salvation. The second statement describes a further dimension: this same eternal life is in the Son, and at salvation the baptism of the Holy Spirit places every believer into union with Christ.

section: C. The Double Portion of the Royal Family
text: The result is a double portion. As royal family of God, the Church Age believer has eternal life imputed directly at salvation and also shares the eternal life of Christ through positional union with Him. The same principle applies to divine righteousness: divine righteousness is imputed judicially at salvation, and the believer also shares the righteousness of Christ through union with Him. The royal family thus possesses a double portion of both plus-R and eternal life — a status unique to the Church Age and to the dispensation of the royal family of God.

section: D. Placement in the Equation
text: D. Placement in the Equation

section: D. Placement in the Equation
text: Although the imputation of eternal life occurs at salvation — the same moment as the judicial imputation of divine righteousness — it is classified within the Z radical rather than the Y radical. The judicial imputation of divine righteousness belongs to the second hope: confident assurance of blessing in time at maturity. The real imputation of eternal life belongs to the third hope: confident assurance of blessing and reward at the judgment seat of Christ in eternity. The distinction is not temporal but teleological: divine righteousness is the pipeline for time; eternal life is the foundation for eternity.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Thirty-Two
text: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Thirty-Two

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Thirty-Two
text: 1. Omniscience is not foreknowledge. Omniscience is the divine attribute by which God knows all the knowable — every reality and every alternative across all of history. Foreknowledge is a description of the content of the divine decrees, dealing only with what actually occurs. They intersect at one point: reality. Conflating them produces irreversible theological error in the interpretation of Romans 8:29–30 and the doctrine of the decrees.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Thirty-Two
text: 2. The second judicial imputation establishes the grace pipeline. At the moment of faith in Christ, the justice of God imputes the perfect righteousness of God to the new believer. This imputation is judicial because divine righteousness has no antecedent affinity with the believer — it is not intrinsically the believer's own. The imputation places divine righteousness on the receiving end of the grace pipeline, with the justice of God on the giving end, and the pipeline is encapsulated by the integrity of God.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Thirty-Two
text: 3. No human work penetrates the grace pipeline. The encapsulation of the grace pipeline by divine integrity means that no legitimate Christian service, no legalistic system, no sacrificial giving, no moral performance, and no act of self-denial can produce divine blessing or introduce merit into the pipeline from the human side. The royal ambassadorship is expressed through production, but production is not the means of blessing.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Thirty-Two
text: 4. Logistical grace is not the same as divine blessing. Between salvation and maturity, God provides everything necessary to sustain the believer's physical life and spiritual advance. This provision — food, shelter, clothing, transportation, a right pastor, the preserved Word of God — is logistical grace. It is genuine divine provision warranting gratitude, but it is categorically distinct from the real imputation of divine blessing that flows through the grace pipeline at maturity.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Thirty-Two
text: 5. Blessing without capacity produces misery. The justice of God does not impute blessing for which the believer has no capacity. Capacity is built through maximum doctrine resident in the soul via the daily function of GAP. Blessing received through association with a mature believer, without personal capacity, becomes a source of divine discipline rather than divine favor.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Thirty-Two
text: 6. The love of God follows the imputation of divine righteousness. The divine attribute of love requires a perfect object. When divine righteousness is imputed to the believer at salvation, the love of God is directed toward that righteousness resident in the believer. The anthropopathism of love in Scripture explains divine policy toward the world; the attribute of love is reserved for what is perfect. All blessing, however, flows from the justice of God — not from the love of God.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Thirty-Two
text: 7. Imputed righteousness is the basis for the real imputation of divine blessing at maturity. The a fortiori argument of Romans 8:32 establishes that if the justice of God accomplished the greater — two judicial imputations with no antecedent affinity — it will certainly accomplish the less: the real imputation of divine blessing to divine righteousness at maturity, where the affinity already exists. Matthew 6:33 encapsulates this entire sequence: seeking the kingdom yields salvation adjustment; his righteousness is the judicial imputation; and all these things are the real imputations of blessing in time and eternity.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Thirty-Two
text: 8. Eternal life is a real imputation to regeneration. Just as human life at physical birth is imputed to the divinely prepared home of the human soul, eternal life at the new birth is imputed to regeneration as its home. God the Holy Spirit is the agent of regeneration. Life is always a real imputation; it is never imputed without an antecedent home. The affinity between believing and eternal life in the salvation passages describes this real imputation.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Thirty-Two
text: 9. Royal family believers receive a double portion of eternal life. The real imputation of eternal life to regeneration is supplemented by the believer's positional union with Christ through the baptism of the Holy Spirit at salvation. The eternal life that is in the Son is shared by every believer who is in union with the Son. This double portion — imputed eternal life and the shared eternal life of Christ — is unique to the Church Age royal family of God.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Thirty-Two
text: 10. The imputation of eternal life belongs to the third hope. Though the imputation of eternal life occurs at the same moment as the judicial imputation of divine righteousness, it is classified in the Z radical and is part of the third hope — confident assurance of blessing and reward at the judgment seat of Christ. Divine righteousness is the pipeline for time; eternal life is the foundation for eternity. Both are given at salvation; their ultimate expressions are time and eternity respectively.
